Islam took up their cause, made their rights law and put safeguards around them, at a time when the nations of the world had left these two groups deprived of rights that were natural and due.

### Phrase by phrase

**"For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave"**. The Arabic says "what the two parents and the nearest relatives leave". Some explain "men" here as the young ones and the kin. Another explanation says the relatives include brothers and sisters, uncles and aunts. The verse does not give the amounts. One explanation says Allah stated the principle first, because people did not usually give women and children any share of an estate, and then He explained the exact shares afterward.

**"and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave"**. The Qur'an could have said in one sentence that men and women both have a share. It chose two separate sentences, even though this looks like repetition. The point is to stress that a woman's right to inherit stands on its own and is as important as a man's. In the time of ignorance before Islam, as one explanation says, women and children were simply left out.

**"whether it is little or much"**. This corrects another custom of ignorant people. Certain items were reserved for special heirs. A horse or a sword, for example, could be inherited only by young men, and others were shut out. The words make it plain that in everything the dead person owned, large or small, every heir has a standing right. No heir may set aside anything for himself before the whole estate has been formally divided by the rules.

**"˹These are˺ obligatory shares"**. The Arabic word is mafrūḍan, determined or made obligatory. The shares set out in the Qur'an have been fixed by Allah. Nobody has the right to add to them, take from them, change them or swap them by personal opinion or by analogy. The word also shows a further principle. Ownership passes to the heirs through the law of inheritance automatically and by force of law. It does not need the heir's acceptance, consent or satisfaction. Even if he declares that he will not take his share, he is still its owner in the eyes of the Sharīʿah (the revealed law). If he does not want to keep it, he may, once he has become the owner, give it away, sell it or share it out by the rules.

### The custom this verse ended

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Qatādah said that the idolaters used to give a share of the estate to grown men and deny it to women and children. Allah then revealed this verse. The pre-Islamic Arabs seem to have lived by the rule that the one who deserves to inherit is the one who rides a horse, fights the enemy and gathers the spoils. This is recorded in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī. Women and children could not live by such a rule. By it, only an adult young man could inherit. A girl was out of consideration, whether she was grown or a minor, and a boy was out as well if he was young and immature.

### The widow who came to the Prophet ﷺ

Several reports tell of the case that led to the verse. One says that Aws ibn Thābit died and left behind two daughters, a young son and a wife. Two of his cousins on the father's side came and took the whole property and gave nothing to his wife or children. This fitted their custom, since a woman could not inherit at all, and a boy who was a minor did not count.

The widow still hoped the two cousins would at least marry the two daughters, so that she would be free of that worry. They refused. She went to the Prophet ﷺ, told him her sad story and explained her children's destitution. The verse of inheritance had not yet come down, so the Prophet ﷺ gave no answer. His heart was at rest, and he was sure that revelation would remove this injustice. Then this verse was revealed.

Another account gives other details. Aws ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī died, leaving a wife called Umm Kujjah, also written Umm Kuhhah, and three daughters. Two men, Suwayd and Arfajah, who were his cousins and the executors of his estate, took all his wealth. They gave his wife and daughters nothing. Umm Kujjah went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said that she was the widow of Aws ibn Mālik, that he had left her with daughters she could not support, and that Suwayd and Arfajah, who held a large fortune, would not feed her or look after the girls. The Messenger ﷺ called the two men. They said in their defence, "O Messenger of Allah, her children cannot ride a horse, bear any burden, or hurt an enemy." He told them to go for now, as he would wait for what Allah would reveal about the matter. Then Allah revealed the verse. In another report from Jābir, recorded by Ibn Mardawayh, Umm Kujjah came to the Messenger ﷺ and said, "I have two daughters whose father has died, and they own nothing," and the verse came down in answer.

After this, the second verse of inheritance followed with the details of the shares. The Prophet ﷺ acted on the Qur'an's rulings. He gave the wife one-eighth of the whole. The rest he divided between the son and the daughters, so that the boy had half and the two girls shared the other half equally. The cousins were not the nearest relatives, in comparison with the children, and they were excluded. All of this is recorded in Rūḥ al-Maʿānī.

### Two principles in two words

The verse uses two words, "the parents" and "the nearest relatives", and they state two basic principles of inheritance. The first is the bond of birth between children and their mother and father, given by the word for the parents. The second is general kinship, given by the word for the nearest relatives. On the correct reading, that second word covers all kinds of family relationship: the tie of birth, other family relations, and relations made by marriage. The parents are named separately because of their importance.

The word "nearest" also sets down another principle. Kinship by itself is not enough to make a claim. The heir must be the nearest. If nearness were not the test, the estate of every dead person would have to be shared out among the whole human race, since everyone descends from one father and mother, Ādam (Adam) and Ḥawwāʾ (Eve). In theory that is impossible, and if it could be done, everyone would receive one worthless speck. So the rule is that when there are relatives of different degrees, the nearer are preferred to the farther, and in the presence of the nearest, the most distant get no share. When several relatives are all counted as nearest together, even if their kind of nearness differs, all of them are entitled, as with the father and mother alongside the children or a wife, since each is among the nearest in his own way.

The same word shows that women and children cannot be shut out of inheritance. Kinship is the same in a boy and a girl as far as the fact of being related goes. A boy comes into the world through his parents, and a girl does too. If the right to inherit rests on being related, there is no sense in denying it to a small child or a girl.

### Nearness, not need

The word "nearest" also tells us that the estate is not divided by need. It is divided by closeness of kinship. So the more needy relative is not automatically more deserving. The one who is nearest to the dead person is entitled to the share before one who is farther, even if the farther one is poorer. If need or benefit replaced nearness as the test, it could never become a settled rule or a firm law. Poverty, need and usefulness are not permanent, since conditions and levels change, and a crowd of claimants would arise and leave those in charge struggling to decide.

### The orphaned grandson

Once this Qur'anic principle is clear, the problem of an orphaned grandson's inheritance resolves itself. It has been made to look like a disputed question for no good reason. A grandson may be needier than the son, but under the rule of the nearest relative he has no claim on the estate while the son is alive, because he is not the nearest. Other arrangements take care of his needs, and one of them appears in the next verse. Only some modern, Westernised thinkers have opposed this position. The whole Muslim ummah has held, on the evidence of the Qur'an and the hadith, that a grandson does not inherit in the presence of a son of the dead man, whether the grandson's own father is dead or alive.

### Inheritance is a gift that comes before deeds

The fixing of inheritance does not depend on virtue or good character, and it does not change because of a fault, a defect or a sin. Suppose a man dies leaving two sons. Their rights are equal, even if one is devout and God-fearing and the other is wicked and disobedient. The God-fearing one does not receive more for his fear of Allah, and the wicked one does not receive less for his wickedness.

The deeper meaning is that inheritance is a gift from Allah that arrives before any action or virtue, so the pious and the wicked share in it alike. In the same way, faith is a gift for Muslims that arrives before any action. Allah said: "Then We granted the Book to those We have chosen from Our servants. Some of them wrong themselves, some follow a middle course, and some are foremost in good deeds by Allah’s Will. That is ˹truly˺ the greatest bounty" (35:32).

### In short

- The verse ends the pre-Islamic custom that only adult men who could fight were heirs. Men and women both receive a share of what parents and close relatives leave, large or small, and Allah has fixed those shares.
- Women's right is stated in its own sentence to show that it stands independently. Ownership passes to the heirs by law, with or without their consent, and no heir may set aside a part of the estate before it is divided.
- The nearest relative excludes the farther ones, and closeness of kinship decides, not need. This is why a grandson does not inherit alongside a son, although other provision is made for him.
- The verse is said to have come down after the widow of Aws ibn Thābit complained to the Prophet ﷺ that his cousins had taken everything.
- Inwardly, inheritance is a gift that does not follow virtue, just as faith is a gift that comes before deeds.

8.text:
The previous verse fixed who inherits, and the nearer relatives exclude the farther. This verse looks after the feelings of those left out: "If ˹non-inheriting˺ relatives, orphans, or the needy are present at the time of distribution, offer them a ˹small˺ provision from it and speak to them kindly." The Qur'an gives a just rule on one hand, and on the other it shows care for the disappointment of the people the rule excludes. It devotes a whole verse to how they should be treated.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If ˹non-inheriting˺ relatives, orphans, or the needy are present at the time of distribution"**. These are the relatives who have no share in the estate, along with orphans and poor people. In one explanation, the orphans are the orphans of believers and the needy are the needy among believers. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of al-ʿAwfī, described what such a scene is like. An estate is sometimes large. When poor relatives who cannot inherit, orphans and the poor stand by while the heirs take up their shares, their hearts long for a portion. They are desperate, and they are given nothing. Allah the Most Kind and Most Compassionate tells the heirs to give them a share, as an act of kindness, charity and mercy.

Relatives who cannot receive anything under the rules of the Sharīʿah are likely to feel disappointed when the estate is divided. Not everyone knows the details of how shares are worked out, and most relatives would like to have something. If they are there in person, and especially if there are orphans, poor and needy people among them, the sight of the others walking away with their shares while they simply watch is a terrible one.

**"offer them a ˹small˺ provision from it"**. Several explanations say that the heirs should give them something kindly out of the estate before it is divided, because they may be looking at it with desire. It came to the heirs without any work on their part. Those who receive a share have a moral duty to give some of it voluntarily. It becomes an act of charity for the recipients, and a means of reward from Allah for the givers.

At a moment when wealth is arriving without effort, only through Allah's mercy, hearts should want to give whatever they can in His way. A similar thought appears in another verse: "Eat of the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest, but do not waste" (6:141). The presence of distant kin, orphans and the needy at the division should not annoy anyone. A person should be grateful that Allah gave him something he did not work for, and give away part of it as a token of thanks. He should see it as a God-sent chance to make up in a small way for the sense of loss these people feel.

This covers the grandson who was left out of the inheritance. His uncles and aunts ought to be glad to give him something each from their own shares.

**"and speak to them kindly"**. If the heirs are young, one explanation says, the guardians should speak honourable words to the needy by apologising, and telling them that the estate is not theirs to divide as they please, but belongs to the young heirs. Another explanation says that the guardian should promise them that he will speak to the young heir about giving them something. The same idea appears in the explanation that when the legal heir is a minor, a goodly promise is made to the poor: "When the child grows up, we will tell him to give you something." A short explanation asks only that people speak to them in a kind way, without any meanness.

The words also tell us what to do when these people are not satisfied with what they get and start demanding a share equal to everyone else's. The demand is unjust and against the Sharīʿah, and there is no way to meet it. Even so, it should not be answered crudely, in a way that hurts their feelings. The actual rules should be explained politely. They can be told that under the rule of Islamic law they have no share in the inheritance, and that what they were given was a gift.

### Is giving to them required?

Scholars differ on whether this command is a duty. Ibn ʿAbbās said, in a report collected by al-Bukhārī, that the verse was not abrogated. Ibn Jarīr recorded that he said the verse still applies and must be carried out. Ath-Thawrī said that Ibn Abī Najīḥ reported from Mujāhid that carrying it out falls on those who inherit, and that they give from whatever portions their hearts are content to give away. Al-Ḥasan, ash-Shaʿbī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr, Abū Mūsā and Ibn Masʿūd gave the same explanation.

Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, az-Zuhrī, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, Makḥūl, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn Sīrīn said that this payment is obligatory. Others hold that the verse refers to a bequest made at the time of death, and still others that it was abrogated. A further explanation says that it was not abrogated, but that people neglect it too readily, because it is encouraged and not prescribed. According to this latter view, the command is commendable and not obligatory. Ibn ʿAbbās, however, held that it is a duty.

### How to give

The gift must not come out of the common estate. It must be made by the adult heirs who are present, from their own shares. Gifts taken from the shares of minors or of heirs who are absent are not allowed in the Sharīʿah.

### The inner reading

The verse has a hidden hint for sinners. When the people of faith come before Allah in the future, the Real will pardon the obedient and give them the reward of their deeds. He will not shut the poor Muslims among you out of that pardon, if Allah wills, since they too were among the family of faith, ahl al-īmān. In the same way, you were not present on the day of the division, so you have no prior claim. Whatever you know of Allah, He has made you worthy of by His favour, although He knows what slips will occur in your states.

### In short

- After the nearer relatives exclude the farther, the verse asks the heirs to give something from the estate to relatives who do not inherit, to orphans and to the needy who are there at the division.
- Speaking kindly means explaining politely, apologising to the needy if the heirs are minors, or making a goodly promise, and not scolding anyone who asks for more.
- Ibn ʿAbbās and many early scholars held that the gift is a duty and that the verse was not abrogated. Others take it as a bequest, as abrogated, or as encouraged but not required. The gift is made by adult heirs from their own shares.
- It should be seen as a God-sent chance to give thanks for wealth that came without effort.

9.text:
This verse speaks to everyone who stands near an estate or near a dying man's will, and asks them to feel for other people's children as they would for their own: "Let the guardians be as concerned ˹for the orphans˺ as they would if they were to ˹die and˺ leave ˹their own˺ helpless children behind. So let them be mindful of Allah and speak equitably." It tells Muslims in general to make sure that the inheritance of the dead reaches his children fully and fairly, and to avoid any action that may harm the children's share.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Let the guardians be as concerned ˹for the orphans˺ as they would if they were to ˹die and˺ leave ˹their own˺ helpless children behind"**. The early explanations take the verse in two ways. The first concerns people who are present at a will. Ibn ʿAbbās said, in the report of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, that it refers to a man who is near death and dictates a will that harms some of those who should inherit. Allah commands whoever hears such a will to fear Him, to steer the dying man toward what is right and fair, and to be as keen to protect the heirs of the dying man as he would be for his own. Mujāhid and several others said the same.

One explanation names the people involved. They are those who visit a sick person and urge him to bequeath more than a third of his estate. Such people used to go to men on their deathbeds and urge them to give their property to this person and that, until nothing was left for their own children. Allah forbade it. They should fear the ruin of the dying man's children, as they would fear ruin for their own if they died leaving them weak and unable to look after themselves. A short explanation says: urge the dying person to do what you would urge for yourself.

The second way concerns guardians of orphans. The verse asks them to treat the orphans as they would wish others to treat their own children after them, with no harm or injustice. Those who guard orphans' property should protect it and give it to them in full when they are mature. They must take pains over this trust, and never let the least carelessness spoil their duty. One explanation says that executors and guardians should feel the fear they themselves would feel if they were to die leaving small, weak children who might be ruined.

**"So let them be mindful of Allah"**. According to one explanation, this means that people should fear Allah when they look after the orphan's wealth. Ibn Jarīr recorded it from al-ʿAwfī, who reported it from Ibn ʿAbbās. It is a sound opinion, because it fits the warning that follows against consuming an orphan's wealth unjustly. The meaning becomes: just as you want your own children to be treated fairly after you, treat other people's children fairly when the care of them is entrusted to you. Another explanation says: let them fear Allah in the matter of bequeathing more than a third to those who have no right to inherit. Another adds that if guardians treat orphans well, Allah will bring others to treat their own children well after they die.

**"and speak equitably"**. In one explanation, the words mean to speak truthfully. According to others, they ask a person to speak justly to the sick man about his will. They ask him to tell the dying man to give no more than a third in voluntary charity, and to leave the rest to those who inherit, so that they do not end up dependent on others. Another explanation says that whoever is present when a will is made should speak up for what is fair to the children, so that no heir suffers wrong through the will. The giver, for his part, should not deprive himself of this good deed by failing to make a will.

### The hadith of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ

The two Ṣaḥīḥs record that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ when he was ill. Saʿd said, "O Messenger of Allah, I am wealthy and have no heir except a daughter. Should I give two-thirds of my property in charity?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "No." Saʿd asked, "Half?" He said, "No." Saʿd asked, "One-third?" The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "One-third, though even one-third is a great deal. It is better to leave your heirs rich than to leave them poor, begging from other people."

The Prophet ﷺ stopped Saʿd from giving all or half of his property in ṣadaqah (charity) and allowed him only a third. If the whole or half had been given away, the heirs' share would have been used up or cut down. This is recorded in Mishkāt, in the chapter on wills, Bāb al-Waṣāyā. The same principle applies when anyone sees a Muslim making a will or giving away property in a way that would damage his children and other heirs. He should be stopped.

### What a Muslim should store up for his family

The verse shows that what a Muslim should collect for his dependants is not wealth but fear of Allah, taqwā, and righteousness, ṣalāḥ. The verse does not say that they should gather their wealth, multiply their real estate or leave behind household goods. It says that they should fear Allah, for He looks after the righteous.

### In short

- The verse asks guardians, executors and people who attend a will to want for other people's children what they would want for their own.
- It has two applications. People present at a will should urge the dying man to be fair and not to leave away more than a third. Guardians should protect the orphans' property and hand it over in full.
- The Prophet ﷺ refused to let Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ give away two-thirds or half, and he allowed a third, saying that it is better to leave heirs rich than poor and begging.
- What a person should leave behind for his family is taqwā and righteousness more than money.

10.text:
After all the commands about orphans, the verse states the penalty: "Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth ˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies. And they will be burned in a blazing Hell." It carries a severe warning for those who steal or dispose of an orphan's property unlawfully, and it makes plain how serious the earlier commands were.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans’ wealth"**. In the Arabic the word is yaʾkulūna, "they eat". It means that using the orphan's property in any way at all is completely unlawful, whether by eating, drinking, spending or making use of it. It is a sure cause of Allah's anger. The punishment for eating up what belongs to someone else, wrongfully and without right, covers every kind of use. One short explanation reads "unjustly" as extortionately. Others say it means without any right, or spending it wrongly and unjustly. The verse is said to have been revealed about Ḥanẓalah ibn Shamardal.

**"˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies"**. In the Qur'an's wording, whatever they swallow of the orphan's wealth is nothing but fire. One explanation says it is whatever is unlawful. Another says that Allah will put fire in their bellies on the Day of Judgment. Another says the property is called fire because that is where such conduct ends. Whenever you consume an orphan's wealth without right, you are consuming only fire, and it will burn in your stomach on the Day of Resurrection.

**"And they will be burned in a blazing Hell"**. The Arabic verb is yaṣlawna, in the active form, or yuṣlawna, in the passive in another reading. It means that they will enter a blaze, an intense fire in which they will burn. One explanation says they will be exposed to blazing fire in the Hereafter, and another that on the Day of Judgment the flames of Hell will consume them.

### Is the fire only a figure of speech?

Many scholars understood the words as a figure of speech. Eating an orphan's property unjustly is like stuffing one's stomach with fire, because that is what it will lead to in the Hereafter. Others, who looked more deeply and gave their reasons, do not accept a figure of speech here. In their view, whatever is eaten of an orphan's property unlawfully is in reality nothing but fire, though it does not look like fire at the time.

They compare it to someone who says that the matchbox in his hand is fire, or that a piece of arsenic is a killer. Holding a matchbox does not burn the hand, and holding arsenic, even putting it in the mouth, does not kill a man. But a little friction shows that the one who called the matchbox fire was right, and when arsenic has been swallowed, it is clear that whoever called it a killer told the truth. The Qur'an's general statements support this view. Whatever deeds a person does, good or evil, those deeds themselves are the trees, flowers and fruits of Paradise, or the embers of Hell. Their form here is different, but on the Day of Judgment they will come forth in their true forms. The Qur'an says: "They will find whatever they did present ˹before them˺" (18:49). The punishment and reward they see will be, in reality, the result of their own deeds.

According to some narrations, those who wrongly devour an orphan's property will be raised on the Day of Judgment with flames pouring from their bellies and out through their mouths, nostrils, ears and eyes. The Prophet ﷺ said that a group of people would be raised on that Day with fire erupting from their mouths. His Companions asked who they were, and he said, "Have you not read it in the Qur'an?" and recited the words about those who eat up the orphans' property unjustly.

### The two weak ones, and the seven destructive sins

Because the property of an orphan eaten unjustly is in reality the fire of Hell, though it is not felt as fire at the time, the Prophet ﷺ gave very clear instructions to take the strictest care. Abū Hurairah reported that he said:

> "I warn you against the property of the two weak ones, the woman and the orphan."

It is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs that Abū Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Avoid the seven great destructive sins." The people asked, "O Allah's Messenger, what are they?" He answered:

> "To join others in worship with Allah, magic, killing a life that Allah has forbidden except for a just cause, consuming interest, consuming an orphan's property, turning your back and fleeing from the battlefield at the time of fighting, and accusing chaste women, who never think of any harm to their chastity, believing women."

### How orphans are really wronged

The whole first section of this surah is about orphans. It orders the protection of their property, forbids treating it as one's own, and orders that the share they receive in inheritance be given to them. It forbids hastily spending their property out of fear that they will grow up and take control. It forbids marrying orphan girls for a lower dower, and forbids seizing their property. In the end, the surah says that eating up an orphan's property unjustly is filling the belly with fire, because such people will be repaid after death with fire in their bellies.

When someone dies, the right of every heir attaches to everything he owned, down to the smallest part. It is a tragedy when the young children of the dead become orphans. Mostly they meet some injustice and excess in every home. Whoever takes control of the property after the father's death, whether an uncle, an elder brother, the mother, a guardian or a trustee, falls into doing things this section forbids. To begin with, they put off the division of the property for years, and in the meantime spend a little here and there to feed and clothe the children. After that, they open up and spend this jointly held property with great freedom on customs and practices that religion does not approve and on wasteful items. They even spend it on themselves and go so far as to manipulate legal documents and put their own children's names in place of the orphans'. Hardly any home is untouched by these things.

Donations made for orphans in religious schools and orphanages must be spent on the orphans. Not spending them on the orphans is a form of "eating up" their property.

### Rulings about the estate of the dead

Four rulings follow from this.

First, the inheritance includes everything the dead person owned, even the clothes on his body. People tend to give these away in charity without realising that they belong to what he left. In some places, copper utensils are given to the poor well before the estate is formally divided, although minors and absent heirs have rights in all such things. The right method is to divide the property first, according to the shares of the children, wife, parents, sisters and anyone else under the Islamic law of inheritance. Once ownership has passed to those who receive shares, it is up to them to give away part of it in charity on behalf of the dead, if they choose to do so willingly. If they want to do this together, they must make sure they are all adults, since a minor's permission is not valid. Nothing may be taken from the share of an absent heir without his permission.

Second, the sheet spread over the janāzah (the bier) while the dead is carried to the graveyard is not part of the required shroud, the kafan. It is not permitted to buy it with money from the estate, since the estate is held jointly. If someone covers the cost himself, that is allowed. In some places a prayer mat is cut from the cloth bought for the shroud for the imām who leads the funeral prayer, and he keeps it. That expense is an extra and may not come from the undivided estate.

Third, in some areas new utensils are bought to bathe the dead and are broken after use. There is no need to buy new ones, because the bath can be given with utensils already in the house. If for some reason they must be bought, breaking them is not permitted. It wastes property, and it harms orphans and absent heirs, whose rights are attached to the whole estate.

Fourth, any spending before the estate is divided, such as feeding guests or giving charity and alms, is entirely impermissible. Giving charity in this way brings the dead person no reward. Giving it in the belief that it will help the departed soul is a much greater sin. The reason is that, after a person dies, all his property belongs to his heirs in proportion to their rights, and there are orphans among them. Giving things in charity from the joint property, which includes the orphan's share, is like stealing from someone and giving the stolen goods away on behalf of the dead. Divide the property first, and then the heirs may give in charity from their shares for the good of the dead if they wish.

It is better not to give charity from the joint estate even before the division, even with the heirs' permission. The permission of an orphan among the heirs is not valid at all. As for the adults, their permission may not come from a willing heart. They may be left with no choice but to agree, so as not to be shamed in front of others, and they may say yes with a heavy heart to ward off embarrassment.

A story told of a pious elder makes this clearer. He went to visit a sick Muslim, and the man died almost as soon as he sat down. The elder at once put out the lamp burning there and gave someone money to buy oil and light it again. When people asked why, he said that the lamp had belonged to this man while he lived, and it was right to use its light. Now that the man had left the world, his heirs had a right over everything he owned. We could use the lamp only with the permission of all the heirs, and since they were not all there, the lamp was lit at the elder's own cost.

### A lesson in plain speech

In this world a person may seize a weak man's right. But every unlawful acquisition is like filling his belly with fire. The fact that what he took is like fire may not be clear now, but it will become clear in the Hereafter. People have freedom of action in this world, but they cannot control the results of their actions. Whoever wishes to be saved from bad consequences should not wrong others. He should adopt a culture of kindness and be a giver to others as far as he is able. If he cannot do anyone any good, then by Islamic standards he should at least not hurt anyone's feelings. He should speak plainly and truthfully, or else keep quiet.

### The inner reading

Allah is the mighty Compeller, the great Lord, the renowned keeper of His servants, the gentle, the generous, the faithful, the tremendous. He is the Lord of everyone and the bearer of everything, who takes the weak by the hand and joins them in love. In this verse He caresses the weak and shows love to orphans. As for the wrongdoers who pierce the livers of orphans and drink the blood of the poor, He threatens them and warns them of a fearful punishment. He stands in for the helpless and argues with the wrongdoers on their behalf. He keeps company with the weak, supports the despairing, answers the distressed and hears the voice of the grieved. He loves a servant who is beaten down, helpless and destitute, and who sighs coldly, weeps warm tears, raises two empty hands to Him and asks once more for pardon.

A tradition tells of a man who was saying, "O Lord, O Lord! You have written, You have measured out, and You have decreed!" He added that all that was, is and will be is what Allah wants, brings about and writes for His creatures, and that none of it lies outside His predestination or happens without His decree. A call came from the man's inmost heart: "That is tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah. Where is servanthood?" What he said was only tawḥīd, and fit for Allah's Godhood. What, then, was the mark of his servanthood? The man said, "O Lord, O Lord! I have disobeyed, I have sinned, and I ask." What comes from me is fitting for me, he said. I have broken my pledge, I keep no faith, I am unfaithful and worse. What can I do about this story? I am all artifice and colour, and I am too crippled to walk the straight path. Greed has turned me into grasping claws, and I am at war with the way the Apportioner apportions.

The passage goes on to say that it is harsh to eat the wealth of orphans and to crave their possessions foolishly. It then begins a story of ʿĪsā (Jesus), pure and a marvel of his time, passing by a graveyard, but the telling breaks off there.

### In short

- Whoever consumes an orphan's wealth unjustly, in any way at all, swallows nothing but fire, and will be burned in a blazing Hell.
- Scholars differ on whether the "fire" is a figure of speech or the real nature of the wealth. On the second view, deeds will appear on the Last Day in their true forms, like a matchbox that is truly fire.
- The Prophet ﷺ warned against taking the money of the two weak groups, women and orphans, and counted consuming an orphan's property among the seven destructive sins.
- Everything the dead person owned belongs to the heirs. Charity, feasts and other spending out of the undivided estate are not allowed, because orphans and absent heirs have rights in it.
- Inwardly, Allah stands in for the weak and warns those who wrong them, and He loves the servant who comes to Him helpless and in tears.

11.text:
This is the verse that sets the main shares of inheritance for children and parents: "Allah commands you regarding your children: the share of the male will be twice that of the female. If you leave only two ˹or more˺ females, their share is two-thirds of the estate. But if there is only one female, her share will be one-half. Each parent is entitled to one-sixth if you leave offspring. But if you are childless and your parents are the only heirs, then your mother will receive one-third. But if you leave siblings, then your mother will receive one-sixth—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. ˹Be fair to˺ your parents and children, as you do not ˹fully˺ know who is more beneficial to you. ˹This is˺ an obligation from Allah. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise."

The earlier verse gave the principle that men and women both inherit from their parents and nearest kin. This verse gives the detail for the closest relatives of all, the children and the parents. They are the nearest and most direct of all human relationships, so they inherit in every case, and the Qur'an takes up their shares first.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah commands you regarding your children"**. The Arabic word is yūṣīkum, from waṣiyyah, which here means a command. Allah is telling parents to be just toward their own children. In the days of ignorance before Islam, the males received a share and the females did not. Ibn ʿAbbās described the old custom in a report recorded by al-Bukhārī. The dead man's property went to his children, while his parents received something only if he named them in his will. Allah cancelled whatever He wished of that custom. He ordained that a male gets twice what a female gets, that each parent gets one-sixth of the whole estate, that a wife gets an eighth or a quarter and that a husband gets a half or a quarter. Another explanation puts it simply: Allah is setting out for you what your children inherit after you die.

**"the share of the male will be twice that of the female"**. This is a general rule. It makes boys and girls both heirs, and it fixes their shares. When a person leaves both sons and daughters, a son's lot is twice a daughter's. If someone leaves one boy and two girls, the estate is divided into four parts. The boy takes two of them and each girl takes one. In the same spirit, another explanation says that with two females beside him a son takes half the estate and they share the other half, with one sister he takes two-thirds and she takes a third, and if he is alone he takes everything.

**"If you leave only two ˹or more˺ females, their share is two-thirds of the estate"**. Some people said this wording means only two daughters, and that "or more" is idle. That is wrong. Nothing in the Qur'an is useless. If the verse were about two women alone, it would have said that the share of both of them is two-thirds. The Arabic speaks plainly of more than two daughters. For exactly two, the same two-thirds applies, and the proof is in the sunnah, as the next section shows. It is also found in the last verse of this surah (4:176), where two sisters receive two-thirds. A female with a brother already gets a third, so two females on their own are surely entitled to the same two-thirds.

There is another thought on the word "more". One explanation says it guards against a false impression. Someone might think that the more females there are, the bigger their portion, because he wrongly takes the two-thirds for two females to come from the third a female gets beside a male. The remaining third goes to the other rightful heirs, such as the parents and the husband or wife of the dead person. All the daughters share the two-thirds equally.

**"But if there is only one female, her share will be one-half"**. If the dead person leaves one daughter and no other children, she receives half of what her father or mother left. The rest goes to the other heirs. If there is a single daughter, the parents take one-sixth each and a further sixth goes to the father.

**"Each parent is entitled to one-sixth if you leave offspring"**. The Arabic words "to each one of the two" repeat the parents, to show that the sixth is not shared between them. Each one receives a sixth of his own. The word for "child" also covers a grandchild, and the word for "parent" also covers a grandparent. This holds whether the child is a boy or a girl, and whether there is one child or more. After the children, the wife or husband and the parents have taken their shares, some of the remainder can return to the father on top of his sixth. In the science of inheritance, that is called taʿṣīb, inheritance as a male relative on the father's side.

**"But if you are childless and your parents are the only heirs, then your mother will receive one-third"**. The father takes the rest, which is twice the mother's share. Allah has given the mother half of what the father gets. If the dead person also left a surviving spouse, the spouse takes first, a half if it is a husband and a quarter if it is a wife. The mother then receives a third of what remains, and the father the other two-thirds, because the remainder is treated as the whole estate for the parents' purposes.

**"But if you leave siblings, then your mother will receive one-sixth"**. When the dead person leaves brothers or sisters, whether full siblings or half-siblings, their presence does not reduce the father's share. It reduces the mother's from a third to a sixth, and if there are no other heirs the father takes the rest. The siblings themselves inherit nothing, because the father is nearer than they are. The Arabic term for this is ḥajb an-nuqṣān, a block that reduces a share and does not remove it. It applies to full siblings, to siblings from the same father only, and to siblings from the same mother only. It applies when there are two or more. Qatādah said that their presence reduces the mother's share and they do not inherit. With one brother only, the mother's share stays at a third. The early scholars explained the reduction by saying that the father is the one who helps these brothers and sisters get married and pays for it out of his own money, while the mother does not. This is a sound opinion.

**"after the fulfilment of bequests and debts"**. All these shares apply only after the dead person's will and debts have been dealt with. The next sections explain the order.

**"˹Be fair to˺ your parents and children, as you do not ˹fully˺ know who is more beneficial to you"**. Benefit may come to a person from his parents in this life or in the Hereafter, in a way he could never get from his children, and the opposite may be true too. Since benefit might come from either, Allah appointed a fixed share for each. This is why He broke with the practice of the days of ignorance and the early period of Islam, when the estate went to the children and the parents received something only if the will named them. According to one explanation, the benefit meant is rank in the Hereafter. According to another, it is usefulness in this world, with regard to inheritance. A short explanation gives an example. A man may think well of someone and leave him everything, or think badly of another and leave him nothing, and he may be wrong both times.

**"˹This is˺ an obligation from Allah. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"**. These appointed shares, which give some heirs more than others, are a command that Allah has decided and ordained. He is the All-Knowing and the All-Wise, who puts everything in its rightful place and gives each person his rightful share. He knows the division of inheritance, and He is wise in setting the male and female shares at different amounts.

### The science of inheritance

This verse, the next one and the last verse of the surah (4:176) contain the knowledge of al-farāʾiḍ, the fixed shares of inheritance. This knowledge is drawn from these three verses and from the hadiths that explain them. Learning it is encouraged, especially the specific things the verses mention. Ibn ʿUyaynah said that the knowledge of al-farāʾiḍ was called half of knowledge, because it touches everyone.

The verse about those entitled to inherit was given briefly in the previous section, with some of the details. More details come later, near the end of the surah, and the remaining shares were fixed by hadiths. Muslim jurists gathered all the rules from the Qur'an and the hadith and made them a permanent science, ʿilm al-farāʾiḍ, the science of the laws of inheritance. This verse covers the shares of children and parents, along with some related points.

### Why the verse came down

Al-Bukhārī recorded that Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abū Bakr came on foot to visit him at Banū Salamah's dwellings when he was ill. They found him unconscious. The Prophet ﷺ asked for water, did wuḍūʾ (the ablution) with it and sprinkled some on Jābir, and he came to. Jābir asked, "What do you command me to do with my money, O Messenger of Allah?" Then this verse was revealed. Muslim and an-Nasāʾī also recorded it, and the other compilers of the Six collected it as well. It came through Ibn Jurayj, who reported it from Ibn al-Munkadir.

Another report from Jābir was recorded by Aḥmad. The wife of Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "These are the two daughters of Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ, who was killed as a martyr at Uḥud. Their uncle took their money and left them nothing. They will not be married unless they have money." The Messenger ﷺ said, "Allah will decide on this matter." The verse was then revealed, and the Messenger ﷺ sent word to the uncle:

> "Give two-thirds of Saʿd's money to his two daughters and one-eighth to their mother, and whatever is left is yours."

Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah collected this hadith. In another version, an Anṣārī woman near Aswāf said that the two girls were the daughters of Thābit ibn Qays, who had fallen at Uḥud, and that their uncle had taken everything. Yet another report has her naming Thābit ibn Qays, or perhaps Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ, and says the Prophet ﷺ summoned the woman and her opponent and ordered the same division: two-thirds to the girls, one-eighth to their mother, and the remainder for the uncle.

The first hadith of Jābir is more likely about the last verse of the surah (4:176), because at the time Jābir had sisters, and no daughters, parents or children to inherit from him. The hadith is mentioned here only because al-Bukhārī placed it here.

### A mercy greater than a parent's

The verse tells parents to be just and fair with their children, and that shows Allah is more merciful toward children than their own parents are. An authentic hadith tells of a woman among the captives who was searching for her child. She found him at last, picked him up and nursed him at her breast. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then asked his Companions:

> "Do you think this woman would throw her child into the fire willingly?"

They said, "No, O Messenger of Allah." He said:

> "By Allah, Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child."

### Why a male gets twice as much

There is a reason for the difference. Men have to find money for their dependants, for business dealings, for work and for meeting their obligations. That is why they receive twice what women receive.

The way the verse is phrased also shows how much it cares that girls are given their share. It does not say that two females receive the equal of one male. It says that a male receives the equal of two females, so the girl's share is the measuring unit. A modern view notes that ancient tribal societies made the boy all-important, since he was a source of strength to the tribe. They gave him the sole right to inherit and left the girl out completely. People resent this today, and so the boy and the girl are now treated as equal. But if the old rule was unjust, the new rule is unrealistic. A law free from every kind of inequity can be expected only from Allah, whose knowledge and wisdom are without limit. His laws on this subject are a real source of social justice and are also tied, in the deepest way, to the life to come.

### Do not take your sisters' share by "forgiveness"

Some people do not give their sisters a share on the pretext that the sisters have given up their right. This is a mistake. Sisters seldom give up their rights willingly. They do it reluctantly, knowing they will not get anything anyway and asking themselves why they should cause bad blood between brothers and sisters. Such forgiveness is not valid in Islamic law. Their claim against their brothers remains, and those who seize inheritance are terrible sinners. If minor girls hold shares in such an estate, not giving them their shares is a sin committed twice, once by taking an heir's share and once by devouring an orphan's property.

### What the parents receive

The parents' shares fall into three cases. First, the dead person leaves living parents and children, even one boy or one girl. The father and the mother get a sixth each. What remains goes to the children and to the wife or husband. Second, he leaves no children and no brothers or sisters, only parents. The mother gets a third and the father the rest, which is twice her share. If a husband or wife survives, that share is taken out first, and a third of the remainder goes to the mother and two-thirds to the father. Third, he leaves no children but two or more brothers or sisters. The mother then gets a sixth. If there are no other heirs, the father gets the remaining five-sixths. The siblings receive nothing.

### The order: burial, debts, will, then shares

The shares are paid in a fixed order. The cost of shrouding and burying the dead Muslim comes out of the estate first, in a way the Sharīʿah (the revealed law) approves, avoiding both extravagance and stinginess. Then his debts are paid. If the debts equal or exceed the estate, there is nothing to divide and no will can take effect. If something remains, or if there are no debts, his will is carried out, as long as it is not a will to commit a sin. A will is carried out up to a third of what remains. If someone wills his whole estate, the will is valid only for a third. Willing more than a third is not appropriate, and when it is done to shut out the heirs, it is a sin. Whatever remains is divided among the legal heirs. If no will was made, the whole remainder after the debts is divided as inheritance.

The scholars of the Salaf, the early generations, and the Khalaf, the later ones, agree that paying debts comes before carrying out the will. This is clear to anyone who reads the verse carefully.

### Why "nearness" and not "benefit"

Allah fixed these shares in His infinite wisdom, and there are great considerations behind them. If the division had been left to people's opinion, they would have taken usefulness as the measure. But who will actually give or receive the most benefit is hard to know with any certainty. So nearness in kinship was chosen as the test instead of usefulness.

This verse makes it clear that the shares set by Allah are settled commands. Nobody has the right to impose an opinion, or to increase or decrease them. They should be accepted wholeheartedly. This command comes from the Creator and Master of all, and it rests on what is wise and good for human beings. No kind of benefit lies outside His knowledge, and no command of His is without wisdom. A person cannot by himself recognise his real gain and loss. If the division of inheritance were left to personal opinion, people would surely have decided wrongly, because of the limits of their understanding, and fairness and moderation would have been lost. So Allah took this duty on Himself, so that justice and equity prevail in dividing what the dead leave, and so that wealth circulates among capable heirs in a just and balanced way.

### The inner reading

The word for "command" here, waṣiyyah, means an order. Allah set two principles for what the heirs are owed from the estate. One is the obligatory portions, farḍ. The other is inheritance by the group of male relatives, taʿṣīb, whose members are called the ʿaṣaba. Inheritance by the ʿaṣaba is stronger than the fixed portions, because it can take in the whole of the estate, while most of the fixed portions cannot go beyond two-thirds. The division begins with those who hold the fixed portions, who have the weaker claim. Then it moves on to the ʿaṣaba, who have the stronger right. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "What is left over of the shares goes to the nearest male relative."

That is Allah's way, His sunnah, forever. The same pattern appears in His words: "Then We granted the Book to those We have chosen from Our servants. Some of them wrong themselves, some follow a middle course, and some are foremost in good deeds by Allah’s Will" (35:32). He gave them the Book as an inheritance, and then He began with the wrongdoer, ahead of those who take the lead. The wrongdoer has the weakest claim to put forward for generosity, because he is broken-hearted and cannot bear to wait long.

"To the male the equivalent of the portion of two females". If the matter were decided by analogy, qiyās, with those earlier cases where the weak are preferred, it would be more fitting to favour the female, because she is weak and cannot move about freely. But His ruling is one that does not need a reason. "You do not know which of them is nearer in benefit to you". Children benefit you with their service, and parents benefit you with their compassion. Parents give it when you are weak as a newborn, and children give it when you are weak in old age.

### In short

- Allah fixes the shares of the closest heirs. A son receives twice a daughter's share. Two or more daughters share two-thirds, one daughter gets a half, each parent gets a sixth if there are children, and a mother gets a third, or a sixth if there are two or more siblings.
- A husband or wife takes first, and the mother's third is then a third of the remainder. Siblings reduce the mother's share but receive nothing themselves.
- Everything comes after burial costs, debts and a will of up to a third. Debts come before the will.
- The verse is said to have come down for Jābir, who was ill, and for the daughters of Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ, whose uncle took their inheritance. The Prophet ﷺ gave the girls two-thirds and their mother one-eighth.
- Allah chose nearness in kinship over supposed benefit because no one can know who will benefit them most, and no heir may add to or reduce what He fixed.
- Inwardly, the shares follow the pattern of Allah's gifts, which come before deeds and need no justification.

12.text:
The previous verse gave the shares of those related by birth. This verse turns to those related by marriage and then to a third case: "You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless. But if they have children, then ˹your share is˺ one-fourth of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless. But if you have children, then your wives will receive one-eighth of your estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister ˹from their mother’s side˺, they will each inherit one-sixth, but if they are more than one, they ˹all˺ will share one-third of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts without harm ˹to the heirs˺. ˹This is˺ a commandment from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing."

So the passage moves from lineage to marriage, and then to the case of a person who dies with no parents and no children, which the Arabic calls kalālah. Together with 4:11 and the last verse of the surah, this verse is one of the three that hold the knowledge of the fixed shares.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless. But if they have children, then ˹your share is˺ one-fourth of the estate"**. In this part of 4:12, Allah tells the husband that he receives half of what his wife leaves if she dies without a child. If she has a child, he receives one-fourth, after her bequests and debts. The word "child" is not limited to the husband's own children. It covers a child by another husband, and boys and girls alike. It also covers grandchildren and further descendants, as the scholars agree. After the husband takes his share, the rest goes to the other heirs, such as her parents, brothers and sisters, according to their own rules.

**"after the fulfilment of bequests and debts"**. These words come after each case and give the order in which the estate is used. In short, debts are paid first, then the will is carried out, and then the shares are divided. The scholars agree on this order.

**"And your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless. But if you have children, then your wives will receive one-eighth of your estate"**. A wife receives one-fourth if her husband leaves no child and one-eighth if he does, whether the child is hers or another wife's. If the husband leaves more than one wife, each does not get a fourth or an eighth of her own. All the wives share that single fourth or eighth equally. What remains after the husband's or wife's share is divided among the other heirs.

**"And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister ˹from their mother’s side˺"**. This is the case of kalālah. The word comes from iklīl, the crown that goes round the head. It is said to mean that the person's heirs come from outside the first degree of relatives. The best-known definition is that a person who dies leaving no ancestors and no descendants is kalālah. Al-Qurṭubī reports a number of other definitions. Al-Ālūsī, the author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, explains that the word is a verbal noun from kalāl, to become worn out, and that it carries the idea of weakness. Any relationship other than that of father and son was called kalālah, because it is weak beside that bond. The word was also used for the deceased who left neither son nor father, for an heir who is neither the son nor the father of the dead person, and in the end for the property left by such a person. One explanation says it can mean any kin other than parents and children.

The verse says "a brother or a sister", and what is meant is a brother or sister from the mother's side. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ and some others of the Salaf, the early generations, said so, and Qatādah reported that it was also the view of Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq. Saʿd's recitation of the verse has the words "from his mother", as al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī, al-Jaṣṣāṣ and others report. That recitation was not passed down by tawātur, the report of a vast number of people in every age. But the consensus of the whole Muslim ummah makes it worth following. There is another clear proof. Allah mentions the inheritance of kalālah again at the end of the surah. There it says that one sister receives a half, a brother inherits all of his sister's estate, two sisters receive two-thirds, and when there are several brothers and sisters, the male receives twice the female (4:176). That verse is about full siblings and siblings from the father's side only. If those were meant here as well, the two rulings would contradict each other.

**"they will each inherit one-sixth, but if they are more than one, they ˹all˺ will share one-third of the estate"**. A single brother or sister takes a sixth. If there are more, whether it is one brother with one sister or two of each, they all share one-third of the estate. A male does not take twice a female here, and the males and females have equal shares. Half-siblings from the mother's side differ from other heirs in four ways. First, they inherit because of their mother. Second, males and females among them receive the same. Third, they inherit only when the deceased is kalālah, since they have no share if he leaves a living father, grandfather, child or grandchild. Fourth, they never receive more than a third, however many they are.

**"after the fulfilment of bequests and debts without harm ˹to the heirs˺"**. The will should be fair and free of any kind of harm. It must not take from some rightful heirs all or part of their share, and it must not add to the portion Allah fixed for some heirs. Whoever does this is arguing with Allah about His decision and His division. An authentic hadith says:

> "Allah has given each person his due right. So there is no will for an heir."

Other explanations spell out the harm. One is leaving more than a third by will. The words "without harm" warn that even though carrying out the will and paying the debts come before the heirs' shares, this priority must never be misused to wrong the true heirs.

**"˹This is˺ a commandment from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing"**. It is imperative to act on all that has been laid down about the shares, the payment of debts and the carrying out of wills. This is a command of great weight, and nobody should do anything that goes against it. The warning is added that Allah is All-Knowing and Forbearing. He knows everything, and He fixed these shares knowing the true state of every person. Whoever obeys will not find his good deed outside Allah's knowledge. Whoever disobeys will find his wrong conduct set out before Allah, and he will answer for it. A person who has wronged his heirs by a false debt or a harmful will is known to Allah as well. No one should feel safe from His punishment. Allah may not punish at once in this world, because He is Forbearing, but the one who disobeys should not fool himself into thinking he got away with it. Another explanation says that "Forbearing" points to the ignorance and deception that happen among people when they divide an estate. Allah does not hasten His punishment despite them.

### Why the husband is named first

The husband's share is mentioned first, perhaps to show how important it is. After a wife dies, her husband becomes part of another family. If she dies in her parents' house, and her property is there too, her people might avoid giving the husband what is due to him. By naming his right first, the Qur'an may well be condemning that practice.

### Pay the dower first

Before the estate is divided, it must be checked whether the wife's dower, her mahr, has been paid. If her husband did not pay it, it counts as a debt and is paid first from the whole estate, like any other debt. The woman then receives her fixed share as an heir on top of it. If the estate is worth no more than the dower, the whole estate goes to her against that debt. In that case no other heir receives anything, because nothing is left.

### Abū Bakr and the word kalālah

Ash-Shaʿbī reported that when Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq was asked what kalālah means, he answered, "I will give my own opinion. If it is right, then its rightness is from Allah." He went on, "If it is wrong, the error is mine and comes from Shayṭān's evil efforts, and Allah and His Messenger are free of it." Then he said, "Kalālah is a man who has neither descendants nor ascendants." When ʿUmar became khalīfah, he said, "I hesitate to go against an opinion of Abū Bakr." Ibn Jarīr and others recorded this.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded in his Tafsīr that Ibn ʿAbbās said, "I was one of the last people to see ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. He said to me, 'What you said was the right opinion.' I asked, 'What did I say?' He said, 'That kalālah is a person with no child or parents.'" Al-Ḥakam, Jābir ibn Zayd, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, an-Nakhaʿī, ash-Shaʿbī, Zayd ibn Thābit, Ibn Masʿūd and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib held the same view. It is the view of the people of al-Madīnah, Kūfah and Baṣrah, of the Seven Fuqahāʾ and the Four Imams, and of most scholars past and present, so some scholars declare a consensus on it.

### Wills that harm the heirs

A will in favour of an heir is not lawful. If someone makes a will for his son, his daughter, his husband or wife, or anyone else who will have a share of his estate, it cannot be enforced. The heirs receive what is theirs and are not entitled to more. The Prophet ﷺ said in his famous address at his last Ḥajj:

> "Allah has given every person his right. So there is no will for an heir."

This is in Mishkāt, from Abū Dāwūd. If the other heirs agree, however, a will in favour of one heir may be carried out first, and the rest of the estate is divided by the Sharīʿah's method, with that heir also taking his fixed share. The hadiths carry this exception in the words "unless the heirs wish", as al-Hidāyah notes.

If someone makes a will, or a false admission of debt, to deprive his heirs, he does something strictly forbidden and a major sin. There are many ways to do harm through debt and will. A man may lie that he is in debt, so that the money goes to a friend. He may present something he owns outright as something he holds in trust for another, so that it stays out of the estate. He may will more than a third. He may lie about a loan he made, claiming it was repaid so that it will not pass to his heirs. Or, in the illness that ends in his death, he may give away more than a third. Anyone who is about to leave this world should do his best to stay away from all of these.

The words "without harm" appear only with the rules for kalālah, yet the rule is general. It is understood at the two earlier places in these verses where will and debt come first. It applies not just to a person who dies as kalālah, but to everyone who makes a will.

### Why "will" comes before "debt" in the wording

The shares are given three times in this passage, and each time they are said to come after the will and the debt. As stated, one-third of what remains after the funeral costs and debts is used for the will. If the will goes beyond a third, it cannot be enforced. In law the debt comes before the will. If the debts use up the whole estate, there is no will to carry out and nothing to divide.

Yet in the verse's wording the will is named before the debt, and this gives the impression that the will comes first. A report removes the doubt: "You recite the verse with the will first, but the Prophet ﷺ settled the debt before the will."

Al-Ālūsī gives the reason for the order of the words. The will is named first to stress that it must be carried out. The person who benefits from a will gets it without paying anything for it and often has no tie of kinship with the dead person. The heirs might ignore it or put it off, because they do not like to see property that would have been theirs go to someone else. Not everyone has debts, and one who has them in his lifetime has not necessarily left them unpaid at his death. Even if a debt remains, the creditors' claim is one the heirs cannot refuse, so the chance of falling short is small. A will is different. The dead person earnestly wished that part of his wealth be put into something good that would serve as ongoing charity for him. No claimant stands behind it, so the heirs themselves might fall short. To offset that risk, the will is named first, as a special measure.

### The inner reading

Inheritance and the right to receive it rest on one of two grounds, a cause or a bloodline. Marriage is the cause, and kinship is the bloodline. Marriage brings love, as Allah says: "And He has placed between you compassion and mercy" (30:21). Lineage is help and strength, as in the saying, "A man is many through his brothers."

When a relative by blood or a person close through the cause of marriage dies, it wounds the heart and hurts the spirit. The Lord of the Worlds puts balm on that pain. After the suffering He commands comfort through the dead person's wealth. As the pain came from his passing, so the balm comes from his property. This is the Lord's way with His friends. If He lays a hardship on them by prescribing the Law, then after the hardship He makes a treasure appear, to ease it.

Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī said:

> "How could I have known that suffering is the mother of happiness, and that under one disappointment lie a thousand treasures? That hope is the messenger of union, and that beneath the cloud of generosity despair is impossible? That the Lovingly Kind is so forbearing that His gentleness to the sinner is beyond counting? How servant-caressing the Possessor of Majesty is, and how much joy His friends find in Him? That what I seek is in the middle of the spirit, and that the glory of union with Him is my opening?"

A line of verse goes with this:

> One night in all my life, near dawn, the image of that comfort of the spirit came to me and asked, "How are you, wounded one?" I said, "In my passion for You, that is the first opening."

### In short

- A husband receives half of his wife's estate if she leaves no child and a quarter if she does. A wife receives a quarter if her husband leaves no child and an eighth if he does. Several wives share that quarter or eighth equally.
- Where a person leaves neither parents nor children (kalālah) and has a brother or sister from the mother's side, each receives a sixth. If there are more than one, they share a third, with males and females equal. The last verse of the surah covers full and paternal siblings.
- Everything comes after the dower, the debts and a will of no more than a third. A will for an heir is not lawful unless the other heirs allow it, and false debts and other tricks to deprive heirs are a major sin.
- Abū Bakr's definition of kalālah, no descendants and no ascendants, was accepted by ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās and most scholars.
- Allah knows everything and is Forbearing, but His patience is no reason to feel safe. Inwardly, the wealth of the dead is balm for the pain of losing them.

13.text:
After setting out the shares, the Qur'an gives a promise and a warning, as it usually does after stating beliefs and rulings: "These ˹entitlements˺ are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. That is the ultimate triumph." The aim is to press Muslims to obey these rules.

### Phrase by phrase

**"These ˹entitlements˺ are the limits set by Allah"**. The fixed shares of inheritance are Allah's limits. They include what He has set aside for each heir according to the degree of relation to the dead person and the degree of dependence on him. They must not be crossed or broken. Other explanations call the limits the legal rulings and duties Allah has imposed. One says that the rulings about orphans and what came after them are His bounds, laws He has marked out for His servants so that they act on them and do not go beyond them.

On the inner side, His limits, the ḥudūd, are His commands and prohibitions, and the means by which His servants, the ʿibād, show their devotion. The root of servanthood, ʿubūdiyya, is keeping to the limits and keeping the promises, the ʿuhūd. Whoever keeps His limit will not be reached by anything bad or harmful. The root of every affliction is going beyond the limits.

**"Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger"**. The obedience meant here is about inheritance. It means not adding to these fixed shares or cutting them down by tricks and schemes. Instead the person gives each heir his appointed share, as Allah commanded, ordained and decided. Another explanation says it means obeying in the division of estates. A short one says it means following Allah and His Messenger in His instructions and staying away from what He has forbidden.

**"will be admitted into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever"**. One explanation says that the rivers flow beneath the dwellings and trees, and that they are rivers of wine, water, honey and milk. The people there will live in Paradise forever and will never die or leave it. In a variant reading, the verb for "will admit him" is in the first person plural: "We will admit him." Another short explanation says the gardens have rivers flowing beneath their palaces.

**"That is the ultimate triumph"**. This is the greatest salvation, achieved by entering Paradise. It is the great success, and no other success comes near it.

### Who may not inherit

The distribution of an estate is based on nearness of kinship, but there are exceptions. The Sunnah specifies that the people named may receive their share as long as they are not barred by having committed murder, by belonging to a different religion, or by being slaves.

First, the dead person and his heir must not be of different religions. A Muslim does not inherit from a kāfir, and a kāfir does not inherit from a Muslim, whatever family tie they have. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> "The Muslim does not inherit from the kāfir, nor does the kāfir inherit from the Muslim."

This is recorded in Mishkāt. It concerns someone who is a Muslim or a kāfir from birth. If a person who was a Muslim leaves Islam and dies or is killed as an apostate, everything he earned while he was Muslim goes to his Muslim heirs. What he earned after his apostasy is paid into the Bayt al-Māl, the public treasury. If a woman becomes an apostate, all of her property, whether acquired during her days as a Muslim or after, goes to her Muslim heirs. An apostate, man or woman, does not inherit from any Muslim or from another apostate.

Second, a killer is shut out. If someone kills a person from whose estate he would have had a share, he is no longer an heir and receives nothing from the one he killed. The Prophet ﷺ said, "The killer does not inherit." This is recorded in Mishkāt too. Some kinds of accidental homicide, qatl al-khaṭāʾ, are an exception, and the details are in the books of fiqh.

### The unborn child and the woman waiting out her ʿiddah

If a man leaves children and his wife is pregnant, the unborn child counts among the heirs. It is hard or uncertain to know the child's sex or the number of children, so it is best to delay the distribution until the birth. If the estate must be divided at once, one should suppose two cases, a boy and a girl, and give the other heirs the smaller of the two portions. What is left is held for the child who will be born.

If a man divorces his wife by a divorce that can be revoked and dies before revoking it and before her waiting period, her ʿiddah, ends, she receives a share, because the marriage is still in force. If he divorces her during the illness that ends in his death, then even if the divorce is irrevocable or pronounced three times, she still receives a share if he dies before her waiting period ends. For this purpose, the longer of two waiting periods is used. The waiting period after a divorce is three menstrual periods, and after the death of a husband it is four lunar months and ten days. Whichever lasts longer is taken as her ʿiddah, so that she may inherit wherever possible.

If a man divorces his wife irrevocably or by three pronouncements before any illness that ends in his death, and he dies a few days later during her waiting period, she gets no share. If the divorce was revocable, she does inherit. If a wife obtains a separation at her own request, khulʿ, during his final illness, she does not inherit even if he dies during her ʿiddah.

### Fixed shares, residuary heirs and the rest

The Sharīʿah fixes shares for twelve kinds of heir. They are called the aṣḥāb al-furūḍ, those with obligatory shares in the Qur'an. If no such heir exists, or if something is left after they receive their shares, the remainder goes to the ʿaṣabāt, the residuary heirs on the male side. A person sometimes inherits in both capacities. In other cases, the dead person's children and father, or the father's offspring, such as a brother, also become residuary heirs. There are several kinds of ʿaṣabāt, and the books on the shares give the details.

An example shows how it works. Zayd died leaving a wife, a daughter, a mother and an uncle. His estate is split into twenty-four parts. Half of that, twelve parts, goes to the daughter. The wife has an eighth, which is three parts. The mother has a sixth, which is four parts. The residue of five parts goes to the uncle, as the nearest male relative on the father's side.

If there are no residuary heirs, the remainder returns to those with fixed shares in proportion to their shares. This is called radd, return. A husband or wife does not receive any of this return. If there is no one in either group, the estate goes to the dhawū al-arḥām, relatives on the mother's side. This is a large group that includes the children of a daughter or sister, paternal aunts, maternal uncles and maternal aunts. There is a lot more to say on this subject than can be covered here, but the remarks above should be enough.

### In short

- The fixed shares of inheritance are Allah's limits. Obeying them by giving each heir his appointed share, with no tricks, leads to Gardens and the great triumph.
- Those who differ in religion do not inherit from each other, and a killer does not inherit from his victim. The Sunnah also bars slaves.
- An unborn child counts as an heir, and the estate should wait for its birth. A wife in her waiting period may inherit, depending on the kind of divorce and whether the husband was in his final illness.
- After the fixed shares, the remainder goes to the residuary heirs, then back to those with fixed shares, then to maternal relatives.
- Inwardly, servanthood is keeping Allah's limits and promises, and every affliction begins with crossing them.

14.text:
This verse is the other side of the promise before it: "But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds their limits will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever. And they will suffer a humiliating punishment." The shares of inheritance are not only matters of family arrangement. They are among those on which a person's entry into Paradise or Hell can depend.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger"**. The disobedience meant here concerns the division of estates. Another explanation says it covers anyone who does not follow His laws or who doubts them. According to another, the person has changed what Allah ordained and has disputed with His judgment. This is the conduct of those who do not accept what Allah has decided and divided.

**"and exceeds their limits"**. This means going against His rulings and duties through deviation and disobedience. It means overstepping the limits He has made.

**"will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever"**. The Arabic can be read in two ways, as "He will admit him" or as "We will admit him". One explanation says the person remains in the Fire until whenever Allah wills. A grammar note on both this verse and the last explains that the singular pronouns and verbs agree with the word for "whoever", while the plural in "to stay there forever" agrees with the general plural meaning of that word.

**"And they will suffer a humiliating punishment"**. This is a punishment through which the person will be put to shame. It is also said to mean a severe torment. It is an eternal, painful torment with humiliation, and this is why Allah punishes those who dispute what He decided and divided.

### The unfair will

Aḥmad recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "A man may do the deeds of righteous people for seventy years, but when it is time to write his will, he commits an injustice. His last deed is his worst, and he enters the Fire. And a man may do the deeds of evil people for seventy years, yet he is fair in his will. His last deed is his best, and he enters Paradise."

Abū Hurayrah said, "Read, if you wish: 'These are the limits set by Allah,' up to 'a disgraceful torment.'"

Abū Dāwūd has a chapter on injustice in wills in his Sunan. There Abū Hurayrah reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "A man or a woman may act in obedience to Allah for sixty years. Yet when they are near death, they leave an unfair will, and so they earn the Fire."
