Abū Hurayrah then recited the verse about wills "without harm", and the words "that is the great success". At-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah also recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan gharīb.

### Two punishments, one now and one later

There are two punishments, one that comes at once and one that is postponed, and shame joins them. If created beings tried to degrade the disobedient as much as their own disobedience has already degraded them, they could not manage it. This is why a poet said that a person who spends a night in sin wakes up already wearing his disgrace, wa-ʿalayhi madhallatuhu. And of one who wakes up and spends the day in pious acts, people say that he has his dignity upon him, wa-ʿalayhi mahābatuhu.

### Following Allah's law, not family convenience

Paying orphans what they are due, keeping to wills and handing the inheritance to the heirs are among the matters on which a person's going to Hell or Paradise depends. Islamic law allows a will for a third of one's property. But anyone who makes a will with the aim of depriving someone of his rightful inheritance commits a sin that could condemn him to Hell. A person must follow Allah's law in this matter, and not his own desires or the convenience of his family.

### In short

- Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger in the shares of inheritance and goes beyond His limits will be put in the Fire to stay there, with a humiliating punishment.
- This covers changing what Allah fixed, doubting His laws, or disputing His judgment.
- The Prophet ﷺ warned that a man may do righteous deeds for decades and then lose everything by an unfair will at the end of his life.
- Disobedience brings two punishments, one in this life, in disgrace, and one later. A person is to follow Allah's law, not his own wishes or his family's convenience.

15.text:
The earlier verses set right the wrongs of the days of ignorance toward orphans and in matters of inheritance. The people of that time also treated women cruelly and kept other evil customs, such as marrying women who were forbidden to them. This verse and the next deal with a woman's proven offence and how it is handled: "˹As for˺ those of your women who commit illegal intercourse—call four witnesses from among yourselves. If they testify, confine the offenders to their homes until they die or Allah ordains a ˹different˺ way for them." The correction of such customs continues through the next two or three passages.

The verse speaks of zinā, which covers both adultery and fornication. The penalty described here was the first one given, in the early days of Islam. It was later replaced, as the sections below explain.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹As for˺ those of your women who commit illegal intercourse"**. The Arabic word is fāḥishah, a lewd act, and here it means zinā. Explanations differ on which women are meant. One says free, married women. Another says women whether married or unmarried. A third says simply women who commit adultery.

**"call four witnesses from among yourselves"**. Four Muslim men are to be called as witnesses. One short explanation adds that they must be trustworthy, and another that they must have caught the pair in the act. The authority before which the case comes must call four qualified witnesses to prove the offence. All of them must be men, and a woman's testimony is not valid here.

**"If they testify, confine the offenders to their homes until they die"**. At the beginning of Islam, when a woman committed adultery and it was established by sufficient proof, she was confined to her home, with no leave to go out, until she died. Other explanations say that she was kept from mixing with people, or even held in prison until death. The order of revelation is also noted. The command to punish the offenders came first, and the order to confine the women came after. The Qur'an gave two limits for the confinement, death, or a way that Allah would appoint. If Allah prescribed another punishment while she was alive, it would replace the confinement.

**"or Allah ordains a ˹different˺ way for them"**. The "other way" is the later ruling that replaced this one. Ibn ʿAbbās said that confinement was the first ruling, until Allah revealed Sūrat an-Nūr, which put flogging for fornication and stoning for adultery in its place. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd ibn Aslam, Qatādah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah all gave a similar account, and the matter is agreed upon. Short explanations state it in plain terms. Imprisoning a free, married woman until death was replaced by stoning, or the virgin receives a hundred lashes and a year's banishment while the married woman is stoned.

### Why four witnesses, and all of them men

Zinā is an extremely grave offence. It violates honour and modesty and brings shame on a family. For that reason, Islam set a very strict standard of proof for it. First, the witnesses must be men, and women's evidence is not accepted. Second, the number is raised to four. That is a hard condition, and it can very seldom be met. The strictness is there so that the woman's husband, his mother, another wife or a sister cannot bring false charges against her out of personal spite. It also stops other ill-wishers from using the charge to settle a private score.

If fewer than four people testify, their evidence is not valid. The accuser and all the witnesses can be treated as liars, and the penalty for false accusation, the ḥadd of qadhf, then applies to them for wrongly accusing a Muslim. Sūrat an-Nūr says clearly that those who cannot produce four witnesses are liars. Some of the elders give a reason for the number four. The case involves two persons, a man and a woman, so it falls under one rule for two cases. Each case needs two witnesses, and so this one needs four.

### The veil over sins

There is also a reading from the allusive side. Allah lowered a veil of generosity over the sins of His servants, and He did it by requiring an excessive number of witnesses to prove this lewd act. Following the witnessing procedure in the law makes it almost impossible to establish such a case. When Māʿiz ibn Mālik came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have committed fornication," the Prophet ﷺ said, "Maybe you only kissed." On another occasion he said, "Smell his breath." In this is the strongest proof of the veil that is drawn over ugly acts.

### The "way" that Allah made

The "way" was later set out in the clear words of the Prophet ﷺ, which describe the married and the unmarried separately. ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit said that when revelation came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it weighed on him and his face showed the strain. One day Allah sent down a revelation, and when the strain had passed, the Prophet ﷺ said, as Aḥmad recorded:

> "Take it from me: Allah has made a way for them. The married with the married, the unmarried with the unmarried. The married receives a hundred lashes and stoning to death, and the unmarried a hundred lashes and banishment for a year."

Muslim and the compilers of the Sunan recorded another wording from ʿUbādah, in which the Prophet ﷺ says "Take from me, take from me", and at-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Muslim's version is also given with the words "Come and listen to me! Come and listen to me! Allah has now made a way for them."

The Prophet ﷺ gave the ḥadd of zinā in the case of Māʿiz ibn Mālik and in the case of a woman from the tribe of Azd. Both were married, so both were stoned. A couple from the Jews of Madīnah was also stoned for zinā, and that judgment was based on a ruling in the Torah.

The ruling for the unmarried offender is in Sūrat an-Nūr itself: "As for female and male fornicators, give each of them one hundred lashes" (24:2). A verse about rajm, stoning to death, was also revealed earlier, but its recitation was later abrogated. The ruling itself stayed in force. ʿUmar said that Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ with the truth and sent down the Book to him, and that the verse of rajm was part of what was revealed. The Prophet ﷺ stoned, he said, and we stoned after him, and the revealed ruling of rajm stands against everyone who commits zinā while married, man or woman. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded it, as cited in Mishkāt.

So the commands to "torture" and to "confine to homes" in these verses were replaced when the legal ḥadd was revealed, which is one hundred lashes or rajm. Further detail will come with the discussion of Sūrat an-Nūr.

### What the verse did not fix

These two verses do not give a definite ḥadd. They say only "punish them" and "confine the women to their homes". They name no particular method for the punishment, so that was left to the authorities. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means that the offenders are rebuked in words and shamed, and also punished physically, for example by being struck with hands and sandals. This sounds like an illustration, and the whole matter was left to the judgment of those in authority.

### Justice in punishment

Anyone who commits an act that Islamic teaching counts as a sin is to be dealt with under the rule of law and not at will. It is unjust to call a person a criminal without meeting the legal conditions, and there is no permission to go ahead hastily even against a proven criminal. Punishment exists to uphold justice, and tyranny or injustice can never serve that goal.

### In short

- The verse gave the first ruling for a woman who commits zinā: four male Muslim witnesses, then confinement to her home until death, or until Allah appointed another way.
- The four-witness rule is deliberately hard to meet, to stop spite and false charges, and false accusers are themselves punished.
- Sūrat an-Nūr and the Prophet's ﷺ words replaced confinement with a hundred lashes and a year's banishment for the unmarried and stoning for the married, as in the cases of Māʿiz ibn Mālik and the Azd woman.
- Punishment must follow the rule of law, and the strictness of proof is read as a veil of mercy over people's sins.

16.text:
This verse gives a second rule and then opens the door of repentance: "And the two among you who commit this sin—discipline them. If they repent and mend their ways, relieve them. Surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful." The two verses together (4:15 and 4:16) were first read as dealing with illegal relations between a man and a woman. Some scholars, however, think this verse refers to two men.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And the two among you who commit this sin"**. The Arabic uses a dual form, "the two". Scholars understood it in two ways. One view takes it to mean the unmarried man and woman who commit zinā. Another takes it to mean two men, whether married or unmarried. Mujāhid said that the verse was revealed about two men who do it, as if he were pointing to the act of the people of Lūṭ.

Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh Pānīpatī and some other commentators hold that the verse is about homosexual acts between two males. The Arabic pronoun for "those two of you" is masculine and presumes males on both sides. Those who read both verses as being about zinā answer that masculine wording in general usage includes the feminine. Whichever side is right, the possibility that this verse refers to homosexual acts cannot be ruled out. One explanation judges the reference to two men to be the more obvious reading. It argues that the particle "of you" is attached to a masculine pronoun, that both parties suffer the same punishment, that both can repent, and that both are told to be left alone afterward. All of this fits men, since detention was stipulated for women in the previous verse. Ash-Shāfiʿī, however, was of the opinion that it refers to an adulterer and an adulteress.

**"discipline them"**. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbās said that this punishment includes cursing the pair, shaming them and striking them with sandals. Other explanations speak of insults and beating with sandals, of maligning and upbraiding, or of words and blows to humiliate and discipline them. No particular method is given, and the matter was left to the authorities. This ruling stood until Allah replaced it with flogging or stoning. A short explanation says that the unmarried were to receive a hundred lashes in its place, and another says that the unmarried are whipped a hundred times and banished for a year, and the married are stoned. If a lewd act means adultery, this verse is replaced by the prescribed punishment. If it means homosexual intercourse, ash-Shāfiʿī held that it is replaced as well. In his view, though, the person on the receiving end is not stoned even if he is married. He is flogged and banished.

**"If they repent and mend their ways, relieve them"**. The repentance meant here is to stop the evil act, after which the offenders' actions become righteous. "Relieve them" means do not abuse them verbally after that, since a person who truly repents is just like one who has no sin. It does not mean that repentance cancels the punishment. The repentance is mentioned after the punishment, as the Arabic connecting particle shows. So if the offenders have repented after the punishment, they must not be disgraced or punished any further. If they have not repented, reproach is still in order after the punishment.

The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record a related ruling: when the slave-girl of one of you commits zinā, let him flog her and not chastise her afterwards. The lashes she receives erase the sin she committed.

**"Surely Allah is ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful"**. Allah overlooks sins. He turns, with relenting, to those who repent and is compassionate toward them. A person who turns away from a sin and asks forgiveness is like a person who has not sinned.

### The act of the people of Lūṭ in the reports

Reports about this act are severe. The collectors of the Sunan recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever you find doing the act of the people of Lūṭ, kill both the one who does it and the one it is done to."

Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has cursed seven kinds of His creatures from above the seven heavens. He cursed one of them three times, saying, "Cursed is the one who does what the people of Lūṭ did", three times, and He cursed the others once, which is enough for them. This is cited in At-Targhīb wa-t-Tarhīb. Abū Hurayrah also reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that four kinds of people spend their mornings under Allah's wrath and their evenings under His rage. The Companions asked who they were, and he said, "Men who imitate women, women who imitate men, one who goes to animals, and one who goes to men."

According to Ḥāfiẓ Zakī ad-Dīn in the same work, four caliphs, Abū Bakr, ʿAlī, ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr and Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, condemned those guilty of sodomy to burning. He also relates, from Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, that Khālid ibn al-Walīd wrote to Abū Bakr about a man in a certain place in Arabia with whom people did what is done with women. Abū Bakr called the Companions together, ʿAlī among them. He said that no group had committed a sin like this except one, and that they all knew how Allah dealt with that group. He proposed that the man be burned. The other Companions agreed, and Abū Bakr ordered it so.

The people of Lūṭ were the people to whom the prophet Lūṭ was sent. Besides rejecting the message and the messenger and ascribing partners to Allah, they were addicted to this unnatural practice. When Lūṭ's teaching had no effect on them, the angels acted as Allah commanded. They lifted the towns off the ground, turned them upside down and threw them back down. The details will come in the discussion of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

Jurists differ on the fixed punishment for this act, and the books of fiqh give the details. The punishments reported are as severe as any: burning in fire, crushing under a wall, throwing from a height, stoning and beheading with the sword.

### Other acts the reports warn against

Other narrations give very severe warnings against anal intercourse with women. Ibn ʿAbbās reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah does not look with mercy on a person who does it with a man or a woman. Khuzaymah ibn Thābit reported that he said three times that Allah is not embarrassed by the truth, and then said, "Do not go to women anally." Abū Hurayrah reported that he said, "Cursed is the one who goes to women anally." Abū Hurayrah also reported that whoever goes to a woman in her menstruation, or in her anus, or goes to a soothsayer, a kāhin, and believes his claims about the unknown, has rejected what was revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ.

### Forgiveness for those who repent

If a sinner admits his fault and reforms, it becomes essential to treat him with sympathy and forgiveness. It is not right to judge anyone by his past. Allah Himself pardons those who sincerely repent and turns in kindness to those who mend their ways. Human beings therefore have no right to sneer at former offenders or make fun of them. A person who taunts them may yet prove to be a wrongdoer himself.

### The inner reading

The command to use different kinds of punishment is the strongest way of gently communicating the warning to stay away from the act. A servant is meant to be on guard and not become deserving of the greater punishment.

### In short

- The "two" in the verse are understood either as an unmarried man and woman who commit zinā or as two men. The possibility of a reference to homosexual acts cannot be ruled out.
- The early punishment was discipline by words and blows. It was replaced by flogging and banishment for the unmarried and stoning for the married, though ash-Shāfiʿī gave a different treatment for the receiving partner.
- Repentance and reform end the reproach. It does not cancel the punishment, but afterward the offender is not to be shamed or abused.
- The reports on the act of the people of Lūṭ are very severe, jurists differ on its fixed punishment, and similar warnings are given about anal intercourse.
- Allah accepts repentance and is Most Merciful, and no one has the right to taunt a person who has repented.

17.text:
After the earlier verses on offences, repentance comes into view. The previous verse mentioned it, and these two verses say when it is accepted and when it is not. The first says: "Allah only accepts the repentance of those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repent soon after—Allah will pardon them. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise." The second, 4:18, gives the other side.

The verse promises that sincere repentance is accepted, and the scholars explain that the two conditions it names, "ignorantly" and "soon after", are much wider than they sound.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah only accepts the repentance of those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺"**. The word for "ignorantly" is jahālah, and it looks as though it limits repentance to those who sin by mistake or without knowing. The explanation of the Companions is that it does not mean the person fails to know that the act is a sin, or that he lacks the intention or will to do it. It means that heedlessness toward the evil end of sin and its punishment made him bold enough to commit it, although he knew it was a sin and approached it deliberately. In other words, jahālah here means carelessness or foolishness.

There is support in Sūrat Yūsuf. Yūsuf (Joseph) addressed his brothers in a way that calls them jāhilūn, ignorant ones, although what they did was neither an error nor a lapse of memory. They did it knowingly and with full intent. They were called ignorant because they were heedless of the bad end of what they were doing (verse 89).

Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Qatādah report that the Companions used to say that every sin a servant commits, he commits out of ignorance. ʿAbd ar-Razzāq narrated, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, that the Companions agreed that every sin, whether done on purpose or not, is committed in ignorance. Mujāhid said that every person who disobeys Allah, even willfully, is ignorant while he does it. Ibn Jurayj related the same from Mujāhid, and said that ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ told him something similar. Abū Ṣāliḥ said that Ibn ʿAbbās commented that a person makes the error only because he is ignorant. Mujāhid, the master of exegesis, added that this is so even if the person looks like one of great learning on the outside.

Abū Ḥayyān explained further in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ. It is like the hadith that a person who commits zinā does not do so as a true believer. At the moment he gives in to the temptation, he has been thrown far from what his faith demands. This is why ʿIkrimah said that everything a person does in this world outside obedience to Allah is ignorance. The reasoning is clear. A person who disobeys Allah prefers short-lived pleasures to lasting ones. Anyone who takes a punishment that never ends in exchange for a short series of pleasures cannot be called sensible, however well he knows the evil of the act and however firm his intention.

The result is that every sin a person commits, on purpose or by mistake, comes from nothing but jahālah. The whole Muslim ummah therefore agrees that the repentance of a person who sinned deliberately can also be accepted. The same wording is explained in short as: sins done in disobedience out of foolishness and impulse, or even if they do so on purpose without knowing the punishment.

**"then repent soon after"**. The words are min qarīb, "from near". The verse sets a condition that one must repent soon, without delay. How soon is "soon"? The Prophet ﷺ answered this himself. Aḥmad recorded that Ibn ʿUmar said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Allah accepts the repentance of His servant as long as his soul has not reached the throat."

At-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah also collected this hadith, and at-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan gharīb. Ibn Mājah said by mistake that it came through ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr. The correct narrator is ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

Early scholars said the same. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means until just before the person sees the angel of death. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said that everything before death is "soon". Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said it is until just before the last breath leaves the throat. ʿIkrimah said that all of this life is "soon". Ibn Marduwayh narrated from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say that a believing servant who repents a month before his death, or a day or a moment before, will have his repentance accepted by Allah, provided that it is genuine and sincere.

So by the Prophet's own explanation, nearly a person's whole lifetime counts as "near", and any repentance offered well before death is accepted. Repentance made in the throes of death is not.

Ashraf Thānawī explains in his work on the Qur'an that a person near death faces two states. The first is utter hopelessness, when every medicine and effort has failed and he realises that death is at hand. This is the state of conscious suffering. The second comes after that, when the pangs of the soul's departure begin and the rattle in the throat, the ghargharah, which announces death, draws near. This is total despair. The first state comes within "soon", and repentance in it is accepted. The second does not, because angels and things of the Hereafter may start to appear to the dying person, and these are not included in "soon". The Qur'an itself points to this in the next verse, where it says that repentance is not accepted once the sure signs of death are visible. The words "soon after" also warn that a person's life is limited, and that death, which he thinks is far away, may be quite near.

**"Allah will pardon them"**. Allah's relenting that He has taken upon Himself is a form of promise that is certain to be kept. Strictly, Allah does not owe anything to anyone. One short explanation says that He overlooks the sins of these people. Another says that the repentance He accepts is the kind He has bound Himself, in His generosity, to accept. A third says that Allah forgives these people by overlooking their disobedience.

**"And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"**. He knows His creatures and what they do. One explanation says He is Knower of your repentance and Wise in accepting it before death, while He does not accept it when a person is in the pangs of death or after he has died. Another says He is Wise in His decree and His sacred laws.

### What repentance is

After the literal explanation, it is necessary to say what tawbah, repentance, really is. In his Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm ad-Dīn, Imām al-Ghazālī describes three situations with regard to sin. The first is total sinlessness, where no sin has ever been committed. That belongs to the angels and the prophets. The second is when a person takes the initiative, ventures into sin, repeats it and persists, never feeling shame or regret and never thinking of stopping. This is the way of the satans and devils. The third belongs to human beings, the children of Ādam (Adam), who regret a sin soon after committing it and firmly resolve not to go near it again. So failing to repent after a sin is the way of devils alone. This is why the whole ummah agrees that repentance is obligatory. The Qur'an says: "O believers! Turn to Allah in sincere repentance, so your Lord may absolve you of your sins and admit you into Gardens, under which rivers flow" (66:8).

Allah's mercy is generous. A person may spend his whole life disobeying Him. If he repents sincerely before he dies, he is not only forgiven. He is admitted to the circle of favoured servants and made an heir of Paradise. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that one who repents from a sin is loved by Allah, and that one who has repented from a sin is like one who never committed it. This is recorded by Ibn Mājah. According to some reports, when a servant repents and his repentance is accepted, he is not only excused from any reckoning for it. The very record the angels wrote of it is erased from his book of deeds, so that he is not disgraced either.

The repentance must be genuine and sincere, and it stands on three pillars. First, a person must feel regret and shame for what he has done. A hadith says, "Repentance is remorse." Second, he must leave the sin at once and firmly resolve to stay away from it in the future. Third, he should think of making amends for what has gone before and do what he can to put right what was wrongly done.

For example, if someone has missed a prayer or a fast, he should make it up, which is called qaḍāʾ. If he cannot remember the number of missed prayers and fasts, he should estimate it and then make them up in earnest. If it is impossible to do it all at once, he may offer one extra qaḍāʾ prayer with each salah at its time, and that is called ʿumrī qaḍāʾ, a lifetime's make-up. In the same way he should make up obligatory fasts as time allows. If he did not pay the zakah due on his wealth, he should pay it for previous years, all at once or in instalments. If he has taken someone's right, he should return it. If he has hurt someone, he should seek that person's forgiveness. If a person does not regret what he did, or regrets it but does not give up the sin for the future, his repentance is not repentance, even if he says it a thousand times. A Persian poet put it well:

> Repentance on the lips, a rosary in the hand, and a heart full of the taste of sin. Sin laughs at my way of asking for forgiveness.

Once a person repents as described, he becomes a servant dear to Allah, whatever sins he has been in. If he slips again, out of human weakness, he should renew his repentance at once, hoping that Allah, the Most Forgiving, will relent toward him this time as every time before. Another Persian couplet says:

> This is the court of My presence, not the court of despair. Even if you have broken your repentance a hundred times, come again.

The same point is made in another way. Repentance is not just words such as "I repent" or "tawbah". It is not lip service. It is an intense realisation of wrongdoing. A sinner who truly repents feels an agony like self-punishment, and Allah will surely pardon one who repents out of deep fear of Him. The heart of contrition is that the wrongdoer turns to his Lord so that his Lord also turns to him. Tawbah is for the one who does something wrong under the pull of a moment's feeling or desire, but whose conscience soon makes him see his fault, so that he leaves evil ways and returns to righteousness, reforming his life by the divine law. That is real penitence. Such a person is like one who strayed away and came home.

### The inner reading

Repentance marks the road. It leads to the Court, opens the treasure, pleads for union, crowns every joy and underlies freedom. It has three steps. First comes regret in the heart. Second comes apology with the tongue. Third comes cutting oneself off from bad things and bad people. A report says that whoever repents but does not put aside bad friends is not a repenter. Whoever repents but does not put aside food and drink is not a repenter. Whoever repents but does not leave his bed and drive sleep from his eyes is not a repenter. Whoever repents but does not spend whatever wealth is left over after his food is not a repenter.

Repentance begins when you free your heart from everything that exists and turn it to the Real, and when you train every drop of blood and piece of flesh in your seven limbs. It goes ahead of the fire that rises from the bottom of Hell, so that today, with the water of your eyes, you do to yourself what the fire would do to you tomorrow. Repentance is also a message sent to you from the Presence:

> "O knight! How long will you wage war? How long will you break the covenant? Come back and make peace! O falcon taken up into the sky, come back, do not go! My fingers hold the end of your thread! O free man, how long have you slept? Wake up, it is morning, and you are thirsty for the wine of yearning. Look, it is time for the morning draught! How long will your heart and your covenant stay broken? It is time to take advice and to repent sincerely."

### In short

- Allah accepts the repentance of those who sin out of "ignorance", which the Companions explained as heedlessness of the end of sin, so even a deliberate sinner can repent, and the ummah agrees on this.
- "Soon after" means any time before death comes into view. The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah accepts repentance as long as the soul has not reached the throat.
- Repentance rests on regret, giving up the sin with a firm resolve, and making amends, such as making up missed prayers and fasts, paying unpaid zakah and returning what belongs to others.
- Repentance is a duty for every person. It is the way of human beings, and failing to repent is the way of devils, and a person who repents is loved by Allah.
- Inwardly, repentance is turning the heart from all else to the Real, and it is Allah's own call back to Himself.

18.text:
This verse shows the limit of repentance: "However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, “Now I repent!” nor those who die as disbelievers. For them We have prepared a painful punishment." The previous verse said when repentance is accepted. This one describes those whose repentance is not accepted, those who go on sinning fearlessly throughout their lives and start offering repentance only when death is standing over them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying"**. These are people who kept running wild with their lives and wasted every chance to repent while there was still time. When death arrives, the pangs of the soul's removal begin and the angels become visible, and then they start to repent. When hope of staying alive disappears, the angel of death comes forward, the soul reaches the throat and then the chest, and it is gradually pulled out. At that point no repentance is accepted and there is no way out of that certain end. Short explanations say the same. Allah does not turn in mercy to those who persist in disobedience, overstepping the limits and insisting on it, and who do not stop until they are dying and then say they regret it. The Arabic conveys that forgiveness, the overlooking of sins, is not for them. That is the state that lies outside what the previous verse called "soon".

**"and then cry, “Now I repent!”"**. When such a person sees his predicament and says, "Now I repent," it would not help him, and it will not be accepted from him. Allah has likewise decided that no repentance will be taken from the people of the earth on the day the sun rises in the west. As He said: "On the Day your Lord’s signs arrive, belief will not benefit those who did not believe earlier or those who did no good through their faith" (6:158). It is similar to the people who, when they saw the punishment, said, "˹Now˺ we believe in Allah alone and reject what we had been associating with Him" (40:84).

This is very much like Firʿawn (Pharaoh) and his people. While they were drowning, they cried out that they now believed in the Lord of Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron). They were told that their declaration of faith meant nothing at that point, since the time for it was over.

**"nor those who die as disbelievers"**. When a disbeliever dies as a disbeliever and polytheist, his sorrow and his repentance will not benefit him. If he tried to ransom himself with the earth full of gold, it would not be accepted from him. Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Ibn ʿAbbās said that this part was revealed about the people of shirk, those who ascribe partners to Allah. What is a declaration of faith worth when it is made in the middle of a struggle with death, with the soul being pulled from the body? Such a confession is out of tune with the time and is worthless, because their punishment is already prepared. In the Hereafter too, if they repent when they see the punishment, it will not be accepted.

Aḥmad recorded, from Usāmah ibn Salmān, that Abū Dharr heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

> "Allah accepts His servant's repentance, or forgives His servant, as long as the veil does not drop."

They asked, "And what is the dropping of the veil?" He said:

> "When the soul is taken while the person is a polytheist."

**"For them We have prepared a painful punishment"**. It is a severe, eternal and enormous torment. One explanation says that these words came down about Ṭuʿmah and the men with him who had abandoned Islam.

### The inner reading

Repentance is accepted until death is present, and on the level of learning, one must repent before death, even if it is only for a moment. On the level of practice, one must repent before the soul has formed the habit of looking at itself and worshipping itself. When a person is satisfied with himself and gazes at himself out of habit, the door of repentance is closed against him and the water of rescue is held back. Stop being a companion of those who nurse the self and worship their own habits. Kiss the dust beneath the feet of those who have given up the self.

Not everyone who has repented on the road of the Sharīʿah, and so reached pardon and forgiveness, has reached truthfulness in love, on the level of the Ḥaqīqah, the inner reality. Dāwūd (David), the prophet, wept and pleaded for a long time. At last Allah said to him, "O Dāwūd! Why do you weep when I have forgiven you, made your opponents content and accepted your repentance?" He said, "Lord, I know. But give me back the sweet moments I had in Your company and the breaths I had with You in seclusion!" Allah said, "Dāwūd, take heed. That is a love that has passed." So let the eyes weep freely from now on, since the days of clear joy cannot come back. A line of verse says:

> Oh pain, oh regret! Of all that standing and sitting in prayer I have dust on my head and wind in my hand.

### In short

- Repentance is not accepted from those who keep sinning knowingly until death arrives and then say, "Now I repent", nor from those who die as disbelievers.
- Once the soul is being pulled out, or once the signs of the Hour appear, it is too late, as it was too late for Firʿawn when he was drowning.
- The last part is about the people of shirk, as ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Ibn ʿAbbās said. The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah accepts repentance until the veil drops, which is when the soul is taken from a polytheist.
- Inwardly, repentance must come before the self becomes a habit of self-worship, and even the repentant long for the sweetness they once had, as Dāwūd did.

19.text:
After a series of rulings about women, the surah turns to the excesses women suffered at the hands of husbands and even of heirs: "O believers! It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will or mistreat them to make them return some of the dowry ˹as a ransom for divorce˺—unless they are found guilty of adultery. Treat them fairly. If you happen to dislike them, you may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing." The aim is to correct disorders in society. The husbands are addressed in particular in the words "treat them fairly", and 4:20 and 4:21 conclude the subject.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! It is not permissible for you to inherit women against their will"**. Ibn ʿAbbās described the old practice in a report recorded by al-Bukhārī. When a man died, his male relatives had the right to do as they wished with his wife. One of them might marry her, give her in marriage, or stop her from marrying, since they had more right to her than her own family. This verse was revealed about that practice. In pre-Islamic times they could also marry the woman without a dowry, or marry her off and keep the dowry themselves. They could stop her from marrying until she surrendered whatever she had inherited, or until her death left them free to take her estate. One explanation specifies that the women meant here were those of one's fathers. Another explanation gives the cases that led to the verse. It was said to be about Muḥsin ibn Abī Qays al-Anṣārī and Kabshah bint Maʿan al-Anṣāriyyah, since before Islam they used to inherit the women of their fathers. If a widow was rich and beautiful, the eldest son married her without any dowry. If she was neither rich, young nor beautiful, he did not marry her. He left her untouched until she bought her freedom with her own money.

The word "against their will" is read in two ways by reciters, as karhan or kurhan, with the same sense. It is not meant as a condition, as if inheriting women would be fine with their consent. It states the fact. To take over the life and property of women as a self-appointed owner, with no legal or rational basis, could only ever be by force. No woman in her normal senses would agree to it, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ points out. The Sharīʿah does not treat her approval as valid here. If a woman out of her mind agreed to be owned by someone, Islamic law would not allow it.

**"or mistreat them to make them return some of the dowry ˹as a ransom for divorce˺"**. Allah forbids harshness toward a wife that is meant to force her to hand back all or part of her dowry, or to surrender one of her rights under pressure and oppression. The Arabic says "do not prevent them", and this includes stopping a divorced woman from marrying again in order to take back what you or a relative gave her. Some husbands, though they had divorced her, would not let the woman marry again, so that she would break down and give back the dowry or forgo what was still owed. Both returning a dowry already paid and giving up an unpaid one are forbidden (ḥarām) when forced. Money or property taken this way is not lawful for the man, and no right is forgiven by it.

The same applies to gifts. What was given to the wife as a gift, and made hers, cannot be taken back by her husband or his heirs. This rule covers only what was handed over to her as an owner. If something was lent for temporary use, such as jewellery, without making her the owner, it does not become part of her ownership, and asking for it back is not forbidden.

**"unless they are found guilty of adultery"**. The Arabic word is fāḥishah, an open lewd act. Saʿīd ibn Abī Hilāl, Zayd ibn Aslam, as-Suddī, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Abū Qilābah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, ash-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said that it means illicit sex. So if the wife commits adultery, the husband may take back her dowry. He may also make things hard for her until she gives it back in return for a khulʿ, a divorce she buys. In Sūrat al-Baqarah Allah says: "It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah" (2:229).

Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah and Ibn ʿAbbās took fāḥishah to mean disobedience and defiance. ʿĀʾishah is also reported to have understood it this way, as insolence and indecent abuse toward the husband. Abū Qilābah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī took it here to mean immodesty and adultery. Ibn Jarīr chose the view that the word is general and covers all these things: adultery, disobedience, defiance, rudeness and the like. According to him, the husband may make things hard for a wife who does any of these until she gives up all or part of her rights and he separates from her, and this view is good. Other explanations say the same. If she does something clearly shameful that forces the husband to think of divorce, it is her fault, and he has the right to keep her in the marriage until he gets back what he gave her or she gives up the unpaid dower. Where fornication is established by witnesses, one explanation adds, the old penalty was imprisonment, and that was later replaced by the verse on stoning. If a woman does this, the husband may force her to buy her release or to give up her dowry.

**"Treat them fairly"**. This is to speak kindly to them, treat them well and make yourself pleasing to them as far as you can, as you would like them to do the same for you. Allah said in another verse: "Women have rights similar to those of men equitably" (2:228). Others explain it as being decent in speaking to them and in providing for them and housing them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "The best of you is the one who is best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family."

### The Prophet's ﷺ way with his wives

It was the Messenger's ﷺ habit to be kind and cheerful with his wives, to joke with them, to be gentle, to spend on them and to laugh with them. He raced ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Faithful, out of kindness toward her. ʿĀʾishah said that he raced her and she won, before she put on weight. Later she raced him again, and he won, and he said, "This one is for that one."

Sometimes, while he was in one wife's house, all of his wives would gather there and eat together before returning to their own homes. He and his wife slept in the same bed, and he took off his upper garment and slept in his lower garment. After the ʿIshāʾ prayer and before sleeping, he would talk with the wife whose night it was. Allah says: "Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever has hope in Allah and the Last Day, and remembers Allah often" (33:21).

### What lay behind the old ways

The most glaring injustice before Islam was that men acted as owners of the life and property of women. A woman taken in marriage was passed on like a piece of property to her husband's heirs after his death. They became her new owners and the inheritors of her property too. They could marry her, or give her in marriage to someone else for a payment. A son of the husband by another wife could marry her himself after his father's death. When a living human being is treated as property, what happens to ordinary property is easy to imagine. This one basic social ill caused hundreds of other unjust practices, some of which follow.

If a woman received a share of an inheritance or a gift from her parents, she stayed deprived of it. Everything given in her name was devoured by the men of her husband's house. If she somehow came into possession of her share, the men stopped her from remarrying, so that she could not take it out of the house. They wanted her to die there and leave her property for them to take.

In some places a husband disliked his wife for reasons of whim and not because of any fault in her. He no longer treated her as a wife, but he did not release her by divorce. His aim was to wear her down until she returned the jewellery and dower money he had handed over, or, if he had not yet paid them, dropped her claim before she could hope to be released. After the husband died, his heirs would not allow his widow to remarry, either to protect an inflated sense of honour or to release her only after taking something for themselves.

All of this rested on one assumption, that a man owns the woman's property and her very life. The Qur'an struck at the root of the evil. It declared that it is not lawful to take women as inheritance by force.

The Qur'an did not use an ordinary prohibitive command here. It said that this is not lawful for you. Along with stressing how serious the sin is, this may point to a ruling. If a man marries an adult woman without her consent, the marriage is not lawful. In fact it is void. It does not create a husband-and-wife relationship, and the rules of inheritance and lineage do not follow from it.

### A call, an admonishment, an allusion

The words of the verse can be read as five things. "O" is the call, "you" is the admonishment, "who" is the allusion, "have faith" is the witness, and the rest is the ruling. The ruling means that women are weak and are held beneath your strictness. Do not torment them, and do not dominate them through scheming and deceit. Do not be harsh, and do not demand of them what the Sharīʿah does not approve. Live with them honourably, with the teachings of the religion, and model your manners on the character of those who submit to Allah. Show them the road of religion and teach them the manners of a Muslim and the Sharīʿah. Protect them from the Fire, as Allah says in another place: "O believers! Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones" (66:6). Keep the courtesy of companionship and put up with some hurt from them, but do not load them with the burden of serving you.

Outwardly the verse speaks of women, but by allusion it speaks of all Muslims. It means: watch out that you never see yourself as having a due from any other Muslim or a superiority over him. Do not expect people above you to wait on you, and do not impose yourself on people below you. Do not bully the weak, but be considerate to them, comfort them and stay close to them. A revelation came to Dāwūd (David): "O Dāwūd, if you see someone broken on My road, or someone whose heart is lost in My work, take care to serve him." The passage breaks off there.

### "You may hate something which Allah turns into a great blessing"

Your patience in keeping wives whom you dislike has good rewards for you in this life and in the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAbbās said that it means the husband may come to feel compassion for his wife and Allah gives him a child through her, and that child carries enormous good. Others say the same: Allah may give you a righteous child from her. An authentic hadith says:

> "No believing man should hate a believing woman. If he dislikes one trait in her, he will surely like another."

The advice is meant for husbands and wives, but it is general guidance too. The Qur'an often gives guidance on one specific matter and sets down advice of a general nature that concerns a person's whole life. Living together is an essential condition of human life, because no one can survive alone. Since temperaments differ, irritations will inevitably arise. The only workable approach is to overlook complaints, avoid friction and work to keep the peace. A person often notices a fault in his companion and becomes annoyed. If he reflects, he will see that few situations lack an unfavourable side. Hardships can be a test of patience. Sometimes they push a person to turn to Allah in repentance, and sometimes their very vexation teaches an important lesson.

### Property and people are different

The heirs of a dead man may inherit his property. But his widow is not part of the estate, to be handled however they decide. Property has no feelings and is a proper thing to inherit. Human beings have their own feelings and independent existence, and they have the right to decide their own future. If a woman has some physical or temperamental flaw, it should be tolerated, so that she has the chance to use her other gifts to play her part in building the household. A person should overlook her unpleasant aspects and try to get along. The secret of the progress and strength of any family or society is that its members overlook each other's faults and give everyone the chance to use his or her abilities. Those who take the way of patience and tolerance in this world for Allah's sake are the ones who will be admitted to Paradise.

When someone does not like his life partner and decides to separate instead of putting up with her, he often exaggerates the other's faults to justify his decision. Charges are made up so that the weaker person becomes anxious and leaves. In the same way, false reasons are put forward while cutting the marriage bond. All of this goes against the covenant. A covenant is sacred to Allah, and whether it is written or unwritten, it is binding in its essence. It applies equally to both sides and leaves them no choice.

### In short

- It is not lawful to inherit women as property. A widow is not part of an estate, and no one may marry her, marry her off or stop her marrying against her will.
- A husband may not make life hard for a wife to make her give back her dowry or give up what he owes. The exception is a clear fāḥishah, understood as adultery, or as disobedience and abuse.
- Husbands are told to live with their wives honourably. The Prophet ﷺ was the best example, with kindness, play and racing ʿĀʾishah.
- A dislike may hide a blessing, such as a righteous child. The general lesson is to be patient with the people we live with.
- Inwardly, the verse tells every Muslim never to see himself as owed service or as above another.

20.text:
This verse goes on to the dowry: "If you desire to replace a wife with another and you have given the former ˹even˺ a stack of gold ˹as a dowry˺, do not take any of it back. Would you ˹still˺ take it unjustly and very sinfully?" If the woman has shown no defiance or immodesty, and the husband simply wants to marry another woman, he may not claim anything back from her in return for the divorce, even though he gave her a lot. He may not force her to give up the dowry still owed either. She has done nothing wrong, and the cause that makes the dower due has already taken place, since they married and were alone together.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you desire to replace a wife with another"**. One explanation says: if you wish to marry a woman and divorce the wife you already have, or to marry another woman in addition to her. Another says that a man may divorce one woman and replace her, but he may not take anything back. The Arabic phrase also fits the case of exchanging one wife for another.

**"and you have given the former ˹even˺ a stack of gold ˹as a dowry˺"**. The Arabic word is qinṭār, a very large sum. One explanation calls it a hundredweight. The meaning of qinṭār was explained in the discussion of Sūrat Āl ʿImrān. The verse clearly shows that the dowry may be large. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb used to discourage large dowries, but later changed his view.

Aḥmad recorded that Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ as-Sulamī heard ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb say:

> "Do not make dowries for women too large. If that had been an honour in this world or a part of taqwa, the Prophet ﷺ would have had more right to it than you. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never gave any of his wives, and none of his daughters received, more than twelve ūqiyah. A man used to pay a large dowry and so hide hostility toward his wife."

Aḥmad and the collectors of the Sunan collected this hadith through various chains, and at-Tirmidhī said it is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā recorded that Masrūq said that ʿUmar stood on the minbar of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked, "O people, why do you go to extremes with women's dowries?" He reminded them that the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions paid four hundred dirhams or less, and that if paying more had been part of taqwa or an honour, the people would not have outdone them. "So I do not want to hear of a man paying more than four hundred dirhams," he said. He came down from the minbar, and a woman of Quraysh said to him, "O Leader of the Faithful, you have forbidden people to pay more than four hundred dirhams in a dowry?" He said, "Yes." She said, "Have you not heard what Allah revealed in the Qur'an?" He said, "Which part?" She said, "Have you not heard Allah's words, 'and you have given the former a stack of gold'?" He said, "O Allah, forgive me." He went back and stood on the minbar and said, "I had forbidden you to pay more than four hundred dirhams in dowries. So let each man pay from his money what he likes." The chain of this report is strong.

**"do not take any of it back"**. This forbids taking back any part of what was given. Taking it back would be an injustice and a clear sin. Another explanation says that taking back what was given would be an act of wrong and a plain transgression.

**"Would you ˹still˺ take it unjustly and very sinfully?"** The wrongdoing is described in stages. The first stage is in these words, which ask whether you want to take it by false charge and open sin. This looks back to 4:19, which laid down that a husband has no right to take back the dowry unless his wife has done a shameful act. By that rule, if you take back the dowry from your wife, you are implying that she did a shameful act, because that is the only case where your claim would be right. Since she did not, your claim is a false accusation, and that is an open sin. In Arabic the two words for "unjustly" and "sinfully" are put in the accusative, as a description of how the taking is done. The question is asked as a rebuke and a rejection of such a claim.

### The inner reading

This verse is the full realisation of generosity in the religion of friendship, and it smooths the foundation of chivalry. It is as though Allah says, "Do not add to the cruelty of separation by taking back a woman's livelihood. That is no act of the generous, and the chivalrous would be ashamed of it. You have already left the scar of parting on a poor woman's heart, so do not also cut her hand off from her means of support. Taking back what you gave would put a scar on a scar."

Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī once divorced a wife and afterward sent her a great deal of money. He said of her, "The trial of our separation is enough. I must not put the suffering of poverty on her as well." They say the money was 40,000 dirhams. The woman threw the money on the ground and said, "Paltry goods from a departed lover!"

### In short

- A husband who wants to replace a wife may not take back any part of the dowry he gave her, however large, because she has done no wrong and the marriage has been consummated.
- Taking it back would amount to accusing her of a shameful act, and that is why the verse calls it an open sin.
- The verse shows that a dowry may be large. ʿUmar first tried to limit it to four hundred dirhams, and gave way when a woman of Quraysh reminded him of this verse.
- Inwardly, a generous person does not add to the pain of parting by taking back what he gave, as Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī showed.

21.text:
The verse gives a second reason why the dowry cannot be taken back. It follows 4:19, which allowed the husband to claim it back only when his wife had done a clearly shameful act, and 4:20, which called any other claim an open sin: "And how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately and she has taken from you a firm commitment?"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately"**. The question means: how can you take back the dowry from a woman you have been with, and who has been with you? As-Suddī, Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās and several others took it to mean sexual intercourse, which validates the dowry. Other explanations speak of the love, enjoyment and sharing of secrets that has passed between the couple, and say that greed for wealth that is rightfully hers after all of this is forbidden and shameful. If the dowry was given against the marriage, she certainly deserves it, and it is hers now because she gave herself to her husband. To think it could be returned makes no sense. If the money was given as a gift, it cannot be returned either. What spouses give each other as gifts cannot be taken back, and such a claim is neither permitted by the Sharīʿah nor enforced by law. The marriage bond itself prevents the taking back of what was given as a gift.

**"and she has taken from you a firm commitment"**. This is the covenant of marriage, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. It is the marriage tie, which is solemnly witnessed in the name of Allah before a gathering of people after a khuṭbah. One explanation says that Allah took from men, when they married women, a firm pledge that they would either keep them in goodness or release them in kindness. Another explanation says that through this word of Allah and His sacred law, the women became lawful for the men. The earlier companionship has a firm sanctity, so out of respect for what is due to it, a man should stop and keep to what the covenant requires.

### The couple who swore oaths of mulāʿanah

A report in the two Ṣaḥīḥs shows the principle at work. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said three times to a couple who were swearing oaths of mulāʿanah, "Allah knows that one of you is a liar. Will either of you repent?" The man said, "O Messenger of Allah, my money," meaning the dowry he had given his wife. The Messenger ﷺ said:

> "You have no money. If you spoke the truth, the dowry is in return for what you enjoyed of her. If you lied, then the money is even further from you."

### The covenant of marriage

The Prophet ﷺ spoke of this covenant in the speech he gave at the Farewell Ḥajj. Muslim recorded from Jābir that he said:

> "Be kind to women. You took them by Allah's covenant, and you made them lawful to you by Allah's word."

To sum up this verse (4:21), once the covenant has been made and closeness in private has brought the couple together, to force the woman to give back what was given to her is plain injustice and tyranny. All Muslims must stay away from it.

### In short

- A husband cannot take back the dowry after intimacy, because she earned it and became its owner.
- Gifts between spouses are not recoverable either, since the marriage bond prevents it.
- The "firm commitment" is the covenant of marriage, sworn in Allah's name. The Prophet ﷺ told men at the Farewell Ḥajj to be kind to women because they took them by Allah's covenant.
- Forcing a wife to give back what she was given is open injustice.

22.text:
The verse now goes back to another practice from the days of ignorance: "Do not marry former wives of your fathers—except what was done previously. It was indeed a shameful, despicable, and evil practice." These verses give the rules about women who are forbidden in marriage. Some are forbidden forever and never become lawful under any condition. The others are not permanently forbidden, and they become lawful in certain circumstances. The permanently forbidden are of three kinds: by blood, by fosterage and by marriage. The kind mentioned at the end stays forbidden only until the woman is married to someone else.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not marry former wives of your fathers"**. In the days of ignorance, people saw nothing wrong in marrying their father's wife after he died. Allah forbade this shameful practice, an evil that brings His anger. How can a man go on calling a woman "mother" for years and then sink so low as to make her his wife after his father's death? The prohibition is made out of honour and respect for fathers, so their sons may not have relations with their wives after they die. A woman becomes forbidden to her husband's son as soon as the marriage contract is made, and there is a consensus on this.

The ruling is that marrying a father's lawfully wedded wife is unlawful. The verse does not require that the father had consummated the marriage. The fact that he married her is enough to forbid her to the son, and she will never be lawful for him. In the same way, it is not correct for a father to marry his son's wife, even if the son's marriage was only a formal nikāḥ and she has not yet come to live with him.

Ibn ʿAbbās described the situation in a report recorded by Ibn Jarīr. In the days of ignorance, people forbade what Allah forbids in marriage, except for marrying a stepmother and having two sisters as rival wives. Allah revealed "Do not marry former wives of your fathers" and "nor two sisters together at the same time" (4:23). ʿAṭāʾ and Qatādah are reported to have said the same. So this practice is forbidden for this ummah, and it is disgraced as an awful sin.

**"except what was done previously"**. The past is past, and what was done in the age of ignorance is forgiven. One explanation says that you will not be held to account for it. The saying that what has passed has passed is not just about marriage. It is a general rule of wisdom. Whenever a change takes place in life, in a family or in a nation, many past affairs look wrong by the new standards. Orders based on things that no longer matter cause endless problems. The right approach is to forget the past and put one's effort into reforming the present and the future.

**"It was indeed a shameful, despicable, and evil practice"**. Similarly Allah says in other verses: "Do not come near indecencies, openly or secretly" (6:151), the warning against al-fawāḥish, and "Do not go near adultery. It is truly a shameful deed and an evil way" (17:32). In this verse He adds a further word, maqtan, which means offensive. It is a sin in itself, and it makes a son hate his father after he marries his wife. People usually dislike those who married a woman before them. This is one reason the Mothers of the Faithful were not allowed to marry anyone after the Messenger ﷺ. They are the Mothers of the Faithful because they married the Messenger, who is like a father to the believers. His claim is greater than any father's claim, and love for him comes before each person's love for himself. Another explanation says that maqtan means it results in severe hatred from Allah.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said that maqtan means that Allah will hate the person, and "an evil way" is for those who take this way. Whoever does this has turned away from the religion. He deserves the death penalty and the seizure of his property for the Muslim treasury. Aḥmad and the compilers of the Sunan record from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib that his uncle Abū Burdah was dispatched by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to deal with a man who had married his stepmother, with orders to put him to death and take his property.

### The people it was revealed about

The verse is said to have been revealed about Muḥsin ibn Abī Qays al-Anṣārī, and Allah then showed them which women are forbidden to marry. Another account names several men. Ḥiṣn ibn Abī al-Qays married the wife of his father, Kubayshah bint Maʿn. Al-Aswad ibn Khalaf married his father's wife. Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah married his father's wife Fākhitah bint al-Aswad ibn al-Muṭṭalib. Manẓūr ibn Zabbān married his father's wife Mulaykah bint Khārijah.

Ashʿath ibn Sawwār said that when Abū Qays, one of the righteous men of Madīnah, died, his son Qays proposed to his father's wife. She said to him, "I consider you my son. I will consult the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and see what he commands." She went and told him, and Allah revealed this verse.

### The inner reading

The verse points to the protection of honour and keeping within the limits of respect. If a man naturally hates that another man should take his wife to bed, then sons are all the more forbidden to disregard their fathers' rights and seek to bed their fathers' wives.

### In short

- A man may not marry a woman who was lawfully married to his father, whether or not the father consummated the marriage, and a father may not marry his son's wife.
- What was done before the revelation was forgiven. The past is past, and it is wise to put one's effort into the present and the future.
- Allah calls this practice shameful, offensive and an evil way, and one explanation holds that a man who does it has turned away from the religion.
- The verse is linked to several men of Madīnah who had married their fathers' widows, among them Muḥsin ibn Abī Qays.
- Inwardly, it protects honour and respect, as no son should do to his father what no man would want done to himself.

23.text:
This verse completes the list of women who are forbidden in marriage: "˹Also˺ forbidden to you for marriage are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal and maternal aunts, your brother’s daughters, your sister’s daughters, your foster-mothers, your foster-sisters, your mothers-in-law, your stepdaughters under your guardianship if you have consummated marriage with their mothers—but if you have not, then you can marry them—nor the wives of your own sons, nor two sisters together at the same time—except what was done previously. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:23).

It sets out the degrees of women who can never be married, because of blood, because of suckling or because of marriage. Ibn ʿAbbās reported that Allah said, "I have forbidden you seven kinds of relatives by blood and seven by marriage," and then recited this verse. Aṭ-Ṭabarī recorded the same words from him about the seven degrees of blood relation and the seven of marriage.

Many natural desires make themselves felt in human beings, and sexual desire is one of them. Islamic law sets a limit for every human feeling, and it has set limits for sexual relations as well. Only the union of a man and a woman that is made through a solemn and recognised social agreement, which is marriage, is valid. Along with satisfying a natural desire, the law requires an atmosphere of chastity in family life. So certain close relatives are declared forbidden, to keep them beyond and above sexual desire. Some of the women in this verse are forbidden forever and can never become lawful under any condition. Others are forbidden only for a time.

### Phrase by phrase

**"your mothers, your daughters, your sisters"**. Marrying one's own mother is unlawful, and the word "mothers" takes in all grandmothers, on the father's side and the mother's. "Daughters" means one's real daughter, the daughter of one's daughter and the daughter of one's son. In short, a daughter, granddaughter or great-granddaughter, whether through a son or a daughter, is unlawful. Adopted children are different. Marrying an adopted son or daughter, or their children, is permissible, as long as it is not unlawful for some other reason. A girl born from adultery is treated as a daughter, and marrying her is not valid. Marrying a stepdaughter, meaning a daughter the wife brought from another husband, has rules of its own that come later.

Sisters are forbidden whether they are real sisters, half-sisters on the father's side only (ʿallātī) or half-sisters on the mother's side only (akhyāfī).

**"your paternal and maternal aunts, your brother’s daughters, your sister’s daughters"**. A paternal aunt is the real sister of one's father, or his half-sister from the father's side or from the mother's side. All three kinds are forbidden. A maternal aunt is the sister of one's mother, in the same three kinds. Nieces are also forbidden, whether the brother or sister is a real sibling or a half-sibling of either type. Aunts include the sisters of one's grandfathers and grandmothers, and nieces include their children, as one explanation spells out.

**"your foster-mothers, your foster-sisters"**. A woman who nursed you is forbidden to you, just as the mother who bore you is. A woman who nursed one of your siblings is, in the same way, a mother to the whole bond, and her daughters become your sisters through suckling. The details are given in the section below.

**"your mothers-in-law"**. The mother of one's wife is forbidden to him as soon as the marriage contract is made, whether or not he ever had relations with his wife. The word "mothers" includes the wife's grandmothers, whether on her mother's or father's side, by blood or by suckling. The same applies to the mother of a woman he slept with thinking she was his wife, or with whom he committed adultery, or whom he touched with desire. Short explanations of the verse say the same: the mother-in-law is forbidden whether or not the marriage with her daughter was consummated.

**"your stepdaughters under your guardianship if you have consummated marriage with their mothers—but if you have not, then you can marry them"**. When a man marries a woman and has relations with her after the marriage, her daughter from another husband becomes forbidden to him, and so do her granddaughters, on either side. If he divorced the mother before ever being with her, her daughter and granddaughter are not forbidden to him. But if, after the marriage contract, he touches his wife with desire, or looks at her private parts with desire, that too counts as having relations with her, and it makes her daughter forbidden. "Having gone in unto them" means sexual relations, as Ibn ʿAbbās and several others said.

The words "your women" are general. They cover not only a lawfully wedded wife. If a man had relations with a woman who was not truly his wife, either because he wrongly believed that she was, or through adultery, the daughter and granddaughter of that woman also become forbidden to him.

The words "under your guardianship" describe the usual situation, a girl brought up in the stepfather's house. They do not limit the ruling. The Arabic term rabāʾib, the plural of rabībah, means a wife's daughter from another husband who is being raised in one's care. The majority of scholars say that the stepdaughter is forbidden to her stepfather, if he has consummated his marriage to her mother, whether or not she was in his care.

**"nor the wives of your own sons"**. The wife of one's own son is forbidden. The word "son" also covers grandsons, on the father's or mother's side, so their wives are forbidden too. The words "from your own loins" are in the verse to exclude the adopted son. Marrying his wife is lawful. A foster son, though, is treated like a son by birth, and his wife is forbidden.

**"nor two sisters together at the same time"**. It is also forbidden to have two sisters together as wives. They may be real sisters, half-sisters on the father's side or half-sisters on the mother's side. They may be sisters by blood or by suckling. Allah prohibits taking two sisters as rival wives, or as rival female servants. If one sister has been divorced, a man may marry the other, but only after the first one's waiting period, the ʿiddah, has ended. A marriage during the ʿiddah is not permitted.

**"except what was done previously"**. Whatever happened in the days of ignorance is not held against anyone. The same words appear in 4:22 and carry the same sense. Now that people have accepted Islam, their past deeds are not counted, but they must keep away from those practices from now on.

**"Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"**. Anything people did wrongly before Islam is overlooked by Allah once they embrace Islam, and they can be sure He will turn to them with the full reach of His mercy. Another explanation says that He forgives what happened in the days of ignorance and shows mercy for what happens in Islam, if they repent.

### How suckling creates a prohibition

Ibn ʿAbbās's words show that the verse treats milk kinship like blood kinship. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded that ʿĀʾishah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Suckling makes unlawful what birth makes unlawful."

In another wording recorded by Muslim: "Suckling establishes the same prohibitions that blood does." Another report in Mishkāt (page 273), from Muslim, says that Allah has made unlawful through suckling what He has made unlawful through kinship. The principle gives a whole network. When a woman nurses a boy or girl in the nursing period, she is their foster-mother and her husband is their foster-father. Her children become their brothers and sisters, her sisters become their maternal aunts, her husband's brothers become their uncles on the father's side, and his sisters become their paternal aunts. Every marriage that is forbidden between blood relatives becomes equally forbidden between milk relatives.

Scholars differ on how much nursing is needed. Less than five separate feedings do not create the prohibition, according to one view. Muslim recorded that ʿĀʾishah said that among the verses revealed, there was "Ten feedings make marriage unlawful", and that it was later replaced by five, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died while this wording was still recited as part of the Qur'an. A hadith from Sahlah bint Suhayl says that the Messenger ﷺ told her to nurse Sālim, the freed slave of Abū Ḥudhayfah, five times. Another explanation also names five feedings within the first two years, and adds that the prohibition covers the foster-sisters' daughters. Among the Ḥanafī jurists, the quantity and the number of feedings make no difference, and the prohibition stands in every case. This is the view stated in the explanation of the word for foster-mothers.

Scholars also differ on the age. The nursing must take place at the usual time in early childhood. The Prophet ﷺ said that fosterage is only from hunger, meaning that the prohibition applies when the child has no way to grow except by nursing. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded it. It must happen before the age of two, as in the verse in Sūrat al-Baqarah that says mothers breastfeed their children for two whole years (2:233). According to Imām Abū Ḥanīfah the period runs from birth until two and a half years. Other jurists, including his own students Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad, say two years only. If a boy or girl is nursed after that, no prohibition arises.

The rulings that follow from this are as follows:

1. If a boy and a girl were nursed by the same woman, they cannot marry each other. Marrying the daughter of a foster-brother or a foster-sister is also not allowed.
2. It is lawful to marry the birth mother of a foster-brother or foster-sister. It is also lawful to marry the foster-mother of one's own sister's foster-sister, or the foster-sister of one's own sister.
3. The prohibition arises if the child takes the milk during the nursing period through the mouth or the nose. If the milk is given in any other way, or injected, it does not arise.
4. No milk except that of the woman nursing the child creates fosterage. Milk of animals or of men does not.
5. If the milk is mixed with medicine or with the milk of a goat, cow or buffalo, the prohibition arises only if the woman's milk is the larger part or at least equal. If it is less, it does not arise.
6. If a man's breasts happen to produce milk, it does not create a prohibition.
7. If a woman lets a child hold her nipple in its mouth and it is not certain that the child swallowed any milk, no prohibition arises, because a prohibition is not established when the actual nursing is doubtful.
8. If a man marries a woman and another woman claims she nursed them both, and the couple both confirm it, the marriage is ruled invalid. If they both deny it, they are not required to separate. If the woman who made the claim appears God-fearing and practising, it is better for them to separate by divorce.
9. The testimony of two practising Muslims is needed to prove a prohibition through suckling. One man or one woman is not enough. But as it is a serious matter, on which the lawfulness of a whole married life depends, caution is always wise. Some jurists rule that if someone intends to marry a woman and a single practising Muslim testifies that they are foster brother and sister, they may not marry. If one witness comes forward after they have married, it is safe and prudent to separate.
10. By the usual rules of evidence, one man and two women count as two male witnesses, so a foster relationship is proved if one man and two women testify to the nursing.

### Why the Prophet ﷺ could not marry Umm Salamah's daughter

The two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Umm Ḥabībah said, "O Messenger of Allah, marry my sister, the daughter of Abū Sufyān." In one wording the sister is named ʿAzzah bint Abī Sufyān. He asked, "Would you like me to do that?" She said, "I would not give you up for anything. But the person I would most like to share the good with is my sister." He said, "That is not lawful for me." She said, "We were told that you want to marry the daughter of Abū Salamah." He asked, "The daughter of Umm Salamah?" She said, "Yes." He said:

> "Even if she were not my stepdaughter in my care, she would still not be lawful for me. She is the daughter of my brother through suckling, since Thuwaybah nursed me and Abū Salamah. So do not offer me your daughters or your sisters."

In another wording recorded by al-Bukhārī he said, "Had I not married Umm Salamah, her daughter would not have been lawful for me anyway." So he said that his marriage to Umm Salamah was the real reason for the prohibition.

### Is the wife of an adopted son lawful?

The verse forbids the wives of "your sons who are of your own loins". That excludes adopted sons, since adoption was common in the days of ignorance. Allah says: "So when Zaid totally lost interest in ˹keeping˺ his wife, We gave her to you in marriage, so that there would be no blame on the believers for marrying the ex-wives of their adopted sons after their divorce" (33:37).

Ibn Jurayj said he asked ʿAṭāʾ about the words "the wives of your sons who are of your own loins". ʿAṭāʾ said they were told that when the Prophet ﷺ married the former wife of Zayd, who had been his adopted son before Islam stopped that practice, the idolaters in Makkah criticised him. Allah revealed these words, and also: "Nor does He regard your adopted children as your real children" (33:4), and: "Muḥammad is not the father of any of your men" (33:40).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad said the two phrases, "the wives of your sons" and "your wives' mothers", are wide in their reach. Ṭāwūs, Ibrāhīm, az-Zuhrī and Makḥūl explained them the same way. The two phrases take in these women whether or not the marriage was consummated, and there is a consensus on the ruling.

There is a doubt here. Why is the former wife of one's foster son forbidden to him, as most scholars hold, though they are not related by blood? The answer is a saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Suckling makes unlawful what blood relations make unlawful."

### Two sisters, and a woman with her aunt

No one may take or keep two sisters as rival wives. This is the consensus of the scholars among the Companions, their followers and the Imams, past and present.
