Whoever accepts Islam while married to two sisters is given the choice to keep one and divorce the other. Aḥmad recorded a statement of aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Fayruz, who quoted his father: "I became Muslim while married to two sisters, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered me to divorce one of them." Ibn Firoz ad-Daylamī related in the same way from his father that when he became Muslim, he had two sisters as wives, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to part with one by divorce and keep the other. This is in Mishkāt (page 274).

These reports show that, just as it is not lawful after accepting Islam to marry one's father's wife or to join two sisters in marriage, it is also not lawful to keep up such marriages if someone made them before becoming Muslim. Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib said that the Prophet ﷺ sent Abū Burdah ibn Niyar to put to death a man who had married his father's wife.

The Sunnah adds that a man may not marry a woman together with her paternal aunt or her maternal aunt. The Prophet ﷺ said, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded, "Do not combine a woman with her paternal aunt, nor a woman with her maternal aunt." Jurists state a general rule from this. If any two women are such that, were one of them a male, their marriage would be invalid, then those two cannot be combined as wives of one man. According to one explanation, it is permissible to marry each of them separately, or to own both as female slaves, but a man may have relations with only one of them.

### Surrender, not reasons

The allusion in this verse is that the Sharīʿah rests on being a servant, not on one's own effort and reasoning. The law of the religion is handed down, not worked out by reason, and the Sunnah is built on submission, not on looking for causes. Surrender is an easy road. Its home thrives, and its aim is the approval of the All-Merciful. The way of self-exertion and self-determination is hard. Their home is in ruins, and their goal is unwholesome. So leap away from the road of self-exertion and hold to surrender. Avoid self-determination and the hunt for reasons.

Whatever the Sharīʿah has declared forbidden, regard it as forbidden, a decree of Allah's Desire, founded on His Will. If the same thing had been allowed in place of forbidden, it would be just the same, since it would be current in the holy Sharīʿah, with no cause or ambiguity. For He is the Real, and majestic is His majesty. "Allah does what He wills" (3:40), and "Allah commands what He wills" (5:1). He forbids what He wills to whom He wills, and He allows what He wills to whom He wills. His work has no cause, and His decree has no one to object.

### In short

- The verse names the women forbidden in marriage: mothers and grandmothers, daughters and granddaughters, sisters, aunts, nieces, foster-mothers and foster-sisters, mothers-in-law, stepdaughters whose mothers were consummated with, sons' wives, and two sisters together.
- Suckling creates the same prohibitions as blood. Scholars differ on how many feedings and on the age limit, with five feedings within two years in one view and no minimum in the Ḥanafī view, and an upper age of two or two and a half years.
- A mother-in-law is forbidden from the marriage contract onward, while a stepdaughter becomes forbidden only after relations with her mother. The wife of an adopted son is not forbidden, but the wife of a foster son is.
- Two sisters, or a woman and her aunt, may not be married together, and anyone who becomes Muslim with two sisters must part from one.
- What was done before is forgiven, but such marriages must not be kept up. Inwardly, the Sharīʿah calls for surrender and not for hunting for reasons.

24.text:
This verse adds one more group to the list of forbidden women, then opens the door wide for everything else, and it attaches the conditions of dowry and chastity: "Also ˹forbidden are˺ married women—except ˹female˺ captives in your possession. This is Allah’s commandment to you. Lawful to you are all beyond these—as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication. Give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries. It is permissible to be mutually gracious regarding the set dowry. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise."

The earlier verse fixed the permanent prohibitions. The hadiths add a few more, and the verse does not list them. As in the earlier verse, the point behind the rules is that the natural desire between man and woman is allowed only inside a solemn, recognised agreement, in an atmosphere of chastity.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Also ˹forbidden are˺ married women"**. As long as a woman is married to one man, no other man may marry her. The rule covers women who have spouses, whether they are free Muslim women or not. It follows that a woman cannot have more than one husband at the same time. The Sharīʿah is so firm on this that even when a husband divorces his wife or dies, she cannot marry another man until her waiting period, the ʿiddah, has ended.

**"except ˹female˺ captives in your possession"**. The exception covers women acquired in a lawful war. They are permitted after it is certain that they are not pregnant, which means after one menstrual period. This holds even if their husbands are in the enemy camp, in Dār al-Ḥarb, the territory of those at war with the Muslims. When such women were brought to the Islamic state, their marriage to non-Muslim husbands who stayed behind ended with their entry. A Muslim could then marry her, if she was a Christian, a Jew or had accepted Islam. If the head of the Islamic state made her a bondwoman and gave her to a fighter as part of his share of the spoils, he could be with her. In both cases, she had first to go through at least one menstrual period after entering the Islamic state. If she was pregnant by her former husband, the wait lasted until she gave birth.

Two rulings follow. A disbelieving woman who accepts Islam in Dār al-Ḥarb while her husband stays a disbeliever is released from her marriage after three menstrual periods. If a disbelieving woman accepts Islam in Dār al-Islām, the Islamic territory, and her husband remains a disbeliever, the authority should invite the husband to think of accepting Islam. If he refuses, the Muslim judge separates the two. The separation counts as a divorce. She then completes her ʿiddah and is free to marry any Muslim she chooses.

**"This is Allah’s commandment to you"**. The prohibition is one that Allah ordained, so one should hold to His Book, not cross His limits, and stay with His laws and decrees. The unlawfulness of marrying the women He has named is fixed by Him.

**"Lawful to you are all beyond these"**. Women other than the forbidden types named are lawful, as ʿAṭāʾ and others said. Examples are the daughter of a paternal or maternal uncle, the wife of an uncle after his death or divorce, and the wife of an adopted son once he has divorced her or died. If one's wife dies, one may marry her sister. The generality of the words does not mean that marriage is unrestricted. A man may not have more than four wives at the same time, as the opening of the surah has already explained. The verse leaves out some other prohibitions that appear in the hadiths, and the verses themselves hint at them.

**"as long as you seek them with your wealth in a legal marriage, not in fornication"**. The reason the forbidden women are listed is to send people looking for lawful women with their wealth, and to marry them. Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ points out two things from this. First, a marriage cannot exist without a dower, and even if the parties agree to marry with none, a dower is still required. Second, the dower must be something that counts as property, māl. According to the Ḥanafī school, the mahr must not be less than ten dirhams. Some explanations give other senses of "seek with your wealth", one being marrying up to four wives, another being buying female captives with your money, and a third being marrying women for a stated period, zawāj al-mutʿah. The lawfulness of that last practice was later abrogated, as the next sections explain.

The words "in a legal marriage" mean that a man seeks lawful women with his wealth in order to guard his modesty and chastity. This is the crucial purpose of marriage, and it must be achieved only through marriage. Fornicators spend money too, but that spending is plainly unlawful, and enjoying a woman obtained through it is never lawful. The words "not in fornication" do two things. They forbid zinā, and they point out that its only purpose is to chase lust and waste seed on an unlawful pleasure. Its aim is not to have children or preserve the human race. Muslims must stay chaste and use their strength where it belongs, for the good of human procreation, by having a wife in marriage, or a bondwoman if one happens to own one. Another explanation puts it as being with them as legitimate husbands, and not indulging in adultery without proper marriage.

**"Give those you have consummated marriage with their due dowries"**. The Arabic word is istamtaʿtum, from a root meaning to derive benefit. In this verse it means sexual relations. The full dower becomes due when the husband has had that benefit. If, after the contract, the wife never came to live with him and he divorced her before that, the dower he owes drops to half. Once the benefit has been received, payment of the dower is obligatory in every case. Falling short is against the letter and spirit of Muslim law. The universal human sense of honour also says there should be no failure or delay in paying the wife once the marriage has achieved its purpose. The Sharīʿah also gives the woman an extra right. If the dower is to be paid promptly, she may refuse to go to her husband until it has been paid to her. Other verses say the same thing. Allah says "And how could you take it back after having enjoyed each other intimately" (4:21), and tells husbands to give women their dowries (4:4). Elsewhere He forbids taking back anything of what was given (2:229).

**"It is permissible to be mutually gracious regarding the set dowry"**. The fixed dower is not an absolute figure to which nothing can be added or taken away. A husband can add to it of his own accord. The wife, if she wishes, can freely and gladly give up part or all of it. The words also allow a woman to agree freely to put off a dower that was meant to be paid at once. According to Ibn Jarīr's report from al-Ḥaḍramī, some men set a dowry but then fell into financial difficulty, and Allah said that there is no harm concerning mutual agreement after the requirement. If she gives up a part of it, the men may accept it. Short explanations say the same: you are not at fault in agreeing together after the obligation is waived, lowered or raised.

**"Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"**. Two points stand out. First, Allah knows everything. His commands are to be obeyed. If someone acts against them, and even if no judge or ruler or other person finds out, Allah knows all about it, so one must fear Him at all times. Second, His rulings are all based on wisdom. His wisdom is too deep for everyone to grasp. The rules on what is lawful and unlawful must be believed, accepted and obeyed, whether or not one understands the reason. The Creator and Master of the command knows the reason in any case. The words fit well here, after a list of prohibitions. One explanation says that Allah knows the reason for allowing marriage for a fixed term and is wise in making it unlawful later. Another says that He knows what drove people to want it and is wise in forbidding it.

### Why one woman cannot have several husbands

Some people say that if men may have more than one wife, women should be allowed more than one husband. This goes against the verse. Plurality of wives has been recognised in all faiths and societies as a blessing. For a woman, several husbands at one time would be a burden for her and a disgrace for the men involved. It also leaves no way for children to have a sound line of descent. When many men have access to one woman, a child's fatherhood cannot be attributed to any one of them. When lineage cannot be established, there is no one who is made responsible for the mutual rights and duties.

Nature and reason give three more arguments. First, the basic purpose of marriage is to have children. Several women can become pregnant by one man, but one woman cannot become pregnant by several men. She conceives by one only, so the procreative ability of all her husbands but one is wasted. All that is left for them is the satisfaction of desire. Second, a woman is more delicate than a man. For a large part of the year she is not physically able to be intimate. There are times in married life when she cannot give one husband his rights, let alone several. Third, a man is stronger and healthier. If his strength is above average and one wife cannot satisfy him, he should have the chance, by lawful means, to marry two or three. If he is not allowed this, he will go to forbidden ways and ruin society. The likelihood that a woman would cause such ruin is remote.

### The captive women of Awṭās

Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī gave the circumstances in which the exception for captives was revealed. Aḥmad recorded his words: "We took some women captive near Awṭās who already had husbands, and we did not like being with them for that reason. We put the question to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse came down. After that we lived with these women." At-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr and Muslim, in his Ṣaḥīḥ, recorded this wording.

Other reports of the same event add details. In one, the Companions asked, "O Prophet of Allah, how can we be with women when we know their families and their husbands so well?" and the verse came down. In a third, narrated by Abū Saʿīd in a version that mentions Ḥunayn, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent an army to Awṭās on the day of Ḥunayn. The army met the enemy, defeated them and took many women captive. Some of the Companions were uncomfortable with the thought of relations with these captives, since their husbands were idolaters. Allah revealed the verse on this occasion.

### Temporary marriage (mutʿah)

The word in the verse for "have benefited" is from the same root as mutʿah, and this raises the question of temporary marriage. Mutʿah means a marriage that ends on a set date. Mujāhid said that the words "so with those among them whom you have enjoyed, give them their required due" were revealed about mutʿah marriage. The weight of the evidence is against this reading.

The two Ṣaḥīḥs record that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade mutʿah marriage and the eating of the meat of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar. Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ that ar-Rabīʿ ibn Sabrah ibn Maʿbad al-Juhanī said that his father went with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the conquest of Makkah, and that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "O people, I had allowed you mutʿah with women before. Now Allah has forbidden it until the Day of Resurrection. So whoever has any woman in mutʿah, let him release her, and let him not take back anything of what he gave her."

The root of istimtāʿ, to derive benefit, applies to any benefit drawn from a person or from property. The simple meaning in this verse, as the whole Muslim ummah has understood it from the early elders to their successors, is the one given above: sexual relations in a lawful marriage. A group among Muslims, the Shīʿah, holds that the word means conventional mutʿah and that the verse proves it lawful. This is a far-fetched argument that rests only on the shared root, and the verse itself refutes it.

Before Islam, mutʿah was a short-term arrangement in which a man and a woman had a sexual relationship for a fixed period, in return for money or something else. It was never meant to create the lasting rights and duties of marriage, and the Qur'an and Sunnah forbade it clearly. Just before the word in question, the verse says "in a legal marriage, not in fornication". The Qur'an's word here for lust, taken literally, means "flowing water", which points to seeking release out of desire. These words show that the only relationship the Qur'an approves is one aimed at chastity through the lasting bond of marriage, not one that satisfies lust for a short time. A mutʿah contract does not create lasting rights and duties, does not set up a family, and does not aim at children and chastity. It only satisfies desire for a short time. The woman is not even treated as a wife who could inherit, and the man does not count her among his recognised wives. Where the purpose is only gratification, men and women are driven to keep hunting for new partners in a temporary arrangement. So mutʿah can never guarantee modesty and chastity. It is their enemy. For these reasons the words are enough to rule out mutʿah as the verse's meaning.

The author of al-Hidāyah attributed to Imām Mālik the view that mutʿah is permissible. This is wrong, as the commentator on al-Hidāyah and other respected scholars have said. He attributed it by mistake.

Some claim that Ibn ʿAbbās held mutʿah lawful until his last years. This is not so. At-Tirmidhī gave a chapter to mutʿah, with two hadiths. The first is that of ʿAlī about Khaybar, which is also in al-Bukhārī and Muslim. In the second, Ibn ʿAbbās says that mutʿah belonged only to Islam's first period, ending when the verse came down. He added that any private parts other than a wife's or a bondwoman's are unlawful. Ibn ʿAbbās did hold mutʿah permissible for a time. Then, on the good advice of ʿAlī, recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, and under the force of that verse, he gave up his earlier position, as the narration in at-Tirmidhī shows. It has been remarked that the group which holds mutʿah lawful claims to love and follow ʿAlī, and yet on this very question it goes against him, the narrator of the prohibition.

Rūḥ al-Maʿānī reports from Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ that mutʿah was lawful before the battle of Khaybar, that it was made unlawful during it, that it was allowed again at the conquest of Makkah, and that after three days it was declared unlawful forever. The Qur'an also states that those who guard their private parts, except from their wives and their bondwomen, are not blameworthy. That statement is so explicit that it leaves no room for another reading, and it shows plainly that mutʿah is unlawful. Looking for flimsy support in some rare and unreliable recitations is entirely wrong.

To sum up, there is no decisive proof that "you have benefited" refers to conventional mutʿah. It is a remote possibility, and it cannot override the decisive proof just cited. A settled principle of Islamic jurisprudence adds weight here. Where two readings are equally possible, the one that supports the prohibition is preferred.

A time-bound marriage, called nikāḥ muwaqqat, is also unlawful. The difference is only in the wording. Mutʿah is made with the word mutʿah, while a time-bound marriage is made with the word nikāḥ, which is used for ordinary marriage, and then limited to a set period.

### Reason is not the measure of Allah's laws

There are many educated but ignorant people today, among Muslims and non-Muslims, who go around digging for the causes of divine rulings. When they fail to find any, they sidestep the need to comply by saying that the word of Allah, Allah forbid, does not fit the needs of the modern age, or is unsuitable. The closing words of the verse have silenced such people for good. They say: you are ignorant, and your Creator is All-Knowing. You lack understanding, and Allah is All-Wise. Your own reason must never be made the test of what is true.

### The inner reading

When you stay mindful of Allah's limits, the ḥudūd, respect your agreements, the ʿuhūd, and obtain the mutual consent of women in the manner the law lays down, there will be no hostility in it among people. No punishment will follow from the Real, because it is lawful and carries no further restriction.

### In short

- Married women are forbidden, except captive women after a waiting period of one menstrual cycle, as the verse was revealed about the captive women of Awṭās. A woman cannot have two husbands.
- All other women are lawful, up to four wives, if a man seeks them with his wealth in marriage for chastity and not for fornication. A dower is always required, it must be property, and the Ḥanafī school sets its minimum at ten dirhams.
- The full dower is due after consummation and half if the couple divorce before. The couple may agree to add to the dower or to forgo part of it.
- Temporary marriage (mutʿah) was allowed early on and then forbidden for ever, as ʿAlī and others reported. The verse itself, with its words "in a legal marriage", does not support it. A time-bound nikāḥ is also unlawful.
- Allah knows everything and is wise in all He decrees, and human reason is not the measure of His laws.

25.text:
This verse continues the rules of marriage with a dispensation for those who cannot afford a free woman, and it adds the punishment for bondwomen who commit zinā: "But if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman, then ˹let him marry˺ a believing bondwoman possessed by one of you. Allah knows best ˹the state of˺ your faith ˹and theirs˺. You are from one another. So marry them with the permission of their owners, giving them their dowry in fairness, if they are chaste, neither promiscuous nor having secret affairs. If they commit indecency after marriage, they receive half the punishment of free women. This is for those of you who fear falling into sin. But if you are patient, it is better for you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful."

The status of a bondman or bondwoman differs from that of a free man or woman, which is why the verse deals with the punishment as well as with the marriage.

### Who the "bondwomen" are

The bondmen and bondwomen in this discussion are those of the Sharīʿah, in its legal sense. Disbelieving men and women taken prisoner in jihād were given to the fighters as part of the spoils by the Amīr al-Muʾminīn, the head of the Muslims. Those prisoners became bondmen and bondwomen, and their children also stayed in bondage, with a few exceptions that the books of fiqh set out. Today Muslims have left the Sharīʿah's way of carrying on jihād, and they have put the decisions of war and peace into the hands of the enemies of their religion. The text says that for this reason they have been deprived of what used to be a bondman or bondwoman. Domestic servants in our time are free and are not bondmen or bondwomen. In some parts of the world, children are sold or enslaved. This is entirely forbidden, ḥarām, and it does not make them bondmen or bondwomen.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman"**. The Arabic word ṭawl means power, capability and means. The sense is that a man who lacks the means to marry free women, faithful and chaste, may marry believing bondwomen who belong to believers. This shows that a man should, as far as he can, marry a free woman and not a bondwoman. If he must marry a bondwoman, he should look for a believing one.

Scholars differ on how strong the discouragement is. Imām Abū Ḥanīfah held that marrying a bondwoman, especially one from the People of the Book, when one has the means to marry a free woman, is makrūh, not desirable. Imām ash-Shāfiʿī and other Imams held that it is unlawful, ḥarām, to marry a bondwoman if one can afford a free woman, and that a bondwoman from the People of the Book is never permitted.

In short, avoiding marriage with a bondwoman is better for a free man in every case. If he has no choice, a Muslim bondwoman is better. The reason is that the child of a bondwoman automatically becomes bound to her owner. There is also the risk that the child of a non-Muslim bondwoman will follow his mother's religion. To free the children from bondage and keep them Muslim, their mother should be free, or at least a Muslim. For this reason scholars hold that a marriage with a free woman of the People of the Book is valid, yet avoiding it is better. In our times the point is obvious, since Jewish and Christian women often marry Muslim men in order to draw the husband and his children into their religion.

**"then ˹let him marry˺ a believing bondwoman possessed by one of you"**. One explanation says that the word "believing" with free women is in line with the usual practice and does not restrict the ruling. But with the bondwomen, the word rules out unbelieving women. It is unlawful to marry them, even if a man cannot find a believing woman and fears falling into fornication.

**"Allah knows best ˹the state of˺ your faith ˹and theirs˺. You are from one another"**. Allah knows the true reality and the secrets of all things, while people know only what is on the surface. So a man should settle for the outward show of faith and leave what is inside to Allah, who alone knows a person's real worth. Many a bondwoman may be better in faith than a free woman. This is said to encourage marriage with them. Faith is the measure of precedence, and a bondman or bondwoman may be far ahead of free men and women in it. So the choice of a believing bondwoman should not be treated as something contemptible. Her faith should be appreciated.

The words "you are from one another" mean that human beings, free or bonded, come from one kind, all children of Ādam (Adam), born of a single soul. One is better than another only through faith and taqwā, awareness of Allah. Other explanations say that it means some of you follow the religion of others, or that you are strengthened by one another. Some of the scholars say that these two sentences are there to get people used to the idea of marrying bondwomen and rid them of scorn for it.

This links to a wider principle. Outward glamour is not the scale by which to judge a person's honour and importance. The real measure of greatness is the unseen faith in a person's heart, known to Allah alone. So who is great and who is not lies beyond human understanding. That unknown side will be judged and made known in Allah's court. Realising this removes a person's sense of superiority, which is usually the root of most social evils.

**"So marry them with the permission of their owners, giving them their dowry in fairness"**. The owner is responsible for his bondwoman, so she cannot marry without his permission. The same rule holds for a male slave. A hadith says:

> "Any male slave who marries without his master's permission is a fornicator."

If the owner is herself a woman, those who may give a free woman in marriage with her consent become responsible for giving away her bondwoman as well. A hadith says that a woman does not give another woman in marriage, or herself, for only an adulteress gives herself in marriage. If an owner refuses permission, the marriage is not valid, because a bondwoman does not control her own person.

The dowry must be paid with a good heart, promptly, honestly and in full, without hedging or delay. Nothing may be kept back, nor should the matter be belittled because she is owned. No trouble is to be caused to her over it because she is a bondwoman. Imām Mālik held that the dowry is the bondwoman's own right. Other Imams say that her owner becomes the owner of what is paid as her dowry.

**"if they are chaste, neither promiscuous nor having secret affairs"**. Marriage with believing bondwomen is to be made with women who are chaste, honourable women who do not commit adultery. "Promiscuous" describes women who are not honourable and do not refuse illicit relations with anyone who asks. Ibn ʿAbbās said that these are the prostitutes, who do not object to having relations with whoever wants them. "Having secret affairs" means taking boyfriends. As-Suddī, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ash-Shaʿbī, Mujāhid and Abū Hurayrah gave similar explanations. Others describe the open fornicators and those who keep lovers in secret. Although the verse speaks of seeking chaste bondwomen, it is also much better to stay away from marrying a free woman who commits fornication.

**"If they commit indecency after marriage, they receive half the punishment of free women"**. This refers to bondwomen who have married, as Ibn ʿAbbās and others said. The punishment that can be halved is the one that consists of lashes, and stoning to death cannot be halved. The "free women" meant are unmarried free women, whose punishment for zinā is one hundred lashes, as Sūrat an-Nūr says (24:2). The punishment for a married free person is stoning. All four Imams agree that, since stoning cannot be halved, the punishment for a bondman or bondwoman who commits zinā, married or unmarried, is fifty lashes. The verse speaks of bondwomen, and the bondman follows by clear analogy. One explanation adds that the fifty lashes come with banishment for half a year. Another says that Allah did not make marriage a condition for the punishment, to show that stoning does not apply to bondwomen.

**"This is for those of you who fear falling into sin"**. The dispensation to marry a bondwoman is for a man who fears he will fall into fornication. The Arabic word ʿanat originally means distress. It is used for zinā because of the distress that it brings, in the punishment in this world and in the Hereafter. So marrying bondwomen is for those who fear this, if they meet the conditions, and who find it hard to be patient and abstain. It is not for those who have no such fear about free women. Imām ash-Shāfiʿī's opinion is that it is unlawful for such a person to marry a bondwoman, and the same holds for a man who has enough to marry a free woman.

**"But if you are patient, it is better for you"**. If a man, even though he fears falling into zinā, holds back and stays morally clean, rising above the pull of his desire, that is better than marrying bondwomen. It is better to refrain and be patient, since otherwise the children become slaves of the girl's owner. In another way of saying it, patience is better because the children will then be free.

**"And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"**. Marrying bondwomen is makrūh, but if someone goes ahead with it, Allah will forgive him. He is also Most Merciful, because He allowed marriage with them and did not forbid it completely. One explanation says that He forgives the adultery you might commit, and that His mercy is in giving a legal dispensation, in case of need, to marry the captives. The same words are explained as Allah making room in these matters.

### What this verse shows about temporary marriage

The verse says that if a man cannot afford a free woman, his second choice is a bondwoman. This also shows that mutʿah, temporary marriage, is not permissible. If it were permissible, a man who could not afford a free woman could take the easiest course and enter a mutʿah, which would satisfy his desire at a much lower cost than a regular marriage.

The verse also names the mark of a bondwoman: being chaste while in wedlock, and not a fornicator. Mutʿah, by contrast, is spillage and plain whoredom. One woman is used by several men over short periods, and any child cannot be credibly traced to anyone. The benefit of having children is lost, and the unique store of human strength all those people hold is wasted, only to indulge a wanton pursuit of desire. The details are given in the commentary on the previous verse.

### The inner reading

Concessions are granted for the weak. The strong are asked to make serious efforts and to take up what is most complete and strict in the law, since they have no work except to uphold the right of the Real, ḥaqq al-ḥaqq. When something external distracts them from their attention to the heart, so that they take what is easier and lesser, it moves them farther from their attention to the innermost self. It is a desertion of the most important and noble matters. When a person comes down from the strongest and most complete way to what is merely permitted to him, he is really sliding into a state of indulgence.

Then the verse ends with "But if you are patient, it is better for you". This means to be patient in bearing what is hard in one's situation. It is a gentle way of speaking to the servant, because Allah did not say "Be patient". He said that patience is better for you.

### In short

- A man who cannot afford a free believing woman may marry a believing bondwoman, with her owner's permission and with her full dowry, and she must be chaste, neither promiscuous nor taking secret lovers.
- Abū Ḥanīfah called it makrūh to marry a bondwoman if one can afford a free woman, and ash-Shāfiʿī called it ḥarām. The best course is patience, since the children of a bondwoman would belong to her owner.
- Faith, and not status, is what counts. Allah knows each person's true state and all are children of one father.
- A bondwoman who commits zinā after marriage gets half the free woman's punishment, which is fifty lashes, since stoning cannot be halved.
- The verse shows that temporary marriage is not permitted, as there would have been no need for the bondwoman option if it were.
- Inwardly, concessions are for the weak, and the strong are asked to hold to the most demanding way.

26.text:
After the long run of marriage rules, three short verses step back to show the purpose behind them. Allah is pointing to His favours: the rules are for your own good, even where you cannot see how in every detail. The first says: "It is Allah’s Will to make things clear to you, guide you to the ˹noble˺ ways of those before you, and turn to you in mercy. For Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise." The verses also encourage people to follow the rules, and they warn against those who mean harm and want you to stray from the straight path.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is Allah’s Will to make things clear to you"**. Allah makes plain to the believers what is lawful, ḥalāl, and what is unlawful, ḥarām, in this surah and in others. He is setting out His commands clearly and openly. One explanation reads it as explaining what is lawful for you. Another says it means explaining that patience, and refraining from marrying captive women, is better for you than marrying them. Others say it covers the rules of your faith and whatever serves your good, in this world and the next, and they describe the sacred law as His way of life for you.

**"guide you to the ˹noble˺ ways of those before you"**. The ways meant are the righteous ways of those who came earlier, and how they kept the commands that Allah loves and is pleased with. Allah is placing you on the road of the noble prophets and the righteous before you. Their ways include their rulings on what is lawful and unlawful. Do not think that these details of the lawful and unlawful are for you alone. Earlier communities were also charged with such rules, and those who acted on them were rewarded with Allah's favour. One explanation points to the People of the Book, who were forbidden to marry captive women. The aim in guiding you to those ways is that you may follow them, and be returned, as Allah says, from disobedience to obeying Him. Allah also wants you to take up the noble qualities and the praiseworthy conduct of the earlier prophets.

**"and turn to you in mercy"**. Allah accepts repentance from sin and error. One explanation says that He will forgive what happened in the days before Islam.

**"For Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"**. He is the Knower and the Wise in His commands, His decrees, His actions and His words. He knows what serves His servants' good, and He shapes His laws to that. He also knows how great their need for marriage is, and He is wise in having forbidden marriage with captive women except when there is need.

### Not a new law

There is nothing new about the moral standards the Qur'an lays down. In every age Allah announced them through His messengers, and the believers in every age followed them. But the earlier heavenly books could not stay free of tampering, so the divine way of life was lost or covered over. Allah revealed it again, in Arabic, through His last Messenger. Today any group that follows these standards joins the long caravan of righteous people who were blessed with Allah's grace and held firmly to His path.

In every community, certain customs take root through centuries of habit, and people grow too used to them to look at them critically. When an original thinker tries to reform society, traditionalists oppose him bitterly. They find it hard to leave familiar ways for unfamiliar ones, and they are hostile to any reform that would take them away from their forefathers' ways. In these situations the strongest reaction comes from the religious class. Once the heart of a religion has gone weak, hair-splitting argument spoils it, and a system of detailed rules built on outward form grows up. Without the real spirit, people go on with the old rituals and think they are following the religion of Allah. This religion of human making is gradually identified with their forefathers and becomes sacred. In the end, the simple and natural religion of Allah is so heavily veiled that it is hard to recognise as the original. So any movement to revive the simple and natural religion meets bitter opposition, because people find their ritual dogma threatened by it. Those whose dogma rests on a self-made faith attack any attempt to revive Allah's plain and straightforward religion, since they expect it to end their dominance and leadership.

### The inner reading

When Allah told the Prophet ﷺ and his community the stories of earlier communities, what they did and how they were dealt with, the believers looked to their own case, since there were among them some who also did what is not allowed. They said, "If only we knew how Allah will deal with us. Will it be disgrace, a change of form, punishment, or what?" So Allah said, "and guide you to the ways of those before you". It is as if He said, We will tell you what We did with them. And "turn to you in mercy" means: as for you, I turn to you, while those before you I have already destroyed completely.

It is also said that Allah wants to make things clear to you by lifting the veil from His secrets, so that what was hidden from others is made plain to you. Or He wants to make clear His singleness in bringing things into existence and creating new things, in which no one else has any part. "The ways of those before you" is the path of the prophets and the friends of Allah. This guidance is entrusting everything to Allah, being content with Him and surrendering completely to His decree and judgment. And "turn to you in mercy" means that He accepts your repentance after having created it in you, and then rewards you according to what He created for you in your repentance.

### In short

- Allah's rules in this passage are meant to make things clear and to put you on the path of the prophets and the righteous before you, and to turn to you in mercy.
- Earlier communities were charged with the same kinds of rules, and Allah rewarded those who acted on them.
- The moral standards are old, and they get covered over by tradition and ritual, so that reform is bitterly resisted.
- Inwardly, the guidance is trust in Allah, contentment and surrender, and His acceptance of repentance is something He creates in the servant first.

27.text:
This verse repeats the offer of grace and sets the people who want the opposite beside it: "And it is Allah’s Will to turn to you in grace, but those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate entirely ˹from Allah’s Way˺." The repetition is deliberate, to bring out the point more fully.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And it is Allah’s Will to turn to you in grace"**. Allah wants to turn to you and forgive your disobedience. One explanation says that He wants to overlook your transgressions, since He made adultery and marrying one's half-sisters on the father's side forbidden for you.

**"but those who follow their desires"**. The scholars name them in different ways. One explanation says that these are the followers of Shayṭān among the Jews, Christians and adulterers. Another names the Jews and Christians, or the Magians and adulterers. Another names the Jews alone, who claimed that a man's marrying his half-sisters on the father's side is lawful in their Scripture. The people meant include fornicators, adulterers, and nations and peoples who hold false creeds. They do not recognise any limit between the lawful, ḥalāl, and the unlawful, ḥarām, and make no distinction between them.

**"wish to see you deviate entirely ˹from Allah’s Way˺"**. They want you to take the terrible road of falsehood instead of the truth, and to give way to their false intentions and crooked ways. They would like you to transgress what is right by doing what is forbidden to you, so that you become like them. Allah tells you to be on guard against them.

### Who wants you to deviate

There are creeds in which it is acceptable to marry women whom it is not proper to marry. There are many atheists who want to do away with the institution of marriage altogether, as something out of step with modern times. Some are not content with what they call "living together". In some countries people go so far as to speak of women as a shared object of enjoyment. All of this comes from those who take orders from their own desires.

Some Muslims are weak in faith, though they say they follow Islam. When they keep company with disbelievers and atheists of this kind, they fall for their claims of desire, and they begin to think that their own religion is out of date and that the position of the enemy is the height of progress. They do not see that they have been made to believe that people with such ideas are modern and forward-looking, and they even begin to wish that their own religion had allowed these things. We seek refuge with Allah from such spineless surrender. The best policy is to heed Allah's warning and stay away from adopting or practising the ideas and ways of people with such disordered dispositions.

### The inner reading

The verse separates the story of the earlier group from that of the later one. Whenever Allah wants to turn toward someone, He does not let an enemy gloat over him, and He does not give him anything bad in the two abodes, this world and the next. As for those who follow their passions, their will, irāda, becomes weak and feeble and is held back before the will of the Real.

The words that follow, about lightening things, are explained in several ways. Allah lightens the weight of the litanies, through intermittent visitations that arrive in your hearts, the wāridāt. Or He lightens what you bear in your struggles, mujāhadāt, with the lights of witnessing, mushāhadāt, that enter deeply into your hearts. Or He lightens the burdens of service with the sweetness of acts of obedience. Or He lightens the difficulties of the trust, the amānah, by carrying its burden for you. Or He eases the hardships of the search with the relief of arrival. About human weakness, He describes by it their need and affliction, ḍurr, but He does not accept it as an excuse, ʿudhr.

### In short

- Allah wishes to turn to you in grace and forgive, and those who follow their desires wish to turn you far from the right path.
- The people meant include fornicators and adulterers, followers of false creeds, and, in some explanations, Jews, Christians and Magians who made lawful what is forbidden.
- A believer must be careful with company that mocks marriage and the lawful and unlawful, because weak Muslims can end up thinking their own religion outdated.
- Inwardly, whoever Allah wishes to turn toward is not left to an enemy's gloating, and He lightens the weight of service with the sweetness of obedience.

28.text:
The third verse (4:28) names a further wish of Allah's, which is to make things easier: "And it is Allah’s Will to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak."

### Phrase by phrase

**"And it is Allah’s Will to lighten your burdens"**. Allah wants to lighten the burden of His legislation, the sacred law, His orders, what He prohibits and what He decrees for you. He gives rulings that everyone obliged to follow them can carry out. He does not burden you with more than you can do. The marriage rules show this. If a man cannot afford to marry free women, he is allowed to marry bondwomen. The parties to a marriage may settle the dowry by mutual consent. A man may marry more than one woman when there is a real need, on condition that justice is not compromised. Mujāhid and others said that this is why Allah allowed free men to marry bondwomen under certain conditions. Another explanation says that Allah wants to make it easy for you to marry captives when there is a need.

**"for humankind was created weak"**. People are weak, and their make-up is full of desire. This is why it suits them to have commands made easy for them. Short explanations say that man cannot do without women, or is unable to hold back from women and from his passions. Ṭāwūs said, in a report recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that the words are about women. Wakīʿ added, "A man's mind leaves him when women are involved." The point is that Allah knows how weak human beings are by creation and by nature, and He makes His law fit that.

### Why marriage suits human weakness

If man were told to stay away from women completely and absolutely, he would be hopeless at obeying Allah's commands. Because of his weakness and limits, he was not only allowed to marry but also encouraged to. Life after marriage brings great benefits of mutual self-realisation to a couple, and above all the blessing of an untainted gaze and a clean character. Their purity toward each other raises the moral quality of life for both, and it makes them strong, self-reliant and happy. Marriage is therefore a shrewd mutual contract that removes the chances of weakness that may affect men and women. It is a method without equal.

### The inner reading: why "man" is described this way

In the Qur'an, wherever the name "man" appears, a displeasing attribute is attached to it. Allah says, "Indeed humankind is truly unfair, ˹totally˺ ungrateful" (14:34). He says, "Indeed, humankind was created impatient" (70:19). He says, "Most certainly, one exceeds all bounds" (96:6). He says, "Surely humankind is ungrateful to their Lord" (100:6), and "Surely humanity is in ˹grave˺ loss" (103:2). The reason is that man comes from dust, and heaviness begins in dust, and darkness has its root there.

The servant takes hope from this. On the day Allah created him, He saw his faults and bought him together with them. As the saying goes, "You bought me with my faults on the first day." The elder of the Ṭarīqah, the path, prayed, "O Lord, You named me ignorant, so what can an ignorant one bring but unfaithfulness?" He went on, "You named me weak, so what can a weak one bring but error?" He asked Allah to take our failure to master ourselves as coming from that weakness, and our boldness and insolence as coming from that ignorance. "You lifted us up when no one asked You to," he said. "Now that You have lifted us, do not let us fall. Keep us in the shadow of Your bounty."

He added that if Allah waters the plant, Allah planted it. If He levels the foundation, Allah raised it. The servant is only what Allah wanted him to be, and having lifted him up, Allah should not throw him down.

### In short

- Allah wishes to lighten the burden of His law, as He does by allowing marriage with bondwomen when a man cannot afford a free woman, by letting couples agree on the dowry, and by allowing a second wife in need on condition of justice.
- Humankind was created weak and desire-prone, so the law is made to fit human nature, and marriage is the lawful answer to it.
- Inwardly, the Qur'an links a fault to the word "man" because he is made of dust, and the servant hopes that Allah bought him with his faults.

29.text:
From the first verse of the surah, the Qur'an has pointed to the creation of all people from one father and mother and the great bond of brotherhood that follows from it, and so to the need to guard everyone's rights. It then spoke at length about orphans and women, then about inheritance, and then about marriage, which is a contract that lets one person into another's life and property. This verse (4:29) now protects human life and property in general: "O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent. And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you." It forbids any unjust intrusion into that area, whether the people concerned are men or women, relatives or strangers, Muslims or non-Muslims with whom there is a peace agreement.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Do not devour one another’s wealth illegally"**. The Arabic literally says "do not eat your wealth between you". The scholars agree that it means nobody should eat up another's property by false means. Abū Ḥayyān notes in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ that the words also mean a person should not squander his own property in that way, for instance by spending it on sin or on plain extravagance. That too is forbidden here.

"Eat" in everyday speech means to use up in any way, whether by eating, drinking or using. Taking another's goods without right is called "eating up", even if the goods cannot be eaten. The word for "false means", bāṭil, takes in, according to Ibn Masʿūd and most of the Companions, every form that the Sharīʿah forbids: theft, robbery, usurpation, breach of trust, bribery, interest, gambling and every false transaction. Allah forbids His believing servants to acquire each other's property by dishonest methods such as ribā, gambling and other wicked ways that look legal, though Allah knows that those who use them are really dealing in interest. Other explanations list transgression, usurpation, false testimony and false oaths, or force, stealing and bribery.

Ibn Jarīr recorded an example from Ibn ʿAbbās. A man buys a garment and says that if he likes it he will keep it, and if not he will return it with an extra dirham. Ibn ʿAbbās said that this is what Allah meant by "do not consume one another's wealth unjustly" (2:188). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that, when this verse came down, some Muslims said, "Allah has forbidden us to eat up each other's property unjustly, and food is the best property we have. So none of us may eat from another's food." After that Allah revealed the verse that says there is no restriction on the blind, the disabled and the sick, and no blame on you if you eat from your homes or your relatives' homes or those of your friends (24:61). Qatādah said the same.

**"but rather trade by mutual consent"**. This means that there is no harm in commercial dealings between buyer and seller by mutual agreement, so that money is earned lawfully. Mujāhid said it means by selling and buying, or by giving someone a gift. Another explanation includes agreeing to lower a price in a sale, called muḥābāt. A variant reading, tijāratan or tijāratun, makes the sense that the goods come from trade effected through mutual goodwill, and such goods you may consume.

A trade is not the only lawful way for property to pass from one person to another. Borrowing, gifts, charity and inheritance are lawful too. But trade is the best known and most common way. The word covers more than buying and selling. Dealings in service, labour and tenancy are also included, since in a sale what one gets is property for property, and in a rental one gets property for service and labour. Trade has been singled out here because trade and labour are the best of the ways of earning a living.

**"And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves"**. By the agreement of the scholars, this covers suicide as well as killing one another unjustly. The first part of the verse spoke of property, and this part covers the right to life. Property is named first, probably because injustice and carelessness are far commoner in matters of property. Unjust killing is far graver, but it happens less often. Allah forbids killing without a just right. Another explanation says that the words also mean committing what Allah forbids, falling into sin and eating up each other's property unjustly, for these destroy a person. Others add that you should not throw yourselves into ruin, and that one should not do what leads to destruction in this world or the Hereafter.

**"Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you"**. The rules in this verse come from divine mercy. They help you guard against these misdeeds, and so against punishment in the life to come and against what could strike you even here, in this life. Allah is merciful in what He commands and what He forbids.

### How the Prophet ﷺ explained "false means"

The Qur'an uses a single word, "falsely" or "illegally", to declare that all wealth acquired by false means is unlawful. The Prophet ﷺ was given the duty of explaining the details, and he explained every kind of impermissible transaction. The many details of forbidden buying and selling in the hadiths are therefore an elaboration of this verse's ruling, and those rulings are in a sense the Qur'an's own. Every ruling of the Sharīʿah in the hadiths explains some Qur'anic ruling, whether or not we know which verse it explains.

### The traders the Prophet ﷺ praised

Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj said that the Prophet ﷺ was asked which way of earning is the purest and most lawful. He said, "A man's work with his own hands, and every honest sale that is not false or fraudulent." Al-Mundhirī records this in at-Targhīb, and al-Maẓharī cites it. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudhrī reported that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The truthful and trustworthy trader will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs." This is in at-Tirmidhī. Anas reported that he said, "The truthful trader will be in the shade of the Throne on the Day of Judgment." Al-Iṣfahānī gave it in at-Targhīb.

There are conditions attached. Muʿādh ibn Jabal reported that the Prophet ﷺ said the cleanest earning is that of traders who do not lie when they speak, who do not betray what is entrusted to them, who do not look for faults in what they buy, who do not praise unrealistically what they sell, who do not delay in paying a debt, and who do not pester those who owe them. Al-Iṣfahānī has it, as cited by al-Maẓharī. Al-Ḥākim recorded, from Rifāʿah ibn Rāfiʿ, that traders will be raised on the Day of Judgment as sinners, except the one who fears Allah, does right and speaks the truth.

### What makes a trade valid

The words "trade by mutual consent" set two conditions for a transaction by which another person's property may lawfully be acquired. The first is that it must really be a trade, which means an exchange of property. Gambling, speculation, interest, and sales of goods that do not exist are forbidden, because they cannot be called trade, even if they carry the name. The second is that both parties must really agree. If the goods exist but the buyer or seller did not consent, the sale is invalid. Jurists call the first kind al-bayʿ al-bāṭil, a void sale, and the second al-bayʿ al-fāsid, a defective sale. Both are included in eating up property by false means.

For the first condition, trade means exchanging one commodity for another. A commodity on one side and none on the other is deception. Interest is the same, since the extra amount is a return for the time allowed in a loan, and time is not a commodity. In speculation and gambling, there is a commodity on one side, but whether there is one on the other side is doubtful. In forward dealing in goods that do not exist, there is a commodity on one side and only a promise on the other. These are fraud, not trade, so jurists rule them void. This explanation removes all the impermissible forms of trade.

The second condition covers cases where both goods exist but the exchange did not take place by agreement. A trade of that sort is wrong and invalid. A third kind looks as if there is a commodity on both sides and mutual consent, but one party's consent was obtained by compulsion, not free choice. This is counted with the second. Take a person or company that gathers up the everyday goods from across a market, builds a stock, raises prices and sells. The goods are not available elsewhere, so the customer has no choice but to buy at whatever price is asked. He walks into the shop and buys with apparent consent, but that consent results from compulsion and is void.

In the same way, if a husband makes life with him so difficult that his wife is forced to give up her dower, her "consent" is not real consent. Or take a man who finds that he cannot get his rightful job done without a bribe, so he agrees to pay one. His willingness is not free choice, and the payment is void in law.

So the words "trade by mutual consent" allow only those forms of buying, selling and trading that the hadiths prove to be lawful. The jurists simply put them in order. All forms of trade that the Sharīʿah forbids are excluded. This one phrase of the Qur'an is the key to the whole treasury of Muslim law on sale and hire.

### The right to cancel before parting

Mutual agreement in transactions is complete when each party has the right to confirm or cancel the deal before they part. The two Ṣaḥīḥs record that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The seller and the buyer have the right to change their minds as long as they have not parted." In al-Bukhārī's wording, when two men make a deal, each keeps that right as long as they have not separated.

### Suicide

Aḥmad recorded ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ's account of the expedition of Dhāt as-Salāsil, on which the Prophet ﷺ had sent him. One bitterly cold night ʿAmr became impure in his sleep and was afraid that washing would kill him. So he performed tayammum, dry ablution with clean earth, and led his companions in the dawn prayer. When he returned and told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ asked, "O ʿAmr, did you lead your people in prayer while you were in a state of impurity?" ʿAmr explained his fear of dying from the cold and said that he had remembered Allah's words "And do not kill yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you," and so he made tayammum and prayed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ only smiled and said nothing. This is the account in Abū Dāwūd.

Ibn Marduwyah mentioned this verse and then reported that Abū Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever kills himself with an iron tool will have that tool in his hand, stabbing himself with it in the Fire of Jahannam forever. Whoever kills himself with poison will have his poison in his hand, drinking it in the Fire of Jahannam forever. Whoever kills himself by throwing himself off a mountain will keep falling in the Fire of Jahannam forever."

The two Ṣaḥīḥs also record this. Abū Qilābah reported from Thābit ibn aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk a saying of the Messenger ﷺ that whoever kills himself with some tool will be punished with it on the Day of Resurrection. The group of compilers collected it.

### A just order, not private vengeance

Property changes hands usefully through supply and demand and through payment for services. Under Islamic law, trade and services are the right way to earn a living. Income by other means, such as theft, deceit, lies, bribery, usury and gambling, is unlawful in Allah's sight. These are only different ways of plundering. Those who use them in place of honest means may succeed in this world, but all that awaits them in the Hereafter is fire and brimstone.

Human life must be respected in the same way, and human beings deserve justice. The right to carry out an execution lies only with an established government, which may punish an accused person after he has been proved guilty under Allah's law. Apart from that, anyone who tries to deprive a person of his life commits an unlawful act, and Allah will set a severe punishment for it. Going beyond all limits and torturing without justification are among the worst crimes in Allah's sight. Those who keep away from these unlawful acts will receive His special favour. They will enter the eternal world of the Hereafter after being forgiven for small slips and weaknesses in this world.

### The inner reading

Everything spent on something other than Allah is capital spent for nothing. The words are also taken to refer to holding back in a heedless way, or spending from a place other than that of witnessing the real truth, the ḥaqīqah. All of that comes to nothing. "And do not kill yourselves" means by committing sins. It is also said to point indirectly to whatever would bring His anger. Another reading is that you kill yourselves by looking to yourselves and paying attention to your lower selves, or by being pleased with them or preferring them to the good pleasure of the Real.

### In short

- Do not take each other's property by any false means, such as theft, bribery, interest, gambling or fraud. Do not squander your own either. The only lawful route named is trade by mutual consent.
- A valid trade needs a real exchange of property and real consent. Deals under compulsion, void sales and defective sales are forbidden, and each party may cancel before they part.
- Truthful and trustworthy traders are praised, with the conditions the Prophet ﷺ listed.
- Do not kill each other or yourselves. Suicide is warned of in the hadiths, and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ prayed after tayammum because of this verse and the Prophet ﷺ smiled.
- These rules are mercy, to keep people safe from punishment in this world and the next.
