The verse that follows warns of the punishment: "And whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire. That is easy for Allah." It is a stern warning and a true promise, and every sane person who hears these words and understands them should take care.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And whoever does this sinfully and unjustly"**. The "this" is killing another person or wrongly taking someone's property. The words "sinfully" and "unjustly", aggression and injustice, are named together, and the second repeats the first for emphasis. They show that the person knows it is forbidden and yet dares to do it. If it happens through forgetfulness or by mistake, the warning does not cover it. One explanation says the offender must be doing wrong knowingly and not from ignorance or forgetting.

**"We will burn them in the Fire"**. In the Hereafter, Allah will cast such a person into a great fire, where he will feel its burning heat and receive his punishment. In the inner reading, Allah will not spare him from a fierce punishment. He will hand the fire over to its rightful inhabitant and give it free rein.

**"That is easy for Allah"**. Casting such a person into the Fire and tormenting him is easy for Allah. He has power over everything.

### In short

- Whoever knowingly takes another's property or life by injustice and aggression will be thrown into the Fire. This is easy for Allah.
- The warning concerns knowing wrongdoing. A mistake or forgetfulness is not covered.

31.text:
The verse that follows gives hope to those who avoid the gravest sins: "If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of your ˹lesser˺ misdeeds and admit you into a place of honour." It is the Qur'an's usual way. After warnings of punishment, it adds encouragement to obey.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you"**. The Arabic word is kabāʾir, the plural of kabīrah, a major sin. Short explanations name the ones for which a punishment is threatened, such as murder, fornication or theft. According to Ibn ʿAbbās, these number as many as seven hundred. Other explanations give the main examples as worshipping others besides Allah, disrespecting parents, killing and taking interest, or the grave things forbidden in this surah. Avoiding major sins also includes carrying out every obligation, farḍ and wājib, since neglecting an obligation is itself a major sin.

**"We will absolve you of your ˹lesser˺ misdeeds"**. If you avoid the major sins, Allah will forgive the small ones and admit you to Paradise. This is why righteous deeds are said to wipe out minor sins. When someone makes wuḍūʾ, the ablution, for prayer, each part he washes expiates sins. Washing the face removes the sins of the eyes, ears and nose, rinsing the mouth removes the sins of the tongue, and washing the feet removes the sins of the feet. Every step to the mosque brings expiation too. These sayings are about minor sins.

Several hadiths explain the verse. Aḥmad recorded that Salmān al-Fārisī said that the Prophet ﷺ asked him, "Do you know what the day of Jumuʿah is?" Salmān answered, "It is the day on which Allah gathered the creation of your father Ādam." The Prophet ﷺ said, "I know what the day of Jumuʿah is. Anyone who bathes, cleans himself as well as he can, then goes to the Friday prayer and keeps silent until the imām has finished, will have all his sins forgiven between now and the next Friday, as long as major sins were avoided." Al-Bukhārī has similar wording from Salmān al-Fārisī. Another explanation says that the forgiven sins are those committed between one congregational prayer and the next, between one Friday prayer and the next, and between one Ramaḍān and the next.

Major sins, in contrast, are not forgiven without tawbah, repentance. For minor sins the condition is that one has made the effort to avoid major sins. This brings a warning. If someone who keeps committing major sins goes on making wuḍūʾ and praying, those deeds will not wipe out even his minor sins, let alone the major ones. On the Day of Resurrection he will carry a heavy load of major and minor sins and find no hand to lighten it.

**"and admit you into a place of honour"**. This is Paradise. The Arabic can be read mudkhalan or madkhalan, an honourable entering or an honourable place. Another explanation calls it a noble gate. A person who is cleansed of all sins, major and minor, can look forward to entering the home of honour and peace.

### What counts as major, and what as minor

Sin in the absolute sense is any act against Allah's command and will. So a "minor" sin is not really minor, since disobeying Allah and opposing His will is always a grave matter. Many scholars have ruled that every act of disobedience is a major sin, and that the distinction between major and minor is drawn only by comparison. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that any act the Sharīʿah forbids is a major sin.

The definition of kabāʾir that the Qur'an and the hadith point to, as the elders explained, is this. A major sin is one for which the Qur'an or the Sunnah prescribes a ḥadd, a punishment to be carried out in this life. Or it is one on which a curse appears. Or it is one for which a stern warning of Hell is given. Any sin whose evil result equals or exceeds that of a major sin also counts. So does a sin done in a rebellious spirit or as a standing habit.

### Why a "minor" sin is never light

A minor sin does not mean something to be done carelessly, lazily or brushed off. A minor sin done with boldness or heedlessness stops being minor and becomes major. A sage compared it to a small scorpion and a large one, or a big ember and a tiny spark. No one can bear the pain of either. So Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī said that the greatest act of worship for Allah is to give up sin. The worship of people who pray and remember Allah and yet do not give up sins is not accepted. The mystic Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said, "The lighter you take a sin, the greater it becomes with Allah." The most righteous elders used to say that every sin is a courier of kufr, calling people to the manners and morals of disbelievers.

In the Musnad of Aḥmad, ʿĀʾishah wrote a letter to Muʿāwiyah in which she said that a servant of Allah who disobeys Him finds that his admirers become fault-finders and his friends become enemies. Heedlessness toward sin is the cause of man's lasting ruin. An authentic hadith says that when a true believer sins, a black dot appears on his heart. If he repents and seeks forgiveness, it disappears. If he does not, the dot keeps growing until it covers his whole heart. The Qur'an calls this rayn, rust: "Their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit" (83:14).

### How many major sins are there?

Someone told Ibn ʿAbbās that the major sins are seven. He said, "Not seven. Say seven hundred, which is better." In his book al-Zawājir, Imām Ibn Ḥajar al-Makkī lists the sins that fall under the definition above, and the number reaches four hundred and sixty-seven. Some scholars counted only the most prominent sins and so reached a smaller number. Others who went into detail and listed all the branches reached a higher one. The Prophet ﷺ himself pointed to many sins as major, and in different places he named them in threes, sixes and sevens, or more. The scholars concluded that no fixed total is meant. Each number in a hadith fits the occasion on which it was stated.

### The greatest sins in the reports

The two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Abū Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Avoid the seven great destructive sins." The people asked what they were, and he said:

> "Joining others in worship with Allah, killing a life that Allah has made sacred except by right, magic, taking ribā, taking an orphan's wealth, turning away from the enemy on the battlefield when the fighting starts, and accusing chaste believing women who never think of anything to tarnish their chastity."

Aḥmad recorded from Anas ibn Mālik that the Prophet ﷺ spoke of the major sins, or was questioned about them, and named associating others with Allah, killing, and being undutiful to parents. Then he asked, "Shall I tell you the greatest of the major sins? The false statement, or the false testimony." Shuʿbah, one of the narrators, said he thought it was "false testimony". The two Ṣaḥīḥs have this from Shuʿbah, from Anas. In another report in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakrah said that his father said the Prophet ﷺ asked, "Shall I tell you the greatest of the great sins?" They said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said, "Joining others with Allah and being undutiful to one's parents." He had been reclining, and he sat up and said, "And I warn you against false testimony and false speech." He kept repeating it until they wished he would stop. In another report, he said the top three are shirk, disobeying parents and false witness or lying.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said, "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'What is the greatest sin?' He said, 'To make a rival for Allah when He alone created you.' I said, 'Then what?' He said, 'To kill your child out of fear that he will share your food.' I said, 'Then what?' He said, 'To commit adultery with your neighbour's wife.'" Because a neighbour's household is everyone's duty to protect, as one's own household is, the gravity of this is doubled. The Prophet ﷺ then recited the verses about those who do not call on another god with Allah, up to the words "except those who repent" (25:68 to 25:70).

Aḥmad recorded a saying that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr heard from the Prophet ﷺ: the greatest sins are to join others with Allah, to be undutiful to parents or to take a life, and the false oath. Shuʿbah was unsure which of these two it was. Al-Bukhārī, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī recorded it. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr also said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Among the worst of the major sins is for a man to curse his parents." They asked, "How could anyone curse his parents?" He said, "He insults another man's father, and that man insults his father in return, or he insults someone's mother and the man insults his mother." This is Muslim's wording, and at-Tirmidhī called it ṣaḥīḥ. It is also recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called cursing a Muslim a sin, and fighting him kufr.

### Other sins the reports name

A narration in al-Bukhārī lists shirk, unjust killing, eating an orphan's property by false means, taking interest, deserting the battlefield of jihād, falsely accusing chaste women, disobeying parents and violating the Kaʿbah as major sins. In some hadiths, a man who lived in the land of disbelief, emigrated to the land of Islam and then went back to live among disbelievers has also committed a major sin.

Other reports include false oaths, holding back water beyond one's need and refusing to share it, learning magic and practising it. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Drinking is the greatest of the major sins," and, "Drinking is the mother of all shameful deeds," because a person who is drunk can fall into any evil. He also said, "The gravest of the major sins is for one to accuse his Muslim brother of a fault that stains his character." A person who joins two prayers at one time without a reason the Sharīʿah accepts, praying one late as a make-up with the next, has committed a major sin. Some hadiths count losing hope in Allah's mercy as a major sin, and so is becoming careless or bold enough to forget His punishment. Another report says that making a will to harm an heir or cut his share is among the major sins.

In a narration of Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ once said three times, "The destitute, the losers, they are ruined." Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī asked, "Who are these unfortunate ones, O Messenger of Allah?" He answered: one who lets his trousers or wrap or shirt hang below his ankles, one who spends something in the way of Allah and then publicises his favour, one who is old and indulges in shameful deeds, one who has authority and tells lies, one who has a family and yet is proud, and one who pledges allegiance to a worthy leader only for worldly gain.

Closing in the same vein, al-Bukhārī and Muslim record that the backbiter will not enter Paradise. A hadith in an-Nasāʾī and in the Musnad of Aḥmad adds that some people will not enter Paradise: the drinker of wine, the undutiful child, the one who cuts ties of kinship without justification, the one who publicises his favours, the one who claims to know the unseen through jinn, devils and other go-betweens, and the dayyūth, a man so content with shamelessness that he never stops his wife and household from immodesty. A hadith in Muslim says that Allah's curse is on one who sacrifices an animal to anyone other than Allah.

### The inner reading

The great sins of the people of service on the path of the Sharīʿah are the ones you have heard of. The great sins of the people of companionship, on the street of the Ṭarīqah, the way of the inner journey, are of another sort and another taste. The people of service are one thing and the people of companionship another. Those who serve are wage-earners, and the companions are the near ones. A saying in the traditions is, "The good deeds of the pious are the bad deeds of the near." Of the same kind is the saying of the elder of the Ṭarīqah, "The hypocrisy of the knowers is better than the self-purification of the seekers."

The basis of this rule is a subtle point about what Muṣṭafā, the Prophet ﷺ, said of clouding of the heart. He said, "My heart is clouded, and I seek Allah's forgiveness seventy times a day." Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq said, "I wish I could see that for which Allah's Messenger sought forgiveness." The mark of the great sins of the knowers is that, in their own journey, a heaviness sometimes comes over them, and their natural disposition is overpowered by human traits. Their lives become open to habits and customs, and the truths of their faith get mixed with the impurities of personal motives and signs of their own shares. In that state, unless a guide of true discipline, honest poverty and ecstatic joy comes forward to greet them and take their hands, they will not climb out of the pit of their own selfhood. If you want to climb out of the pit of rank like a man, take hold of the pearl-studded, musk-scented chain.

The great ones of the religion have said that a man will not become an elder of the Ṭarīqah, fit to take disciples, until he has reached this dangerous place and left behind the station of heaviness. Only a man who has lost the way a thousand times and found it again can lead a lost person back. First one needs the way to the way, and after that the way itself. A person who has never left the way knows the way, but not how to get back to it. This is the secret of the prophets' slips and their falling into heaviness. Allah knows best. This is a knock at a magnificent gate, and blessed is whoever finds it opened and is guided to it.

### In short

- If a person avoids the major sins, Allah wipes out his minor sins and admits him to a place of honour. Righteous deeds such as wuḍūʾ, prayers and the Friday prayer wipe out minor sins, while major sins need tawbah.
- Many scholars hold that no sin is truly small. A minor sin done boldly or as a habit becomes a major one, and each sin leaves a black dot on the heart until repentance clears it.
- A major sin is one that carries a prescribed punishment, a curse or a warning of Hell. Ibn ʿAbbās said seven hundred is nearer the truth than seven, and Ibn Ḥajar al-Makkī listed 467.
- The Prophet ﷺ named the greatest sins as shirk, killing, undutifulness to parents, false testimony and lying, interest, taking an orphan's property, fleeing from battle, accusing chaste women, and adultery with a neighbour's wife.
- Inwardly, the great sins of the near ones are different from those of the servants, and the way out is to follow a guide who has lost and found the road.

32.text:
After the rules on inheritance, in which a male receives the share of two females, this verse deals with the feelings those differences can stir up: "And do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others. Men will be rewarded according to their deeds and women ˹equally˺ according to theirs. Rather, ask Allah for His bounties. Surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things."

The verse came as an answer to several remarks from women of the time. Aḥmad recorded that Umm Salamah, also written Umm Salmah and Umm Salama, said, "O Messenger of Allah, men go out to fight and we do not, and we receive half of the inheritance." Allah then revealed the words "do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others". At-Tirmidhī also recorded it. Her point was not an objection. She wished she could be a man and have the merits that belong to men. Other women said that if they had been men they would have joined the jihād and had its reward. Another woman asked the Prophet ﷺ, "A man gets a double share in inheritance, and a woman's witness counts as half of a man's. Does that mean that we get half the reward for all our acts of worship?" The verse answers both kinds of remark. Its first part answers Umm Salamah, and the words "men will be rewarded according to their deeds" answer the second woman.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others"**. Allah forbids a person to crave the wealth, mount or wife of his brother, or anything that his brother has. Instead, one should ask Allah for abundant bounty, and say, "O Allah, give us the like of what You gave him, or better," leaving the matter to Allah. Another explanation says the verse was about Umm Salamah, who said, "If only it were prescribed for us as it is for men, so that we might be rewarded as they are." Allah forbade such talk. The merits in which He has made one group excel another are such things as praying in congregation, attending the Friday prayer, joining military expeditions, jihād, and enjoining good and forbidding evil. The "some of you" and "others" in the verse are men and women. A further explanation says Allah forbids what leads to mutual envy and hatred, in worldly matters or in religion.

The ruling is a wide one. The verse closes the door on craving things, traits and merits that Allah has given to others, because effort cannot gain them. When a person finds himself short in wealth, comfort, looks, merit or knowledge, he naturally feels a surge of envy, and he wants to be at least equal to the other person or ahead of him. But some merits have nothing to do with a person's own effort. They are gifts of nature, such as being a man, being born into a prophet's family or a ruler's, or being born beautiful. A person who lacks them cannot get them, however long he tries. A woman cannot turn into a man. A person cannot choose to be born into the family of a prophet, nor change his build, nor become tall and handsome.

When a man finds himself unable to match the other, his inner self starts toying with the thought that it would be wonderful if the other person lost those blessings too, so that they would be equal or he would be better off. This is envy. It is a shameful and damaging trait, and it causes many quarrels, disturbances, killings and ruin in the world.

**"Men will be rewarded according to their deeds and women ˹equally˺ according to theirs"**. Ibn Jarīr understood this to mean that each person will earn the wages of his own works. There is a reward if the deeds are good and a punishment if they are evil. Others explain it as a share from the reward for what men have earned in the struggle and so on, and for women, from what they have earned by obeying their husbands and guarding their chastity. Another says that for men the reward comes from works of goodness, and for women from works of goodness done in their homes. One report from Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-Wālibī, says this part of the verse is about inheritance, and that each person will receive his due share. A short explanation puts it simply: neither is rewarded except through what they earn.

In the same way, the later part of the verse supports another point. Effort made to acquire real merits is not wasted. Each man and woman will receive a return for their own work.

**"Rather, ask Allah for His bounties"**. Do not wish for what others were given over you, since the decision has been made and will come to pass, and wishing does not change it. Instead, ask Allah for His bounty. He says that He will give it, since He is the Most Generous and the Most Giving. One short explanation says to ask Him for success and protection, and another says to ask for whatever you need.

The ideal conduct is this. When you see someone excel in one of life's graces, do not wish to match him in that particular excellence. Ask Allah for graces and blessings from Him. His grace takes different forms for different people. For some, wealth is a blessing, because they might have fallen into sin and disbelief if they had become poor. For others, the grace lies in the very poverty they are in, because if they became rich they might have sunk into thousands of sins. In the same way, for some the grace is power and influence. For others, the unnoticed and forgotten, the grace shows itself in that very state, since power and influence might have drawn them into many sins. So when you ask Allah, do not ask for some fixed kind of life. Ask for His grace, so that He, in His boundless wisdom, opens the doors of His blessings for you.

**"Surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things"**. The arrangement Allah has made is the essence of wisdom and justice. Every person who is created and maintained in any condition is in an arrangement that matches what wisdom and justice demand. But man does not fully know the results of what he does. Only Allah knows how fitting it is to keep a person in a given condition. Allah knows who deserves this life, and He gives him wealth, and who deserves poverty, and He makes him poor. He knows who deserves the Hereafter, and He guides him to the deeds that will help him succeed in it, and He knows who deserves failure, and He keeps him from righteousness and what leads to it. He also knows where merit is deserved and what each person is asking for, and He is the Knower of good and bad, reward and punishment, success and failure.

### Striving for good is different from craving

Verses of the Qur'an and sayings of the Prophet ﷺ urge people to compete in good deeds. That is an open field, where one may look at the record of merit that others have left and be encouraged to reach it. It concerns deeds within a person's control, which can be gained by learning, training and work. If someone is impressed by another person's intellectual gifts, practical life and excellent character, he may strive to gain those qualities. That is a desirable and praiseworthy thing, and the verse does not contradict it.

The verse also removes a mistake that a lot of people make without realising what they do. Some are so devoted to acquiring merits that cannot be acquired that they ruin their otherwise peaceful lives in this world. If it gets worse, and they are consumed by envy, which is to wish, "If I don't have this blessing, may it be taken from the other person," then they destroy their chance of salvation in the next life through the grave sin of envy.

There is another kind of person who has no courage, avoids action or has no sense of honour and shame. Such people do not even try to gain the merits that can be gained. When someone gives them good advice, they blame fate and destiny, which is only a cover for their own timidity and laziness. The verse settles this with a wise and just rule. A person's effort cannot gain merits that are outside his control, such as being high-born or handsome. Such things should be left to fate, and one should be content with Allah's decree and thankful to Him. Craving more than that is pointless, ineffectual and meddlesome, and it leaves nothing but sorrow. As for merits that can be acquired by effort, wishing for them helps only when it is backed by the necessary struggle. The verse promises that the effort will not be wasted and that each person will be repaid for his or her work.

### Be pleased with what you were given

Anyone whom Allah chose to be a man should be grateful, and anyone He chose to be a woman should be pleased to be exactly that. Had she been a man, she might have failed in the duties placed on men and ended up a sinner. A person made beautiful should be even more thankful, and a person with plainer looks should not grieve, but think of the good that may be hidden behind it. Beauty does not guarantee good, and it may land its owner in some unwelcome trial or corruption.

A true descendant of the Prophet ﷺ should thank Allah for the great blessing of that tie. A person who does not have it should not worry about it or long for it. It cannot be gained by effort, and if someone still insists on craving it, all he will get is sin, a broken heart and an aching soul. Rather than longing for a line of descent one lacks, a person does better to look to his own deeds and make them good and righteous. Once a person has built up such spiritual strength, he can get ahead of those with a higher lineage.

### Where the crimes of property and life begin

Earlier verses forbade unjust use of someone's property and unjust taking of life (4:29). Al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ points out that this verse aims at closing the very source of those crimes. Theft, robbery and other unlawful ways of seizing property, and killing and destruction, all spring from one particular feeling. A person finds someone else ahead of him in wealth or material gains. He first feels a pinch in his heart and wants to catch up or to become superior. The strength of this desire then pushes him to commit these crimes. The Qur'an stops these crimes at their root by stopping the desire for what cannot be acquired.

### Why people differ

Differences between individuals in this world follow Allah's plan of creation. Some are less gifted in body and mind than others. Some are born into favourable conditions and some into unfavourable ones. Some have great resources, and some barely get by. The ones with less become jealous of those who are above them, and this leads to envy, hostility and conflict in social life. It is wrong to judge oneself or others only by outward things. They matter only in this world, and a person receives them only to leave them behind. What really matters is success in the Hereafter, which has nothing to do with worldly possessions. It depends on deeds done in this world for the sole purpose of seeking Allah's pleasure. So the wise course is to shield oneself from envy, to pray to Allah for strength, and to keep directing one's efforts toward success in the Hereafter.

Wherever people live together, as a family or as a country, someone has to lead. The authority rests undisputedly with one person. In Allah's plan for this world, man has been made head of the family and has been given the inborn abilities needed for this duty. The biological and physical differences between men and women fit that plan. Those who want to go against it will only cause distortion and discord. Nature will go on making men and women according to the divine scheme, whereby men are given the qualities needed as protectors and guardians, and women the quality of cooperation that lets them assist them without harm to the faculties nature gave them. But when men and women are handed contradictory roles in social activity, the result will be nothing but distortion in social life.

### The inner reading

Abū Bakr al-Kattānī said, "Whoever thinks he will arrive without effort is a wisher, and whoever thinks he will arrive by effort is a drudge." Whoever imagines he will reach the goal without toil is a wisher. As the saying goes, the incapable are those who follow their own whims and wish for Allah. Whoever imagines that he will reach the Sought by toiling and seeking is a drudge.

Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī said:

> "He is not found by seeking, but the seeker finds. Until he has found Him, he will not seek. Whatever can be found by seeking is worth little. The servant finds the Real before the seeking, but for him seeking is the first step. The knower finds seeking from finding, not finding from seeking. In the same way, the obedient person finds obedience from self-purification, not self-purification from obedience, and finds the cause from the meaning, not the meaning from the cause. O Allah, since finding You comes before the seeking and the seeker, I seek because restlessness has overpowered me. The seeker is seeking, and the Sought was obtained before the seeking. This is a most marvellous business. More marvellous still, finding has become ready cash when seeking has not yet begun. The Real is seen, but the curtain of exaltedness is in place."

You are an ocean of loveliness, a ripple of beauty, the rule of generosity, the heart of life. The lovers who look for You burn with longing, like Alexander searching for the water of life.

Another reading of the verse is this: you wish for the rank of the masters without travelling their path, holding to their conduct and practising their practices. You want the condition of the great, yet you have not walked their road. You look for the Kaʿbah of union with eyes that have never struggled. You see how fortunate the friends are, but you have not seen what they went through. Your trouble is that you wish to be like those who took pains. You imagine that the pen of the covenant wrote the mark of friendship on the hearts of the passionate for nothing, with no effort. Yet every moment they have been wounded in spirit and heart, and they have drunk a cup mixed with poison. How many nights, to see You, I have been struck on the head by the dogs of Your street! But not everyone is fit for His wounds, and not everyone is worthy to suffer His pain.

May Allah's mercy be on those chivalrous ones who made their spirits the target of the arrow of His trial and knew their hearts as the litter for His burden of pain! In that trial and sorrow they hum this tune:

> If my spirit is worthy to suffer Your pain, this share of passion's good fortune is enough for me.

Yes, everyone's wound is in proportion to his faith, and everyone's burden in proportion to his strength. The stronger someone is, the heavier his burden. That is the hidden meaning of the verse where He says... and the passage breaks off there.

### In short

- Do not crave what Allah gave to others. The merits that are gifts of nature, such as being a man or a woman, one's looks, one's lineage and one's rank, cannot be gained by effort, and craving them breeds envy and many crimes.
- Each of men and women is rewarded for what he or she earns. Striving in deeds within one's reach is praised, and that effort is never wasted.
- Ask Allah for His bounty, His grace and not some fixed state of life, since only He knows what is good for you.
- The verse was revealed in answer to Umm Salamah's wish that women could join the fighting, and to a woman's question about whether her worship earns half the reward.
- Inwardly, the one who sits and wishes and the one who thinks effort alone gets him there are both wrong, and the Real is found before the seeking.

33.text:
The next verse repeats the law of inheritance and ends the old practice of inheriting by pledge: "And We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin. As for those you have made a pledge to, give them their share. Surely Allah is a Witness over all things." Some women, on learning that a man's share is the same as two women's, wished they were men so as to get the double portion. The law was therefore restated, and the verse says in few words that every share in it rests on perfect wisdom and justice. Human reason cannot take in all the factors that make for order or disorder in the created world, so it cannot reach exactly the elements of wisdom considered in fixing Allah's laws. So whoever has been given a share should be pleased with it and grateful.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin"**. The Arabic word is mawālī. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, as-Suddī, Zayd ibn Aslam, Qatādah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās, among others, said that it means heirs. Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to have said that it means relatives. Ibn Jarīr remarked that the Arabs call a cousin a mawlā. The words "what has been left by parents and next of kin" mean what a person inherited from his parents and family. So the sense is: to every one of you, people, We have appointed relatives, such as your children, who will inherit later what you inherited from your own parents and relatives. Another explanation says that Allah has appointed heirs, relations, for each man and woman, to receive what parents and kinsmen leave.

**"As for those you have made a pledge to, give them their share"**. Those with whom you have a pledge of brotherhood were to be given their share of the inheritance, so as to honour the pledges that had been made, with Allah as witness. In the early days of Islam, this was the practice. It was later replaced when the Muslims were told to fulfil the pledges they had already made and to refrain from making new ones. One explanation says that these were allies with whom, before Islam, people had made agreements of mutual help and inheritance. They were to receive their portion, a sixth. Later it was abrogated by the verse that says that blood relatives are nearer to one another, and by 33:6. That verse says: "blood relatives are more entitled ˹to inheritance˺ than ˹other˺ believers and immigrants, unless you ˹want to˺ show kindness to your ˹close˺ associates ˹through bequest˺." Where other heirs exist, an agreement between two parties no longer touches the inheritance in any way.

Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it this way. When the emigrants came to Madīnah, an emigrant would inherit from the Anṣārī who was his brother, while the Anṣārī's own relatives would not, because of the bond of brotherhood the Prophet ﷺ had made between the emigrants and the Anṣār. When the verse "And to everyone We have appointed heirs" came down, it cancelled that pledge as far as inheritance goes. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the verse about those you have made a pledge to remained valid for cooperation and good advice, while inheritance was taken out of it. It became permissible to leave something in a will to a person who had previously had the right to inherit.

A different account is given about adoption. In the pre-Islamic period, people used to adopt men and youths, and set aside part of their wealth for them as they would for their own children. Allah ended this. It is not abrogated, though, if a man gives them something from the third of his wealth. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said that the verse was revealed about those who adopted men who were not their natural sons and then made them heirs. Allah ordered that something be set aside for them in the bequest, while the division of the estate was assigned specifically to the heirs who were immediate or close relatives. He denied adopted sons a share in the estate and allowed them a portion of the bequest instead.

**"Surely Allah is a Witness over all things"**. Allah is aware of all your circumstances and works. He has witnessed every one of you when you gave these pledges and promises.

### Keeping faith

In the beginning of Islam, Allah made relationships formed by mutual commitment equal to the ties of blood in deciding inheritance. That ruling was later replaced, but the rule to respect one another stayed. If this is how Allah treats a pledge between two men, what of the pledge a servant makes with Allah? He said: "Among the believers are men who have proven true to what they pledged to Allah" (33:23). People have recited the line: "Truly, those who have died to the religion of whims find the decree of death a sweet watering place."

### In short

- Allah appointed heirs for everyone from what parents and close relatives leave, and the shares He set rest on perfect wisdom and justice, so each person should be content with his.
- In early Islam, those bound by a pledge of brotherhood or alliance had a share of inheritance. That was later replaced, and the pledge remained valid only for help and good advice, with a bequest from a third of one's wealth still possible.
- Adopted sons are not heirs, but they may be given something in a will.
- Inwardly, if pledges between people are to be respected, so much more is the pledge a servant makes to Allah.

34.text:
The earlier verses on women forbade withholding or wasting their rights. This verse now sets out the other side, a man's place in the family, and the way to handle trouble inside a marriage: "Men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially. And righteous women are devoutly obedient and, when alone, protective of what Allah has entrusted them with. And if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them ˹first˺, ˹if they persist,˺ do not share their beds, ˹but if they still persist,˺ then discipline them ˹gently˺. But if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them. Surely Allah is Most High, All-Great."

The verse begins with a principle and then describes two kinds of wives, the good and those who fall short, and a graded way to deal with the second kind that is meant to keep the matter inside the home.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Men are the caretakers of women"**. The Arabic word is qawwām. It describes a person who holds the responsibility, the duty and the charge of managing a task or running a system, and who looks after everything that goes with it. The word has been translated in several ways, most often as one who rules or decides, and also as guardian, custodian, overseer and protector. Understood as a carer and a functional head, and not as a ruler in the political sense or a dictator, it fits what ordinary experience shows. The man is responsible for the woman. He is her maintainer, her caretaker and the leader who corrects her if she goes astray. Short explanations say that he oversees her proper conduct, and that he has authority over her, to discipline her and keep her within bounds.

**"as men have been provisioned by Allah over women"**. The Arabic says that Allah has made some of them excel others. Men excel women and are better for certain tasks. This is why prophethood belonged to men, as did other important positions of leadership. The Prophet ﷺ said, as al-Bukhārī recorded, that a people who put a woman in charge of their affairs will never succeed. The same applies to appointing women as judges or to other positions of leadership. Other explanations name the ways in which men were favoured, such as reason, the division of booty and estates, knowledge and authority. The inner reading adds that Allah gave men more because the burden falls entirely on them. They have the full strength and the eminence of aspiration, and they carry burdens in proportion to their strength or their aspiration.

**"and tasked with supporting them financially"**. This means the dowry, the spending and the many expenses that Allah set down in His Book and in the Sunnah of His Messenger for men to meet for women. It is these that make it fitting for a man to be her maintainer, as Allah says elsewhere: "But men have a degree (of responsibility) over them" (2:228). Allah has made this responsibility the men's. The women are not required to pay the dowry or spend on others in that way.

**"And righteous women are devoutly obedient"**. The Arabic word is qānitāt. Ibn ʿAbbās and others said that it means obedient to their husbands. Another explanation says they are kind to their husbands and obedient to Allah regarding them. A short explanation says they are devoted to their Lord and to their husbands.

**"and, when alone, protective of what Allah has entrusted them with"**. As-Suddī and others said that she guards her honour and her husband's property when he is away. Another explanation says that she guards her private parts and everything else while her husband is absent, because of what Allah has guarded for them when He told their husbands to look after them well. According to another, it means that the husband is truly protected only when Allah protects him. It is Allah's own help, His tawfīq, that lets women meet these heavy responsibilities. The words mention the husband's absence because that is when a woman is more likely to be careless. The point is to avoid being careful and alert while the husband is in the house and neglecting these rules when he is out of sight.

**"And if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them ˹first˺"**. This is a woman who shows bad conduct toward her husband. She may act as if she is above him, disobey him, ignore him, or dislike him. When such signs appear, the husband should advise her and remind her of Allah's punishment for disobedience. Allah ordered a wife to obey her husband and forbade her to disobey him, because of the greatness of his rights and all that he does for her. Other explanations specify that the rebellion is disobedience to him in bed, and that the advice is given with sacred knowledge and with the Qur'an, so as to make her fear Allah.

**"do not share their beds"**. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said that the abandonment means not having intercourse with her and lying on the bed with one's back to her. Several others said the same. As-Suddī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah and Ibn ʿAbbās, in another report, added that the husband should not speak with her. The words say "in the beds". Jurists conclude that the separation should be limited to the bed and not extended to the house. A woman left alone in the house would be hurt far more, and relations would be strained more. Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥaydah asked, "O Messenger of Allah, what is the right that the wife of one of us has over him?" The Prophet ﷺ said, as the Sunan and Musnad compilers recorded:

> "To feed her when you eat, to clothe her when you clothe yourself, not to strike her face or curse her, and not to leave her apart except within the house."

**"then discipline them ˹gently˺"**. If advice and ignoring her in bed do not work, the husband is allowed to discipline his wife, without severe beating. Muslim recorded that Jābir said that in the Farewell Ḥajj the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "Fear Allah regarding women, for they are your helpers. You have a right over them that they do not allow into your bed anyone you dislike. If they do this, you may discipline them lightly. They have a right over you to be provided with their food and clothing in a reasonable manner."

Ibn ʿAbbās and several others said that the beating is not a violent one. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said it is not a severe one. Other explanations speak of a mild beating that is not exaggerated, one that does not hurt the body or injure the skin or bones. Slapping or hitting the face is absolutely forbidden.

This is a last resort. The first two steps, gentle explanation and leaving the bed, are a way of showing nobility against stubbornness, and the prophets and their righteous followers spoke in favour of them. The third was allowed as a forced choice in a limited form. A saying alongside it is that the good men among you do not beat women, and no such act is reported of the prophets. According to a report from the daughter of Abū Bakr, given by Ibn Saʿd and al-Bayhaqī, beating women was forbidden outright in the early days. But women became far too oppressive as a result, and the permission was restored. The Prophet ﷺ did not like this method, and said that gentlemen would not use it.

**"But if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them"**. When a wife obeys her husband in all that Allah has allowed, he may not look for any means of annoyance against her. He then has no right to beat her or to shun her bed. Other explanations say that "seeking a way" means looking for a reason to strike her unjustly, or seeking a way against her with regard to love. A man should forgive and let go of what happened, and not look for faults on flimsy grounds. The inner reading adds: do not forget her loyalty in the past because of one moment of dislike in the present, since things may well become pleasant again.

**"Surely Allah is Most High, All-Great"**. This reminds men that if they wrong their wives without cause, the Most High and Most Great is the Protector of those women, and He will take revenge on those who wrong them and deal with them unjustly. The advantage Allah gave men over women is not absolute. His own position over men weighs heavily. If a man goes beyond the limits set for him, he is the one who will be punished. Another explanation says: Allah has not loaded you with what you cannot bear, so do not load women with what they cannot bear, such as affection.

### Authority with limits

For any group that lives together, big or small, and for any organised system, it is both reasonable and customary to have a head, a chief or an authority who can arbitrate in a disagreement and make decisions so that matters run smoothly. This is accepted everywhere in the running of countries and governments, and it was also felt in older tribal societies, where the chief was the authority for the tribe. A family is a small sample of such larger bodies, so it too needs someone to head it, support it and run it. Allah in His wisdom chose men for this duty, because their natural abilities are stronger than those of women and children. This is so plain a fact of human life that no sane person, man or woman, can deny it, and denying it does not change reality.

The sum of the matter is that the rights of women are as binding on men as the rights of men are on women, and the two sets of rights are alike, with one exception. Men have a certain precedence in functional authority, and even that is hedged by balancing factors. As other verses explain, this is not the authority of a dictator or a tyrant. A man who exercises it is bound by the supreme law of Islam, the Sharīʿah. He must act by consultation and follow good advice. He cannot act on a whim or on wild instinct. He is commanded to treat women well, in the recognised way. The principle of consulting appears in another verse (2:233), where husbands are told to act in consultation with their wives in family matters. After this explanation, a man's authority should not be a cause of heartburn for women.

### Two reasons for men's responsibility

Because women might take this arrangement unhappily, Allah did not just proclaim the man's authority. He gave two reasons, one that belongs to the wisdom of creation, which no human being controls, and one that comes through a person's own effort.

The first is in the words "Allah has made some of them excel others". It is the wisdom and choice of Allah alone. It is like the sacred precincts of Makkah, where Allah named one house of worship as His House and the qiblah, and like Jerusalem, where the Bayt al-Maqdis was given special honour. The precedence of men is similar. It is a grace from Allah. Men did nothing to earn it, and nothing is wrong with women because they do not have it. It rests on the wisdom of creation and is the Creator's own prerogative.

The second reason is what comes through effort. Men spend their money, pay the dower and bear the burden of meeting all of women's needs. This is why they have the precedence. A comment in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ is worth noting. These two reasons also show that the right to authority is not established by force alone. It can be earned by a person's competence and ability.

The wording is also noteworthy. The Qur'an does not say that Allah made men excel women. It says that He made some of them excel others. The expression hints that men and women are parts of each other. Men's precedence, even where it is proved, is no more than the precedence of a person's head over his hand, or of his heart over his stomach. Just as the head's precedence does not lessen the role or importance of the hand, a man's precedence does not lower a woman's status, since each is part of the other's body. One may say that the man is the head and the woman the body. Some commentators see another hint. The precedence is in terms of the kind, and as individuals a woman may exceed a man in her qualities and achievements, even in those of a caretaker, over some individual men.

The second reason also removes a doubt that might arise from the share of men being double that of women in the verses on inheritance (4:11). All the financial duties lie with men. Before a woman marries, her expenses are her father's, and after marriage they pass to her husband. In that light, the double share is not too much, because it returns to women in the end.

It also points to a principle about functions. By her creation and nature, a woman is not made to go out, work and earn her own living. The qualities of her being do not suit running around offices and markets, doing jobs and heavy labour for a living. To keep her from having to rough it out like men, Allah placed her whole responsibility on men. Before marriage her father looks after her, and after marriage her husband. She has been made the means of human procreation, and the duties of being a mother and keeping the house and family together are on her shoulders. A man cannot handle those burdens. So it cannot be concluded that her status is lowered by making her dependent on a man for her expenses. No value judgment is being made. It is only a functional division of duties, with a precedence that works both ways. In short, the two reasons show that men's precedence neither lowers women's status nor holds any special gain for men, and whatever gain there is goes back to women.

Two things ought to be present when deciding which child of one father and mother is formally authorised to take care of the other. The one with authority should have the mental and physical ability to carry out its demands, and the one under it should agree and be pleased. The first reason in the verse points to the ability of the man. The second points to the agreement of the party who will be under that authority. When a woman agrees to enter the marriage bond, in return for her dower and full maintenance, she is agreeing to the husband's authority and accepting it with pleasure.

### The wife the Qur'an praises

Ibn Jarīr recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "The best of women is the one who pleases you when you look at her, obeys you when you command her, and guards herself and your property when you are away."

Then he recited the verse "Men are the caretakers of women" to its end. Aḥmad recorded from ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "If a woman prays her five prayers, fasts her month, guards her chastity and obeys her husband, she will be told, 'Enter Paradise by whichever door you like.'"

The Prophet ﷺ also said, as al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Hurayrah, that if a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses, the angels curse her until morning. Muslim has it in the words that if a wife spends the night ignoring her husband's bed, the angels curse her until morning. In another saying, the Prophet ﷺ said that if he were to command anyone to prostrate before another, he would command the wife to prostrate before her husband, because of the greatness of his right over her. A further hadith says that for a woman who is dutiful to her husband, the birds in the air, the fish in the sea, the angels in the sky and the beasts in the forest ask forgiveness from the Lord for her.

Protecting her own honour and modesty and everything in her care at home is the base of happiness in a well-run household. Women are weaker than men in some abilities, and yet they tend to be much stronger than men in carrying out these duties. This too comes from Allah's help. That is the reason that women, in general, are less involved than men in sinful immodesty.

### The three steps for a wife's ill-conduct

The Qur'an gives three methods, to be used in the order in which they are named. A good woman accepts the role of the man as leader according to Allah's plan. If she does not, the man must not turn vengeful or slander her with accusations. If he has found her guilty of improper conduct, he tries to reform her. First he counsels her and talks it over with her gently. If that works, the matter ends there. She is saved from a lasting sin, and he is saved from an aching heart.

If she remains stubborn, the next step is to sleep on a separate bed, as a sign of his displeasure and as a warning that may change her mind. This is a mild form of admonition. If she takes the hint, the dispute ends. If she ignores even this and keeps up her crooked ways, the third step permits a token beating, the outer limit of which is that it must leave no mark on the body. The Prophet ﷺ did not like this and said that gentlemen would not do it. But if this last, symbolic reproof restores normal relations, the aim is achieved.

The three options given to men are followed by the words "But if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them". If, after all three steps, the women begin to listen, men should not split hairs or start making more accusations. It is better to let it go, remembering that the authority given to them over women is not absolute, since Allah's authority over them is heavy.

So the verse offers a compact system for settling a quarrel inside the four walls of the home, without a third party having to step in.

### Why the verse came down

Zayd ibn Zuhayr had given his daughter Ḥabībah in marriage to Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ. In a dispute over something, the husband slapped her. Ḥabībah complained to her father, and he took her to the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ ruled that Ḥabībah had the right to hit Saʿd as hard as he had hit her. As they set off home to take their revenge, this verse was revealed. It allowed a beating as the very last option and did not allow retaliation or revenge against husbands. The Prophet ﷺ soon called the two back and told them to follow what Allah had decreed, and he withdrew his first ruling.

Another account ties the passage from "Men are the caretakers of women" to "If they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them" to the daughter of Muḥammad ibn Salamah. Asʿad ibn ar-Rabīʿ, her husband, had struck her face with his hand after she refused to share his bed. She came to the Prophet ﷺ asking for retaliation, and Allah forbade it.

### The inner reading

Men "stand over" women through what Allah has preferred some over others with and through what they spend. He gave men more because the burden is wholly theirs, since they have the perfection of strength and the height of aspiration. They carry burdens in measure of their strength or their aspiration. It is said that resolutions are made according to the measure of the people of resolve.

### In short

- Men are caretakers of women, not as tyrants, but as heads of the family. They must consult and follow the Sharīʿah. The two reasons given are Allah's choice and the fact that men spend on women.
- Righteous wives are devout and protect themselves and their husband's property in his absence, with Allah's help.
- For a wife's ill-conduct there are three steps in order: advice, leaving the bed, and a light, non-violent discipline as a last resort. Striking the face is absolutely forbidden. When the wife changes her ways, the husband must not seek any way against her.
- The verse was revealed after Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ slapped his wife Ḥabībah and her father wanted retaliation. It allowed no retaliation and set the order of steps.
- Allah is Most High and Most Great, and He takes the part of wives who are wronged.

35.text:
The verse that follows provides for the case in which the quarrel is not settled at home: "If you anticipate a split between them, appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers. If they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware." The previous verse dealt with a wife's rebellion. This one deals with estrangement and alienation between husband and wife.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you anticipate a split between them"**. A family feud can drag on, either because the woman is stubborn, or because the husband has been unjust and oppressive. In either case it will not stay inside the walls of the home. Supporters of one side will start to run down the other with accusations, tempers will rise, and what began between two people will turn into a clash between two families. Another explanation says that the verse speaks of a dispute where you cannot tell which of them is at fault. A short explanation says it is a disagreement that is turning into aggression and a clash of natures.

**"appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers"**. The jurists say that when estrangement arises, the judge first refers the couple to a trusted person, who looks into their case to stop any wrongs between them. If the matter goes on or gets worse, the judge sends a trustworthy man from the wife's family and another from the husband's, to meet them and examine whether it is better for them to part or stay together.

The Qur'an addresses the officials of the government, the guardians of the two parties, their supporters and the Muslims in general. It suggests a decent method that cools tempers, closes the way to accusations and makes a settlement possible. The aim is that the quarrel, though it cannot stay in the couple's house, is at least settled within their families and does not go to court and become public. The concerned officials, the guardians or a group of Muslims who have integrity, influence and authority should appoint two arbitrators, one from the man's family and one from the woman's. The word used for both is ḥakam, which points to the qualifications they need. They must be able to decide the dispute, and that means a person who is both knowledgeable and trustworthy. One explanation says the arbitrators should be sent with the couple's consent. Another adds that the husband gives his arbitrator the matter of divorce or of accepting compensation in its place, while the wife gives hers the matter of separation.

**"If they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them"**. The Qur'an does not lay down what the two arbitrators are to do or what their rights are. It adds only this remark, and two things come out of it. First, if both arbitrators have good intentions and truly want peace, they will receive unseen help from Allah, and He will create love and harmony in the couple's hearts. If harmony is not restored, it may be that one of the arbitrators lacks full sincerity. Second, the purpose of appointing them is to bring about peace between husband and wife, and nothing beyond that.

Allah gives preference to the couple staying together. Short explanations say the same: staying together is preferable and better, and the arbitrators should use the best means to bring them back together.

Ibn ʿAbbās explained that Allah commands that a righteous man be appointed from the husband's family and another from the wife's, to find out which of the two is in the wrong. If the man is at fault, they keep him from his wife, and he pays some compensation. If the wife is at fault, she stays with her husband and he pays no compensation. If the arbitrators decide that the marriage should stay or be dissolved, their decision stands. If they decide that it should stay, but one spouse agrees and the other does not, and one of them then dies, the one who agreed inherits from the other, and the one who did not agree does not inherit. Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr collected this.

Shaykh Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said that the scholars agree that when the two arbitrators disagree, the view in favour of dissolving the marriage is not adopted. They also agree that the arbitrators' decision is binding, even if the spouses did not appoint them as agents, when the decision is that the couple stay together. They differ on whether it is binding when the arbitrators decide for separation. He added that the majority hold that the decision is still binding even if the spouses did not appoint them to decide anything.

Another explanation says that, when the arbitrators and the couple wish to put things right, Allah will make them all of one mind. He will grant the couple success and determine for them what counts as obedience, which may be reconciliation or separation.

**"Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware"**. This is a warning to the two arbitrators as well. Neither injustice nor crookedness from them will go unnoticed, since they will stand before the One who knows everything and is aware of everything. Allah knows whether the arbitrators agree or disagree, and He is aware of what the woman and the man are doing, and of what is hidden and what is open.

### Do the two arbiters have the power to divorce?

If the couple has made the arbitrators their representatives and agents in everything, they have admitted that any joint decision of the two is binding on both. The arbitrators then have full authority to decide. If both agree on a divorce, they can divorce. If both decide that the wife should be released with khulʿ, a divorce she buys, it takes effect, and the parties are bound by it. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Imām Abū Ḥanīfah held this view, as Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and others record.

There is a report from the time of ʿAlī that supports the view that the arbitrators have no inherent right except to make peace, unless the parties give them full authority. ʿUbaydah as-Salmānī narrated it, and it is in the Sunan of al-Bayhaqī. A man and a woman came to ʿAlī, each with groups of people. He asked them to appoint an arbitrator from each family. When the two had been appointed, he said to them, "Do you know your responsibility? Do you know what you must do? Listen to me. If you both agree that the couple should stay together and be reconciled, do it. If you find that things cannot be mended, or that they will not stay on good terms later, and you both agree that separating them is the sensible course, do that."

The woman said, "I accept this. Let these two act according to Allah's law, and I will accept any decision they give, whether it matches my wishes or not." The husband said, "I will not accept separation or divorce under any condition. But I authorise the arbitrators to tell me to pay whatever financial penalty they impose, and let my wife come back to me in peace." ʿAlī said, "No. You too must authorise the arbitrators in the same way the woman has done."

Some mujtahid Imams drew from this the rule that the arbitrators have an inherent power to divorce, since ʿAlī asked the parties to give that authority. Imām Abū Ḥanīfah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī held that if the power were inherent, ʿAlī would not have needed to seek the authorisation of the parties. The very effort to obtain their agreement proves that the arbitrators do not have such a power by themselves. They do become authorised if the husband and wife hand it to them.

### Why a family settlement is better than a court

When two people disagree, their minds become biased. They do not think about each other fairly. In such a case the best way to settle it is to bring in an arbiter who is not personally involved, who can think without prejudice and decide from the facts of the case.

This teaching of the Qur'an opens a new way of resolving disputes. It saves people from going to courts and officials, and it lets them settle a lot of their disputes and claims through arbitration inside the family. Muslim jurists say that appointing two arbitrators to make peace is not limited to quarrels between husband and wife. It can be used, and should be used, for other kinds of discord, especially when the parties are relatives. A court decision is a short-term answer to the underlying problem. Such a decision leaves seeds of hatred and hostility in people's hearts, and they come up again after a time in far more unpleasant forms.

ʿUmar issued an order to his judges, "Send disputes between relatives back to them, so that they make peace with the help of one another, since a court's decision breeds heartburning and hostility." The reason he gave, that court decisions tend to create hatred and hostility in hearts, applies to non-relatives too. Wisdom lies in saving all Muslims from mutual hatred. So jurists hold that it is right for officials and judges, before hearing cases formally, to try to find a way for the disputing parties to meet and agree to a settlement. They mention al-Ṭarābulusī's Muʿīn al-Ḥukkām and Ibn ash-Shiḥnah's Lisān al-Ḥukkām.

Though short, the two verses give a complete system of family life. If it were put into practice, it could remove many quarrels and hatreds from the world, and men and women would live in peace among their families, safe from the local feuds that grow into tribal, racial, national and even international ones. In summary:

1. Settle family disputes inside the house, using one method after another.
2. When that is not possible, government officials or relatives make peace between the parties through two arbitrators, so that the quarrel does not leave the wider family circle, even if it leaves the house.
3. When that fails too and the matter reaches a court, the judge must look into the background of both sides and give a just ruling.

A good woman, then, accepts the man's role as leader by Allah's plan. A good man does his part and does not forget that Allah is always watching him. Allah's court of judgment does not distinguish between a man and a woman. The difference between the sexes serves only the good management of worldly life, and has no bearing on repayment and reward in the Hereafter.

### The inner reading

It is said that a husband has a right to his wife's obedience in the body. As for love and inclination of the heart toward him, that is up to Allah. So do not burden her with what Allah has not provided for you from her. Hearts are in Allah's power. He puts love in them toward whomever He wills and makes them hate whomever He wills.

### In short

- When the split between a couple cannot be settled at home, two arbitrators are appointed, one from each family, to look into the case, so that the quarrel stays within the families and out of the public eye.
- They should be knowledgeable, trustworthy and sincere, since Allah promises to restore harmony if both truly want it, and staying together is preferred.
- Scholars differ on whether the arbitrators may divorce on their own, with al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Abū Ḥanīfah requiring the spouses to delegate that power, as ʿAlī required in the case brought to him.
- This kind of family arbitration can be used for other disputes among relatives, as ʿUmar told his judges.
- Inwardly, love lies in Allah's hands, and a husband should not demand from his wife what Allah has not given him.
